Importing data is the best way to quickly get information into Contractor Foreman. If this is new to you, start small with just a couple lines of data before importing everything.

- Open the Excel file
- Go to File > Save As
- Excel will default to “Excel Workbook (*.xlsx)”
- Click this option to see a list of additional formats.
- About half-way down you will see “CSV (comma delimited) (*.csv)”
- Use this option. Do not use the other CSV options that are available.
- Save the file and then close it.
- Now you can import the file. You will be able to verify the data prior to it importing.

heading: Adding a Project in Contractor Foreman
body:
Projects in Contractor Foreman act as the central hub for managing every aspect of your work—from estimates and budgets to scheduling, communication, and documentation. Because every workflow is different, Contractor Foreman gives you multiple ways to create a project, depending on where you start your process (Estimate, Lead, Opportunity, Directory, CompanyCam, QuickBooks, or directly within Projects).
This article explains each method, when to use it, and the standard fields you’ll complete when creating a project.

Punchlists Module – Creating and Managing a New Punchlist

Overview: Purpose of the Punchlist Feature
The Punchlist Module in Contractor Foreman is a structured tool designed to help teams manage and track outstanding work items—often referred to as “punchlist items” or “deficiencies”—that must be addressed prior to project closeout. These items are typically identified during walkthroughs or final inspections, and can span across multiple trades, disciplines, and project phases. Using this module, project teams can:

- Log individual punch list items with detailed descriptions.
- Assign responsibility to subcontractors, vendors, or internal team members.
- Track completion status and deadlines.
- Communicate directly by emailing punch list reports from the system. Accessing the Punchlist Module
To access the Punchlist Module:
Navigate to the Main Menu,

then select Punchlists from the Project Management category. This action will open the Punchlist dashboard where users can view existing punchlists, add new records, and filter based on project, status, or assigned company.

heading: 1. Items Tab
body:
The Items tab is where you can add the items of what you are invoicing. This tab allows for flexibility and customization of the items listed on your invoice. You have several options to add items:
Import from Schedule of Values (SOV): You can import items from your project’s Schedule of Values, which is useful if you’re billing for specific project phases (progress billing) and the only option to generate AIA Style G702 Invoices. Import from Estimate: Pull items directly from the estimate linked to the project to bill for estimated work or materials. Great for small projects where you can invoice the customer 100% of the total value of the project. Cost Items Database: Import items from your pre-set cost items database for consistent pricing. Manual Items: Add any custom or one-time items manually. Time & Materials (T&M) Items: Add T&M items if you are billing based on time and materials used. Also, what is the purpose of a T&M invoice? Add a Discount: You can also apply a discount to individual line items or the total invoice by adding a discount percentage or fixed amount. Additionally, you can select Taxable Items by selecting the checkbox beside each item.

heading: Daily Logs
body:
Daily Logs are an important document to have filled out every day for each ongoing project. Contractor Foreman provides an easy method for tracking daily activities on the jobsite with Daily Logs. You can log weather, Visitors, Task accomplished, materials used and more.
Daily logs are concise, documented records that capture essential details of the day’s work on a construction site. They typically include information about crew activities, weather conditions, equipment usage, materials delivered or used, any incidents or safety issues, and a summary of the progress made. These logs are often filled out by site superintendents or project managers and are stored within the Daily Logs module in Contractor Foreman.
Using daily logs creates a strong, transparent foundation for construction project management, leading to better outcomes and fewer misunderstandings.

heading: Details
body: Under the details of your Daily Logs, you have the ability to enter arrival date and time, departure time and tasks performed. It is important to say that the Tasks performed field is one of the most important to fill. This will be shown in our Project module so we can have a quick view of all the tasks performed by our employees in a chronological order. Tracking weather and delays in daily logs provides a clear record of conditions that may impact construction activities. This helps explain delays or alterations in the work schedule due to weather, protects against claims related to weather-caused delays, and supports accurate project planning and forecasting. It’s also valuable for safety planning, as extreme weather can pose risks to crew members and equipment. Tracking jobsite conditions and safety incidents is essential for maintaining a safe and efficient work environment. Recording these details helps identify and mitigate potential hazards, reducing the likelihood of future accidents. Documenting incidents also provides critical information for investigations and can reveal patterns that guide safety improvements.

Under the people tab or section of our Daily Logs you have the ability to track who was on site, whether they were your own employees, visitors such as customers, inspectors, architects and even subcontractors. This tracking process ensures accountability and coordination across all teams involved in a project. This information provides a clear record of who was present each day, which is useful for verifying work progress, managing labor costs, and allocating resources efficiently. In case of incidents, this record helps in determining who witnessed or was involved. Furthermore, having accurate attendance data supports compliance with contractual obligations and safety protocols, enhancing overall site security and accountability.
*** As noted before, the Daily Logs interact with other modules and the People Tab/Section is not the exception to the rule. When our employees use the Time Cards, their time will be reflected and shown in the “Employee Time Cards” field. Same applies for Subcontractors using the Time Cards. Remember that for subcontractors or employees to clock in and out, they need to be users of the Contractor Foreman.

body:
In construction, it’s important to understand the difference between an estimate, budget, proposal, and bill of quantities. An estimate is a calculation of the project’s cost, usually prepared early to get a general idea. A budget, within Contractor Foreman, represents the maximum amount we plan to spend in order to achieve the desired profit. A proposal is a formal offer from a contractor that includes the scope, pricing, and terms of the work. A bill of quantities is a detailed breakdown of materials and labor, listing exact quantities to support accurate pricing and comparison between bids.
In Contractor Foreman, the Estimate tool can serve multiple purposes: it can be presented as a Proposal to the customer, used as a Bill of Quantities to quantify the required parts and labor, and tied directly to the Budget to ensure the project remains financially viable.

Exclusions: Exclusions in a construction project are elements, services, or items explicitly stated to be outside the scope of the project. These are aspects that are not included in the contracted work and are the responsibility of other parties or not part of the defined project scope.In a residential construction project, exclusions may include items such as furniture, appliances, interior decorations, and additional landscaping features beyond the basic scope.

heading: Posting Payments from the Payments Module in Contractor Foreman
body:
Managing payments directly from the Payments module in Contractor Foreman gives you a centralized way to track and apply funds across multiple invoices. Instead of navigating through individual invoices, this method lets you log payments in one place and assign them to the correct invoice during entry.
This approach is especially useful for companies handling multiple projects or clients simultaneously, as it allows the finance team to streamline data entry, reduce errors, and maintain consistency in financial reporting.

heading: Why Use the Payments Module?
body:
While payments can be posted directly to an invoice, the Payments module provides a broader, more efficient workflow for:

- Recording payments received across different invoices in a single dashboard.
- Reviewing past transactions in one centralized location.
- Quickly identifying outstanding balances and reconciling accounts.
- Avoiding the need to open each invoice individually when processing multiple payments.By using this module, you save time and ensure your financial records stay synchronized with your invoicing system.

heading: How to Post a Payment from the Payments Module
body:
- Open the Payments Module

From the main menu, select Payments .

This will open a list of all payments associated with your account.
- Create a New Payment Entry

Click Add Payment (or the “+” icon depending on your view).

A new payment form will open for you to complete.
- Fill Out Payment Details Provide all relevant information in the payment form, including:

Date: When the payment was received.

Amount: Total amount of the payment.

Payment Type: Choose from Bank Transfer, Cash, Credit, Check, or Other.

Status: Select Received, In Review, Verified, or Failed.

Notes: Add any context, such as partial payments or client-specific details.

Reference #: Enter transaction IDs, check numbers, or payment confirmations.
- Assign the Payment to an Invoice

In the same form, select the Invoice the payment should be applied to.

This ensures the payment is connected to the correct document and project.
- Save the Payment

Click Create Payment to finalize the entry.

The payment will now appear in both the Payments module and within the linked invoice.

heading: Best Practices
body:
- Centralize payment entry: Use this method when processing multiple payments at once—it reduces time spent clicking through individual invoices.
- Verify invoice links: Always double-check that each payment is applied to the correct invoice before saving.
- Use statuses effectively: Mark payments “In Review” until they are fully confirmed, then update to “Verified” for final records.
- Leverage notes and references: These fields help build a clear audit trail for future reconciliation.

Adding an RFI Notice
Purpose
A Request for Information (RFI) is used to formally ask for clarification, direction, or additional details related to project documents, plans, or specifications. RFIs help ensure that the work proceeds accurately and without assumption when project scope or design elements are unclear. It creates a clear, traceable communication trail between the contractor, subcontractor, architect, or engineer. Why Use an RFI Notice? RFIs ensure that any ambiguities, conflicts, or missing details in project documents are clarified before work proceeds. By submitting an RFI, contractors avoid making assumptions that could lead to costly errors, rework, or delays. It also creates a clear, time-stamped record of questions and responses, protecting all parties if disputes arise later in the project.

heading: How to Add a New Incident
body:
- Go to the Incident module .
- At the top of the screen, click the “+ Incident” button.

- In the pop-up window, make sure you select Incident , not Employee Write-Up .

- Enter the Location (best practice is to select the project where the incident occurred).
- Select the Date and Time — note that the date field is required.
- The Incident Number will be generated automatically unless you have customized your settings.
- Under Classification , choose the type that best fits the situation (for example: Accident, Death, Near Miss, Observation, or Self-Reported ).

You can also add a custom classification specific to your company by typing it in and pressing Enter .
- Fill in the Description of the Incident (required field).
- Once complete, click Create Incident at the bottom of the screen.

heading: Details Section
body:
Under Details, you’ll find several information blocks:

- Details Block: Review and confirm the information previously entered. The Cost Code field is for tracking purposes only—it won’t affect project costs unless you manually enter an expense.
- Action Taken: Document the steps taken to correct the unsafe condition or prevent recurrence.
- People: Record everyone involved, including witnesses , people notified (Safety Manager, Project Manager, HR, etc.), and the date/time notified .On the right side of the screen, you can document further information:

- Observation/Injury Details

Description of the injury (if applicable).
Accepted treatment: Indicate if the employee received on-site treatment and describe what was done.
Transported to hospital: Check and describe if applicable.
Returned to work the same day: Mark and describe if confirmed.
Violations: If any, record the OSHA or company safety violation involved.You can also enter Custom Field Values as configured in your company settings.

body: To disable a user’s account in Contractor Foreman, follow these steps to ensure the user no longer has login access while maintaining the integrity of any documents they created or modified. Start by navigating to the Main Menu and selecting the Directory. This section contains all user profiles, including employees and subcontractors, in your system. Once in the Directory, filter the list to find the user you wish to disable by using the drop-down filter located to the right above the contacts list. Set the filter to show only Users. This will refine the list and display only users with login access to the system. After filtering, locate and click on the name of the user you wish to disable. This will open the profile for that specific user. Inside the user profile, to the top right corner of the page, you will find an option labelled Allow Login Access. To disable the account, simply uncheck this box. By doing this, the user will no longer be able to log in or access the system. Even though the user’s account will be disabled, any documents the user created or modified—such as estimates, invoices, or reports—will still remain within the system.

That’s where Cost Codes come in.
text:
Cost Codes > What is the purpose of cost codes and how to use cost codes?

If you want to control your project financially, you must know exactly where your money is going.
That’s where Cost Codes come in.
title: What is the purpose of cost codes and how to use cost codes?

heading: What Is a Cost Code?
body:
A Cost Code is a number (or number + name) used to categorize and track costs for specific parts of a project.
Think of it like a labeled bucket.
Instead of saying:
“We spent money.”

You say:
“We spent $4,500 on Framing Labor.”
“We spent $2,200 on Concrete Materials.”

Each bucket (Cost Code) collects:

- Labor
- Materials
- Equipment
- Subcontractors
- Other costsThis gives you visibility.
And visibility gives you control.

heading: Why Cost Codes Matter
body:
Without cost codes:

- You cannot accurately compare budget vs. actual.
- You don’t know which trade is profitable.
- You can’t measure productivity.
- Future estimates are guesswork.With cost codes:

- You track costs in real time.
- You identify overruns early.
- You protect profit.
- You build historical data for smarter bidding.Cost codes turn data into decisions.

In Contractor Foreman, you have the flexibility to either add your own custom cost codes or import from standard databases of cost codes. The system is designed to be versatile, with a two-tier structure that allows you to use Parent Codes and multiple Child Codes underneath them. This provides a more organized and detailed approach to tracking costs for various project components. For example, you can have a Parent Code for 23 00 00 – Heating, Ventilating, and Air Conditioning (HVAC), and Child Codes like 23 01 00 – Operation and Maintenance of HVAC Systems and 23 05 00 – Common Work Results for HVAC under the same Parent Code. To begin, go to the Main Menu and navigate to the Settings. There, under System Settings, go to Cost Codes. There are multiple methods to add cost codes to your system. Method 1: Manually Adding Parent and Child Codes
You can manually create both Parent Codes and Child Codes by yourself in Contractor Foreman. Here’s how:
Add a Parent Code:
Go to the Action drop-down menu at the top left of your screen. Select “Add Parent Code (Division)”. Fill out the following fields:
CSI Code (e.g., 23 00 00). CSI Name* (e.g., Heating, Ventilating, and Air Conditioning (HVAC)).

Method 2: Import Cost Codes from Standard Databases (NAHB or CSI)
Contractor Foreman supports importing cost codes from two major industry-standard databases, depending on whether your project involves residential or commercial construction:
NAHB (National Association of Home Builders): Best for residential construction. CSI 2016 (Construction Specifications Institute): Ideal for commercial construction. To import cost codes from either database, go to the Action drop-down menu at the top left. Select “Import Cost Codes (From CSI or NAHB)”. Choose either the NAHB or CSI 2016 database as you prefer. A full list of cost codes from the selected database will appear. Browse and select the codes you wish to import, then click “Import Codes”. You can import from one database at a time but can import from both NAHB and CSI as needed to build a comprehensive list of cost codes.

heading: Understanding the Types of Forms You Can Edit
body:
Company Forms: These are forms that your company has either created from scratch or customized from a library form. You can edit and tailor these forms to your company’s needs time to time.
Forms from the Library: You cannot directly edit forms in the library. However, you can customize a library form by first making a copy of it and then editing it.

heading: Editing Company Forms
body: When you want to edit a form that is already part of your company’s collection, click the three dots to the right of the form which you want to edit, and select Edit This Form. It will take you either to the Basic Form Builder or the Advanced Form Builder depending on which builder was used to create the form. For example, if the form you want to customize is created using the Basic Form Builder, it will take you to the Basic Form Builder when you try to edit it.

heading: Editing Forms from the Library
body:
Even though you cannot directly customize forms in the forms library, you can create a copy of a form and customize it for your liking. This is great if there’s already a form in the library closer to what you want to create with slight modifications. Simply click three dots to the right of the form you want to customize, select Copy This Form, and start customising your form. After making changes, save the form, and it will show up in your company forms ready to use.

body: Contractor Foreman makes it easy to import your current contacts into the system, saving you time and ensuring that all of your critical contact information is correctly imported and organized. First, navigate to the Directory module, where all contact information is managed. To import contacts, you will need to use a specific template provided by Contractor Foreman to ensure that your contacts are uploaded accurately. This template is a CSV file that is formatted to import contacts correctly. On the top left side of the Directory, you’ll see the Contacts by Type widget that shows all contact types and the number of contacts you have for each type (Employees, Customers, Leads, Contractors, Vendors, Miscellaneous Contacts, Users). Click the three dots next to the contact type you need to import, and click “View Import Template”. For example, if you need to import employees, click the three dots next to the employee count in the widget and click “View Employee Import Template”. This will download a CSV file for the specific contact type you selected.

heading: How to create a new To Do’s list?
body: There are a few different ways to create a To do’s list using Contractor Foreman. We will review in this article how to create a To Do’s list directly from the To Do’s Module. At the top right corner of the screen you will see a “+ To Do” button. Click on it to create a new To Do’s List. Once you have done that, a side window will pop up. If the To-Do’s list is related to a Project, click on the empty space/blank right below the Project to select your Project. Despite it is not a required field, we suggest always populating this field if applies. In the event the To-do’s list is not related to a Project but to an Opportunity, the Opportunities will be shown on the Project’s drop down menu as well. Task name is a required field, this means that if you do not type anything there, you will not be able to save and create your new To-do’s list. Due date (by when we want it done), Priority and the assigned to field. This last one is very important. All the people listed on the assigned to field will be subject to notifications if they are users of the Contractor Foreman. Please read this article to learn more about Notifications in Contractor Foreman.

heading: Details
body: Task Name: also referred to as the To-Do’s Name, is a concise, clear, and descriptive title that identifies a specific task or activity to be completed. It should be short and easy to understand, providing enough detail to communicate the purpose of the task without unnecessary complexity. Due: The Due Date on a To-Do List indicates the deadline by which a task must be completed, ensuring timely progress and accountability. Assigned To: Specifies who is responsible for completing a task. Those listed will receive notifications via email, SMS, or push alerts based on system settings. Tags: Tags are keywords or labels used to categorize To-Do’s for easy organization and filtering. For example, a To-Do for inspecting plumbing could have tags like “Inspection”, “Plumbing”, or “Phase 1”. Description: The Description gives detailed information about a task, outlining its purpose and any specific requirements. For breaking the task into smaller steps, checklists are available right below, allowing you to track progress and ensure all subtasks are completed.

heading: What is a Work Order?
body:
Work Orders in Contractor Foreman can be used in two different ways, depending on your needs:

- Adding Contract Value (New Scope of Work)

A Work Order is often used to add an entirely new scope of work to an existing project. While Change Orders represent modifications to the original scope of work (e.g., changing the type of flooring already included in the contract), Work Orders are different. A Work Order is a whole new addition to the project that was never part of the original agreement . Example: You’re remodeling the interior of a house, and because of your excellent work, the customer asks you to also build an exterior patio or a swimming pool. This is an additional scope of work, and the value of that work is added to the project through a Work Order.
- Assigning Work Internally to Employees

Work Orders can also be used to assign specific jobs to your team. This allows you to track materials, labor cost, equipment, subcontractor labor, and other expenses linked to that specific task. This is similar to how some companies use “Job Work Orders,” but remember:

Work Orders are not Purchase Orders. Work Orders are not Projects.

body:

Invoice To : Select who will be invoiced.

- Add Site Details

Location, drawing type, page number, URL, and description.

Attach files such as drawings, photos, sketches, or designs.
- Understand the “No Cost Work Order” Checkbox

If unchecked : The Work Order will add its value to the project’s contract value .

Status options include: Open, Estimating, Submitted, Approved, or Completed.

You can only edit a Work Order while it is in Open or Estimating .

Once submitted, approved, or completed, edits are restricted.

Work Orders can be submitted to customers for approval.

Once approved, they become part of the project’s Schedule of Values (SOV) .

Remember: You must mark a Work Order as Completed before invoicing your customer through the SOV.

In construction, a punchlist is one of the most essential tools for quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC). It is used to record and track deficiencies, defects, or incomplete items found in a project, whether they come from the work of your own employees or subcontractors. The purpose is simple: to make sure the work performed on site meets both design requirements and quality standards before final handover to the client.
title: Basics of Punchlists

heading: What is a Punchlist?
body:
A punchlist is essentially a list of deficiencies that need correction or completion. For example:

- A paint job that shows streaks.
- A door that doesn’t close properly.
- A missing electrical cover plate.
- Concrete with cracks or surface defects.Once items are added to the punchlist, they must be addressed and corrected to ensure the project is delivered to the client as promised.

heading: Why is it Important?
body:
Punchlists serve as a safeguard for both contractors and clients:

- For General Contractors (GCs): Punchlists ensure subcontractors meet contractual standards and nothing is overlooked before final payment.
- For Specialized Contractors: They provide a way to verify that the work performed meets the expected quality and aligns with the project scope.
- For Owners/Clients: Punchlists guarantee that the delivered project reflects the agreed-upon design and functional requirements.

title: Basics of Punchlists

heading: Residential vs. Commercial Projects
body:
The role of a punchlist can vary slightly depending on the type of project:

- Residential Projects: In home construction or remodeling, punchlists often cover aesthetic details that homeowners notice immediately—paint touch-ups, trim alignment, flooring finish, or plumbing fixtures. A detailed punchlist ensures customer satisfaction and prevents callbacks.
- Commercial Projects: In larger, more complex builds, punchlists focus heavily on functional compliance —MEP systems (mechanical, electrical, plumbing), code requirements, accessibility, and safety standards. Since multiple subcontractors are involved, punchlists act as a coordination tool to confirm everything works together before occupancy.

Since multiple subcontractors are involved, punchlists act as a coordination tool to confirm everything works together before occupancy.

heading: Punchlist vs. Other Tools (Common Misunderstandings)
body:
It’s important not to confuse a punchlist with other project management tools in Contractor Foreman:

- To-Do Lists – These are general reminders or tasks (e.g., “order materials,” “update the Gantt chart,” “call the inspector”). While useful, they are not about quality control . A to-do list can support project management but doesn’t replace a punchlist.
- Custom Forms & Checklists – These are process-oriented tools. For example, a safety checklist before installing scaffolding, or a crane installation checklist to ensure all permits and precautions are in place. They ensure procedures are followed , but they do not track deficiencies in the finished product.The key difference is that punchlists are product-focused (what needs to be fixed in the work delivered), while to-do lists and checklists are process-focused (what steps need to be taken).

heading: Final Thoughts
body:
The punchlist is more than just a list of “things to fix.” It’s a cornerstone of delivering quality construction projects. Whether you are building a family home or managing a multimillion-dollar commercial project, a well-managed punchlist protects your reputation, keeps clients satisfied, and ensures compliance with standards.

By understanding what punchlists are—and what they are not—you’ll be able to use them effectively alongside other tools like to-do lists and checklists to run your projects smoothly.

heading: Why use Service Tickets?
body:
Service tickets are important because they:

- Let you keep track of one-off or smaller jobs without creating a full project.
- Provide clear statuses (scheduled, in progress, completed, follow-up) so you always know what’s happening.
- Allow you to attach pictures, and labor hours directly from the job site.
- Give you the ability to generate an invoice immediately after the work is completed , speeding up your cash flow.
- The dashboard includes a map location view to see active or scheduled service tickets, making it easier to plan your day or dispatch crews.
- Offer a clock-in option for tracking hours spent on a ticket. While these hours don’t automatically sync into the invoice, they can be entered manually.

heading: Background
body:
In Contractor Foreman, the Expenses module is an essential tool for tracking costs that arise unexpectedly during a project or expenses that were not initially included in the project’s estimate. Tracking these additional costs is crucial for maintaining an accurate record of your project’s financials and ensuring that no costs go unaccounted for.

These expenses can arise from various situations, such as purchasing materials, tools, or supplies that are needed on site, which is not in the estimate. For example, let’s say you run out of gun nails at a construction site. These nails may not have been accounted for in your initial estimate, but you need to buy more to continue work. In this case, you can log this purchase in the Expenses module to keep track of this extra cost.

To access and use the Expenses module in Contractor Foreman, open the main menu, and select Expenses. This will take you to the module where you can view existing expenses or add new ones.

heading: Details Section
body:
Once you are within the Expense record, you will have the ability to add the following:

- Reason: Here you will type the reason why the Employee or the User had to spend money in that Project, for example, “workers run out of drywall screws during installation”
- Type: You can pick one of the 5 different item types that Contractor Foreman uses MLESO (Material, Labor, Equipment, Subcontractor, Other).
- Employee: It is the employee or user who made the expense.
- Cost Code: in Expenses are used to categorize and allocate costs to specific parts of a residential construction project, such as framing, plumbing, or electrical work. This helps in tracking spending accurately, analyzing budget performance, and ensuring accountability. For instance, if $200 is spent on additional plumbing fittings, assigning it to the Plumbing cost code ensures it is logged correctly and aligned with the project budget. Only 1 expense can be associated to 1 cost code.
- Reference Number: in Expenses is used to uniquely identify and track a specific transaction or purchase. It helps in cross-referencing with receipts, invoices, or financial records, ensuring clear documentation and easy retrieval.

heading: Change Order Status
body:
Each Change Order status represents a different stage in the process and may trigger automations that affect other modules in Contractor Foreman.
StatusDescription
On Hold / OpenThe Change Order can still be revised. The total amount is not yet included in the project total.
Pending ApprovalAutomatically assigned when the Change Order is sent to the customer for review.
Unbilled / ApprovedOnce approved by the customer, the Change Order becomes part of the Total Project Amount, Schedule of Values, and Job Cost Report.
BilledApplied when the Change Order amount has been fully invoiced to the client.

To Submit for Approval:

- Click the three-dot icon .
- Select View/Email PDF .
- Choose a template.
- Click Submit for Approval .

Purchase Order Creation
Purpose
This guide provides a detailed, step-by-step walkthrough for creating a Purchase Order (PO) within Contractor Foreman. A Purchase Order is a legally binding document issued by a buyer (your company) to a seller (vendor/supplier), detailing the specific goods or services you are authorizing for purchase. It includes pricing, quantity, delivery expectations, and terms, serving as a critical communication and accountability tool in the procurement process. This documentation is tailored for:

- Project Managers
- Office Administrators
- Site Supervisors
- Purchasing/Procurement Team MembersAnyone responsible for ordering, tracking, or receiving materials, equipment, or subcontracted labor can benefit from understanding this workflow. Background
Contractor Foreman offers a centralized and efficient way to manage Purchase Orders. Whether you’re in the office generating a bulk materials order or in the field ordering last-minute supplies, the PO module helps track every detail in real-time.

Background
Contractor Foreman offers a centralized and efficient way to manage Purchase Orders. Whether you’re in the office generating a bulk materials order or in the field ordering last-minute supplies, the PO module helps track every detail in real-time. Key capabilities include:

- Project-Centric Tracking : Every PO is tied directly to a project, ensuring clean job cost allocation and reporting.
- Status Management : Track POs from draft to approval, fulfillment, and payment.
- Search & Filters : Sort and view POs by vendor, project, approval status, and custom fields.
- Security & Permissions : Role-based access ensures only authorized personnel can edit, delete, or approve POs.
- Field-Ready : Mobile-friendly interface allows for quick entry, file uploads, and updates from a tablet or phone.

body: Sub-contracts in Contractor Foreman are essential for tracking committed costs and managing agreements with subcontractors. A sub-contract represents an agreement between a contractor and a subcontractor for a specific portion of the work within a project. By using sub-contracts, you can effectively monitor financial commitments, streamline billing processes, and ensure that project costs are properly recorded.
text:
Sub-Contracts > Basics of Sub-Contracts

Sub-contracts in Contractor Foreman are essential for tracking committed costs and managing agreements with subcontractors. A sub-contract represents an agreement between a contractor and a subcontractor for a specific portion of the work within a project. By using sub-contracts, you can effectively monitor financial commitments, streamline billing processes, and ensure that project costs are properly recorded.
title: Basics of Sub-Contracts

heading: Purpose of Sub-Contracts in Contractor Foreman
body:
Sub-contracts help project managers track financial obligations accurately. For example, if you have hired a subcontractor to complete all plumbing works for $10,000.00, you can create a sub-contract in Contractor Foreman to reflect this commitment.

- This $10,000.00 will now be recorded as a committed cost for your project.
- As the work progresses, the subcontractor will submit invoices for completed work, which from now on we will call Bills .
- You can generate a bill against the sub-contract, selecting the completed items and their corresponding amounts.
- For instance, if the subcontractor invoices $2,000.00 for completed plumbing work, you can generate a bill for $2,000.00 from the sub-contract, and this amount will be added as an actual cost to your project.By managing sub-contracts in this way, you gain better financial control over your projects, ensuring that all contractual commitments are properly documented and monitored.

heading: How to Create a Sub-Contract in Contractor Foreman
body:
Follow these steps to create a sub-contract in Contractor Foreman:
Access the Sub-Contracts Module
Log into Contractor Foreman and navigate to the Sub-Contracts module from the main menu. Click the +Sub-Contract button located at the top right corner of the screen. Enter Basic Sub-Contract Details
You will now be prompted to enter key details for the new sub-contract:

- Project* – Select the project to which the sub-contract belongs.
- Subject* – Provide a name for the sub-contract (e.g., “Plumbing Works Agreement”).
- Agreement Number* – Assign a unique identifier to the sub-contract.
- Sub-Contractor – Choose the subcontractor from your directory.
- Select whether this Sub-contract is Billable or notAfter entering these details, click “Create Sub-Contract” to generate the contract. You will be redirected to the newly created sub-contract page. Add Detailed Information to the Sub-Contract
Once the sub-contract is created, you can further add more details.

- Adding Sub-Contract Items

You can manually add items related to the sub-contract or import them from various sources, such as:
Cost Items Database – Pull predefined cost items into the sub-contract.

heading: Categories of Contacts
body:
In Contractor Foreman contacts are grouped into specific categories to help keep your different types of contacts organized and easy to manage.

Employees: Your company’s staff members.
Customers: The clients or companies you are doing work for.
Leads: Prospective customers who might become future clients.
Contractors: Subcontractors or other outside professionals working on your projects.
Vendors: Suppliers who provide materials or services for your projects.
Miscellaneous Contacts: Any other contacts that don’t fit into the above categories.
Users: These can be only the employees and contractors who have access to Contractor Foreman with their own account with set permission levels based on their role in the company (click here to see how to create user profiles for your employees and contractors).

heading: Widgets and Information
body:
When you access the Directory module in Contractor Foreman, you will be presented with a list of all the contacts in your system. However, there are several features designed to help you quickly find and manage specific types of contacts:
Filter by Contact Type: A drop-down menu located just above the contact list on the right-hand side allows you to filter contacts by type (e.g., Employees, Customers, Contractors). This makes it easy to narrow down the contact list and find exactly who you’re looking for without scrolling through all the contacts. Contacts by Type Widget: In the top left of the Directory module, there is a widget that shows how many contacts you have for each category. This provides a quick overview of your total number of contacts for each type. Also, If you need to bulk import multiple contacts at once, Contractor Foreman provides an option to import contacts for each type. You can do this by clicking the three dots next to each contact type in the widget and selecting the import option. (Click here to see how to import contacts). Certificates Expiring (Within 60 Days) Widget: This widget shows certificates that are expiring within the next 60 days.

heading: How to add New Contacts
body: To add a new contact of any type, click the “+Contact” button on the top right of the Directory module. Select the contact type you want to create from the list (e.g., Employee, Customer, Vendor). Enter the contact’s information, such as their name, phone number, email address, and any other relevant details. Fields marked with an asterisk (*) are mandatory. Finally, save the contact. Once you’ve saved the contact, you will automatically be redirected to the profile of the newly created contact. From there, you can add even more details. For example, you might add additional contact information, add certificates, and upload important files. Let’s walk through an example of adding an employee to the Directory. Click the “+Contact” button, click “+Employee“, enter the employee’s basic information such as First Name, Last Name, Phone Number, Email, and Address. Once you’ve filled in the necessary fields, click Save. You’ll be redirected to the employee’s profile, where you can now add more details like their job title, employee ID, and wage rate by using the widgets. Also, you will see several tabs in the left panel where you can add certificates, time off requests, documents, files, and notes.

heading: What is the purpose of the Time Cards?
body:
The primary purpose of the time cards in Contractor Foreman is to accurately track and record the working hours of employees, their geolocation and their cost per hour to one or multiple projects.
Time cards ensure that:

- Employee hours are documented – Time cards log when employees clock in, take breaks, and clock out, providing a clear record of their work hours.
- Project tracking – Time cards link employees’ hours to specific projects and locations, helping to allocate labor costs to the correct project.
- Safety monitoring – Time cards also include fields for reporting injuries, helping to keep track of workplace incidents.
- GPS verification – When enabled, GPS tracking ensures employees are physically present at the job site during clock-in and clock-out times, adding an extra layer of accountability.In short, the Time Cards Module helps us to create and manage time cards efficiently, keeping track of the geo-location, time and cost per hour.

heading: Background:
body:
In Contractor Foreman, you have the option of turning on or turning off GPS Tracking (See Settings). If turned on, GPS tracking only logs the current location of where an employee clocked in at and clocked out at. It does not track all movement throughout the day, the GPS gets enabled automatically every 20 to 30 minutes. GPS tracking does not work on the Web Panel (Desktop version.) In addition, phone must have GPS turned on for GPS to work in Contractor Foreman.
NOTE: GPS tracking is only as reliable as the hardware being used. Older devices or devices used underground or in large buildings often have difficulties obtaining GPS signals. This is due to the device being used and not the app.

body: - Contractor Foreman obtains the GPS location when a user is using the app and performs one of the following actions; Clocks In, Clocks Out, Break, Resume, Changes Project, Changes Cost Code. If the user is on break, the Break location is used.Watch the training tutorial video.

heading: What Is an Incident?
body:
An incident is any unplanned or unexpected event that results in, or has the potential to result in, injury, illness, property damage, environmental harm, or loss of productivity. Not all incidents cause harm, but all must be recorded and investigated to identify root causes and prevent recurrence.
Contractor Foreman allows you to classify incidents by type to better track and analyze them. Below are the most common classifications and what they mean:

title: Basics of Incidents

heading: Incident Classifications
body:
- Accident: A work-related event that results in injury, illness, or property damage . Examples include slips, trips, falls, tool-related injuries, or damaged equipment. Accidents must be investigated and documented immediately.
- Near Miss: An event where no injury or damage occurred , but it could have under slightly different circumstances. For example, a worker tripping over a hose but catching themselves before falling. Near misses are key learning opportunities and should always be reported.
- Death (Fatality): A work-related fatal incident , whether immediate or resulting later from the injury. All fatalities must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours and require full investigation and documentation.
- Observation: A proactive note or record of a potential hazard or unsafe condition before an incident occurs. Observations are often reported by supervisors or safety personnel and serve as preventive measures. Example: noticing missing guardrails, exposed rebar, or improper PPE usage.
- Self-Reported (from Time Cards): A report made by an employee themselves , often through the Time Card module, describing a minor injury, unsafe act, or near miss.

heading: Why Tracking Incidents Matters
body:
Recording incidents accurately is one of the most important responsibilities on any jobsite. From the General Contractor’s perspective, it’s not just paperwork — it’s protection. Documentation proves that hazards were identified, corrective actions were taken, and the company fulfilled its duty of care.
Keeping detailed records helps:

- Protect the company against liability and insurance disputes.
- Identify trends and recurring hazards across projects.
- Prevent future incidents through root-cause analysis.
- Ensure OSHA compliance and accurate recordkeeping.
- Reinforce accountability and a safety-first culture across all teams.

heading: The OSHA 300 Log and Why It Matters
body:
The OSHA 300 Log is used to document all recordable work-related injuries and illnesses. Keeping this log updated is a federal requirement and helps employers:

- Track patterns of workplace injuries .
- Demonstrate proactive safety management .
- Ensure compliance and transparency .
- Maintain credible records in case of inspection or legal review.Each entry in the OSHA 300 Log includes details such as the employee’s role, incident classification, location, and type of injury or illness.

heading: Why Employee Write-Ups Matter
body:
Employee write-ups are not about punishment — they’re about documentation, prevention, and improvement. Keeping accurate records of incidents or behavioral issues helps:

- Protect the company and management from liability or false claims.
- Promote transparency and fairness across all employees.
- Provide clear evidence of communication and corrective action.
- Support training and development , helping employees understand expectations.
- Reinforce a culture of accountability and safety .By documenting each event properly, you create a clear history that can be referenced in future evaluations or disciplinary actions, ensuring decisions are consistent and supported by facts.

heading: When to Issue a Write-Up
body:
Write-ups should be used when an employee:

- Violates safety rules or OSHA standards .
- Fails to follow company policies or procedures .
- Repeatedly ignores instructions or performance feedback .
- Displays unprofessional or unsafe behavior toward others.
- Causes damage or disruption on the jobsite.Not every mistake requires a write-up. The goal is to use this tool when verbal coaching has not corrected the behavior or when the violation is serious enough to require formal documentation.

heading: Key Elements of a Proper Write-Up
body:
A complete and effective Employee Write-Up should include:

- Employee Information: Name, role, and project location.
- Date and Time of Incident: When and where the issue occurred.
- Description of the Incident: Clear, factual explanation of what happened — avoid opinions or emotions.
- Action Taken: Immediate steps to correct or prevent recurrence.
- Witnesses and Notifications: Record who saw the event and who was informed (Safety Manager, HR, Project Manager, etc.).
- Employee Acknowledgment: Have the employee sign the write-up to confirm they have reviewed it (not necessarily that they agree).
- Supporting Evidence: Attach photos, notes, or files as needed.

Equipment Logs Module – Comprehensive User Documentation

Section: Basics of Equipment Logs

Purpose
Use the Equipment Logs module to document when and where equipment is used, record operating hours, track maintenance activity, and note fuel/fluid inspections. This helps you:

- Maintain accurate equipment cost tracking.
- Monitor operator usage.
- Keep maintenance records up to date.
- Ensure compliance with company policies and insurance schedules. Important Note on Job Costing: Equipment Logs are not used for recording equipment cost . In Contractor Foreman, equipment cost must be recorded through the Daily Log , where equipment usage hours are entered and multiplied by the hourly rate from the Cost Items Database. This ensures costs flow correctly into project job costing reports. Background
In Contractor Foreman, Equipment Logs support field-to-office communication by allowing operators and project managers to report usage, servicing, and wear-and-tear conditions in real time. These logs integrate with your Cost Items Database to update equipment lifetime use, value, and maintenance records. However, Equipment Logs do not calculate or assign costs to projects.

title: Basics of Equipment Logs

body:
Background
In Contractor Foreman, Equipment Logs support field-to-office communication by allowing operators and project managers to report usage, servicing, and wear-and-tear conditions in real time. These logs integrate with your Cost Items Database to update equipment lifetime use, value, and maintenance records. However, Equipment Logs do not calculate or assign costs to projects. For accurate job costing:

- Set the equipment’s hourly rate in the Cost Items Database.
- Record usage hours in the Daily Log (not the Equipment Log).
- The system multiplies the rate by hours logged to assign costs to the project. Quick Tips

- Required fields are marked with an asterisk (*)
- Click the blue Submit button to save entries.
- Click the green pencil icon to edit a log.
- Deleting logs requires Admin Rights or explicit permission.
- Click the Action button (bottom right) to delete a record. BEFORE YOU BEGIN: Set Up Equipment
Before creating any logs, you must first define equipment in the Cost Items Database under the Equipment category. Here’s how:
Refer to the “Cost Items Database” documentation for step-by-step instructions on setting up new equipment records.

heading: What is a Submittal?
body:
A submittal is a critical document in construction project management. It serves as a formal request by the contractor or subcontractor for the architect, engineer, or general contractor to review and approve specific materials, products, equipment, or systems before they are fabricated, delivered, or installed on site. Submittals play a vital role in ensuring compliance with the design intent, contract documents, and quality standards established for the project. They include a wide variety of items, such as product data sheets, material samples, shop drawings, and technical specifications, and are often required for structural components, finishes, HVAC systems, electrical devices, and more. The purpose of a submittal is to:

- Verify that proposed items meet the project’s technical requirements.
- Prevent costly errors, delays, or rework due to incorrect installations.
- Establish clear communication and accountability between all project stakeholders.To support this essential process, Contractor Foreman provides a powerful and easy-to-use Submittals module. It allows project teams to create, submit, review, and track submittals in one centralized platform.

heading: Submittal Workflow
body:
When you create a submittal, it’s assigned the status Draft by default. Once you start working on it, you can manually change the status to Pending. After completing the submittal and it’s ready to be reviewed, you’ll submit it to the external approver. At that point, the system will automatically update the status to Submitted.
The external approver will receive the submittal and can provide feedback on any of the items included. Keep in mind that a submittal can contain as many items as needed.
Once the submittal is returned, its status will change to Response Received. You’ll then review it to check if the items were approved or declined. If everything is approved, you can mark the submittal as Approved, and the workflow is complete.
If the submittal requires changes or wasn’t fully approved, you’ll mark it as Rejected, create a copy, and restart the workflow with a new revision.Create a New Submittal

heading: Create a New Submittal
body:
To create a new submittal in your Contractor Foreman account, open the main menu and navigate to the Submittals module. This will take you to the submittals dashboard. In the top-right corner, click the + Submittal button. A new pop-up window will appear on the right side of your screen.

Start by entering the submittal number, this is a required field. By default, the system starts numbering from 1 and you can’t change this directly. If you want to customize the numbering system (for example, so each new submittal starts at 1 per project), go to your Submittal Settings and change the numbering system there.
Next, enter the title, select the project, and choose a coordinator. Fields marked with an asterisk (*) are required. Once completed, click the Create Submittal button. This will take you to the submittal you just created, now displayed in full screen.

Each submittal has two tabs: Details and Notes. Let’s start with the Details tab.

Your fastest and most powerful way to extract information
The Reports module in Contractor Foreman exists for one main purpose: to give you immediate access to every piece of information you’ve documented in the system. Whether you’re working with estimates, change orders, daily logs, bills, safety records, or time cards, everything can be downloaded in the form of a report.
This is what makes the Reports module so valuable. It becomes the source of clarity for owners, upper management, project managers, superintendents, and anyone who needs visibility. With just a few clicks, you can understand the status of your projects, the health of your operations, the progress of tasks, and the completion of work, because all the data lives inside Contractor Foreman.

heading: The Best Way to Learn Reports (Recommended Approach)
body:
At Contractor Foreman, we always recommend this method:
Instead of trying to study every single report one by one, use a real project you already have in progress.
This project naturally contains:

- Daily logs
- Time cards
- Estimates
- Costs
- Equipment logs
- Notes
- Subcontractor informationDownload as many reports as you can for that project and review them.
This will help you understand:

- What each report shows
- How the data is connected
- Which ones bring you clarity
- Which ones upper management will want
- Which reports you will consistently useThis approach is always more effective than memorizing long lists.

text:
Files and Photos > How do I add files to a Project?

In Contractor Foreman, adding files to a project can be accomplished through several methods, offering flexibility in how you manage and organize project-related documentation. Whether uploading documents, images, or other media, files can be added directly to a project or through modules associated with that project, such as Daily Logs, Punch Lists and most of our modules.
title: How do I add files to a Project?

heading: Uploading Files Directly to the Project from the Files and Photos Module
body:
To upload files directly to a project where no files have been uploaded yet, go to the Files & Photos module by navigating to the main Menu. This will take you to the central location where all files are stored.

Once inside the Files & Photos module, you will need to create a folder (if no files have been uploaded yet) where you want the files to be uploaded. Click on the “+ Create a Folder” button, select your project and click on the blue “Save” button.

Once we have created the Project Folder, now we can upload our documents by dragging the files to Contractor Foreman or by clicking on the bold text Click & Drag.

If you have previously uploaded any sort of documents, there will potentially be more folders within the main Project Folder. Also, notice that the “Plans” folder was automatically created for convenience and ease of use.

body: The Schedule module provides a Gantt chart interface, which allows you to plan, visualize, and update tasks across your projects. Follow the steps below to get your projects to show on the schedules. From the Main Menu, navigate to the Schedule module. Once inside the Schedule module, you will see a Gantt chart interface, which is similar to other project management tools like Microsoft Project. In the Gantt chart interface, locate and click the button labelled “Select Project” or “Projects” on the top left. A list of your available projects will appear. Select the project(s) you wish to display and work on. Click Save to confirm your selection. If you are viewing the selected project for the first time in the Schedule module, you will be prompted to enter a Start Date and End Date for the project. Enter the desired date range and click Save. A Gantt chart will be generated with a sample task that spans the duration you provided. This will act as a placeholder to help you get started. Once the project is selected and the Gantt chart is generated, you can begin adding tasks, adjusting timelines, and organizing the schedule. Click here to see how to add tasks and how to manage them.

body:
The Schedule of Values (SOV) is a critical tool in Contractor Foreman, widely used in the construction industry to manage and streamline project financials. Its primary functions include:
Tracking the Contract Amount

The SOV provides a detailed breakdown of the project’s total contract value into individual work items or cost categories. This enables accurate monitoring of the contract amount as the project progresses.
Managing Invoicing

The SOV facilitates precise tracking of amounts invoiced to the client versus the remaining balance to be invoiced. This ensures accurate billing aligned with project milestones and prevents discrepancies in financial reporting.
By offering these capabilities, the Schedule of Values helps maintain financial transparency and enhances project management efficiency.
**The SOV is the information that will be shown on the Continuation Page of the AIA G-702 and G-703 form.
text:
Cost Items Database > Basics of Schedule of Values (SOV)

The Schedule of Values (SOV) is a critical tool in Contractor Foreman, widely used in the construction industry to manage and streamline project financials. Its primary functions include:
Tracking the Contract Amount

The SOV provides a detailed breakdown of the project’s total contract value into individual work items or cost categories. This enables accurate monitoring of the contract amount as the project progresses.
Managing Invoicing

The SOV facilitates precise tracking of amounts invoiced to the client versus the remaining balance to be invoiced. This ensures accurate billing aligned with project milestones and prevents discrepancies in financial reporting.
By offering these capabilities, the Schedule of Values helps maintain financial transparency and enhances project management efficiency.
**The SOV is the information that will be shown on the Continuation Page of the AIA G-702 and G-703 form.

heading: Importing items to the Schedule of Values from an Approved Estimate.
body:
You can bring all the line items of an Estimate to the Schedule of Values and there are 2 simple ways to do this. 1. Once an Estimate gets manually approved, you will get a pop-up question asking you if you wish to create the Schedule of Values using every line item in your estimate.

** Please note that the sections created in the Estimate will also be shown in your SOV. In other words, your SOV will have sections and within those sections the individual line items. 2. If you created a Project from the Projects Module, or you did not create the SOV when the Estimate was approved. You can simply open the Project in question, go to the SOV section from the left panel and click on the drop down menu “Add Item to SOV. You will see a list of options. The one we are looking for is “Import from an Estimate” one. Click on it and you will have the ability to select an itemized version of the SOV (every line item shown on your Estimate) or just the subtotals as you had them on your original Estimate. You might wonder, what the difference between the itemized version of the SOV vs the “just sections” version of the SOV is.

We will leave out Change Orders and Work Orders for the simple reason that when either one of those records get approved by the customers, they become part of the Schedule of Values automatically. This goes back to the original definition of the SOV, a tracking tool that allows us to keep track of the up-to-date contract amount of the project. Importing an item from the Cost Items Database allows you to quickly add items to your SOV saving time and efforts. In order to use this function it is important to have built first a solid database with all your typical items. Adding your items manually is one of the most common things to do in Contractor Foreman when we begin to use the platform. Just remember to fill all the required fields marked with a red asterisk and make sure you do not miss the item type (Labor, Equipment, Subcontractor, Material, Other) and cost code for better reporting.

Once a project is completed, users may prefer not to have it clutter their view of ongoing, active projects. Fortunately, the system is designed to filter the open projects list automatically by default. However, users also have the flexibility to customize their view based on company preferences. Here’s how you can manage the visibility of completed projects across different views and modules in Contractor Foreman. By default, when you access the Projects module, the list view, or Projects Dashboard, will display only open projects. However, if you need to view completed projects or all projects (both open and completed), you can switch between different views. Above the project list, you will find an option to toggle between different project statuses:

Open Projects: The default view shows all ongoing projects. Completed Projects: Selecting this option will display only the projects that have been marked as completed. All Projects: This option provides a comprehensive list of all projects, regardless of their status. Also, in the project navigation menu, the system automatically shows only open projects by default.

heading: Viewing Completed Projects in Specific Modules
body:
While the Projects module provides clear options for filtering completed and open projects, you may need to see or hide completed projects when you’re working in other modules of Contractor Foreman, such as Inspections, Invoices, or Change Orders. You can setup each module to show completed projects or hide them.
Go to the Settings of the Projects Module and you will find options for customizing how projects are displayed across different modules. Within the Projects module settings, look for a field called Project Selection Options. This field controls whether completed projects are shown in various modules. Here, you can choose to include or exclude completed projects based on your workflow preferences.

For example, if you want to see completed projects in the Inspections module, you can turn on the option to display completed projects for that specific module. And if you prefer not to see completed projects in the Invoices module, you can turn off the setting for that module.

The great thing about the Daily Logs is that you can add as many employees or Subs as you want to a Project. To add an employee or Subs to Daily Logs you can do so by going to the Daily Logs Module and open the daily log to which you would like to add your employees or subcontractors.
Then go to the People section of your daily log and click on the blank space “Select/View Employees” of the Employees on Site Field.

Then select all the employees you would like to add, add the Employee Work Notes and if you had visitors on site and their respective note.

When it comes to add subcontractors you only have to click on the “Assign Subs to Jobsite” button, select the subs that were on your site and click on Save.
Right after selecting your subcontractors, you will see them under the “Subs on Jobsite”. Go ahead and add the number of Sub’s employees, the number of hours they were working and the Notes of what they did.

Remember that in order to populate the Employee or Subcontractors Time Cards, they (your employees or subs) need to have access to Contractor Foreman as users and use the time card module to clock in and out.

heading: How to retrieve archived Work Orders
body:
If you ever need to reference or reactivate an archived Work Order, you can easily bring it back:

- Go to the Work Orders main dashboard .
- Click on the funnel (filter) icon .
- Under Record Status , switch from Active to Archived (or choose All to view everything).
- Select the Work Order you want and click Unarchive .
This flexibility ensures that even when you archive items, nothing is lost—you’re simply organizing your workspace for better efficiency.

When you’re working inside a Work Order, chances are you’ll need to attach supporting documents, things like photos from the jobsite, design sketches, vendor quotes, or even links to external resources. Contractor Foreman makes this process straightforward, and everything stays organized within the Work Order itself. To upload files:

- Open the Work Order.
- In the left-hand panel, select Files .
- Look just below the Files header—you’ll see a small plus (+) icon . Click it, and a new window will appear on the right side of your screen. From there, you have several ways to bring your documents in:

- Drag & Drop – simply drag the file from your computer into the upload area.
- Browse & Upload – click inside the space to browse your device and select the file.
- Contractor Foreman Gallery – pull in files or photos that are already stored in your CF account.
- Cloud Storage Sync – upload directly from Google Drive or Dropbox .
- Paste a Link – if your file is hosted online, just drop the link into the field provided.

How to Print a Punchlist

Purpose
Printing a punchlist allows users to generate a physical or digital hard copy of all punchlist items associated with a specific project. This is essential for field coordination, contractor accountability, project closeout meetings, and documentation. A printed punchlist can be distributed during on-site inspections, used for manual sign-off, or kept for compliance and audit purposes. Contractor Foreman offers an intuitive method to generate and print punchlists through its integrated PDF generation and export features. Step-by-Step Process to Print a Punchlist
Step 1: Navigate to the Punchlist Module

- From the Main Menu , select Punchlists under the Project Management section.

- This opens the Punchlists dashboard where all created punchlists are displayed in a list or tile view. Step 2: Select the Punchlist to Print

- Locate the specific Punchlist you wish to print.
- You can use available filters (by project, date, or status) to narrow down the search.
- Click on the desired Punchlist to open it and see additional detailed for the punchlist.

How to Add Items to a Punchlist
Overview: Purpose of Adding Punchlist Items
A Punchlist is a structured and trackable list of tasks, deficiencies, or incomplete work that must be completed before a construction project or a phase of it is considered finished. These items are typically identified during walkthroughs, inspections, or quality control reviews. Contractor Foreman’s Punchlist module enables users to systematically document, assign, and monitor these items. Each item can include detailed descriptions, images, deadlines, and responsible parties, ensuring clear communication and resolution. Adding individual Punchlist items is central to this process. Whether you are documenting minor finishing work or critical safety issues, each item added contributes to ensuring that nothing is missed during final project delivery. Step-by-Step Instructions for Adding Items to a Punchlist
Step 1: Navigate to the Punchlists Module

- From the Main Menu , locate and select the Punchlists option.

- This will open the Punchlists Dashboard, which displays existing punchlists by project, status, and other filters. You can either create a new Punchlist or open an existing one to add items.

body: To apply tax to your invoices in Contractor Foreman, you need to set up your tax rates first. To configure your tax rates, from the Main Menu, go to Settings. Under the System Settings heading, click on Financial. There you will see a setting field called Tax Rates. Click on Add Tax Rate + to add a new tax rate. Provide a name for the tax rate (e.g., “Sales Tax” or “VAT”) and input the appropriate percentage for the tax. After entering the necessary details, click Save to store the new tax rate. Now that you have created your tax rate, you can use that tax rate on your invoices. Go to the Invoices module and open the invoice where you want to add tax. Once in the invoice, click on the Items tab in the left panel. In the Items section, you will see all the line items added to the invoice. On the right side of each line item, there is a checkbox to mark it as Taxable. Check this box for the items you want to apply tax to. Below the list of items, you will see an option to select the applicable tax rate. Choose the tax rate you previously created from the drop-down menu.

An estimate template allows you to reuse an already created estimate for future estimates. Here’s how you can create one from an existing estimate. From the main menu, go to the Estimates module. Select the estimate that you want to save as a template. This can be any estimate you’ve already created. Once the estimate is open, scroll down to the very bottom of the page. At the bottom right of the estimate, you will see a checkbox labeled “Save Estimate as Template.” Check this box. That’s it! The estimate is now saved as a template, and you can reuse it when creating future estimates. How to Use an Estimate Template
Now that you’ve saved an estimate as a template, you can use it to create new estimates quickly. Here’s how to do it. Create a New Estimate by navigating to the Estimates module and clicking on the +Estimate button at the top right of the screen. Fill in the basic details for the new estimate, and click “Create Estimate” to create the estimate. Click here to see more on how to create an Estimate. After saving the estimate, you will be redirected to the newly created estimate. On the left panel, click on the Items tab. In the Items tab, click the Add Item to Estimate drop-down menu.

body: Yes, Contractor Foreman fully supports syncing Bills with QuickBooks as part of its accounting integration features. This ensures your financial records are consistent and up to date across both platforms, helping you save time and reduce the risk of errors in your bookkeeping processes.
text:
Bills > Are Bills synced with QuickBooks?

Yes, Contractor Foreman fully supports syncing Bills with QuickBooks as part of its accounting integration features. This ensures your financial records are consistent and up to date across both platforms, helping you save time and reduce the risk of errors in your bookkeeping processes.
title: Are Bills synced with QuickBooks?

heading: How the Sync Works
body:
When you create a Bill in Contractor Foreman—for example, from a Sub Contract, Purchase Order, or directly in the Bills module—it can be synced automatically to your QuickBooks account, provided that you have set up the QuickBooks integration.
Once synced, the Bill will appear in QuickBooks as a standard bill entry, making it easy for your accounting team to process payments and manage cash flow.
text:
Bills > Are Bills synced with QuickBooks? :: How the Sync Works

When you create a Bill in Contractor Foreman—for example, from a Sub Contract, Purchase Order, or directly in the Bills module—it can be synced automatically to your QuickBooks account, provided that you have set up the QuickBooks integration.
Once synced, the Bill will appear in QuickBooks as a standard bill entry, making it easy for your accounting team to process payments and manage cash flow.
title: Are Bills synced with QuickBooks?

heading: Important Note About Sync Limitations
body:
While the sync between Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks is robust, there is one key limitation to be aware of:
We do NOT currently support syncing Bills from QuickBooks to Contractor Foreman if those Bills are associated with multiple Projects (i.e., split transactions are not supported).
This means if a single bill in QuickBooks is split between more than one project, it will not sync back into Contractor Foreman. However, if a Bill in Contractor Foreman is tied to one project, it will sync successfully with QuickBooks.

heading: Understanding Bill Synchronization Between Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks
body:
When entering a bill in Contractor Foreman, users begin by selecting the vendor or subcontractor and filling out key general details: the bill date, due date, payment terms, and bill number. Once these are set, the next step involves entering the individual items on the bill.
For each item, users must select the item type, item name, quantity, unit cost, therefore the total amount, unit, and cost code. Additionally, attachments can be added to the bill if necessary.
Once the bill is completed, it is immediately synchronized with QuickBooks through an automatic integration process.

For each item, users must select the item type, item name, quantity, unit cost, therefore the total amount, unit, and cost code. Additionally, attachments can be added to the bill if necessary.
Once the bill is completed, it is immediately synchronized with QuickBooks through an automatic integration process.

heading: What Transfers to QuickBooks
body:
When reviewing the bill in QuickBooks, the following general details transfer successfully:

- Vendor or Subcontractor (Supplier)
- Bill Date
- Due Date
- Terms
- Bill NumberThese elements appear in QuickBooks exactly as they were entered in Contractor Foreman.

heading: Important Differences in Item Handling
body:
The most significant difference lies in how items are managed between the two systems:

- In Contractor Foreman , items are structured with a type (e.g., Material, Labor, Equipment, Subcontractor and Other), a name, and associated cost details.
- In QuickBooks , all items imported from Contractor Foreman appear under the Item Details section, not under Category Details.This is critical to note, as many QuickBooks users are more familiar with entering bills using Category Details. The switch to Item Details may require a shift in workflow for some users.
Additionally:

- In QuickBooks, the Product/Service reflects the parent code and child code from Contractor Foreman.
- The Description matches the item name.
- Quantity and Rate transfer correctly, allowing QuickBooks to calculate the Amount (Quantity × Rate).
- The Customer field in QuickBooks is automatically populated with the project name from Contractor Foreman.

Change Orders in Contractor Foreman are used to document and manage additional work that was not initially included in the original contract. There are times when you may need to adjust the amount on a Change Order, and this can only be done when the Change Order status is set to Open. Below are the steps to guide you through adjusting the amount of a Change Order.

Navigate to the Change Orders Module, find and select the Change Order that you need to adjust from the list of Change Orders. Once inside the selected Change Order, you can edit existing items, remove items, and add new items to the change order.

If the Change Order’s status is set to Pending Approval, Approved, or Billed, you will not be able to change your change order amount.
Just click on the QTY or Unit Cost for easy and quick changes or click on the Eyeball icon to open the whole cost card and edit more values. Note this is per line item as shown below. Also, you can click on the “Add Item to Change Order” to add a complete new line item to the Change Order.

How to Change the Ship to Address on a Purchase Order
Overview
In Contractor Foreman, Purchase Orders (POs) are more than just financial documents, they’re logistical tools that define where and how your materials or services should be delivered. One key field that drives fulfillment accuracy is the “Ship To” address. Whether you’re delivering materials to a jobsite, staging area, client property, or your warehouse, the Ship To field gives you full control over the delivery destination. Occasionally, it becomes necessary to revise this location after the PO has been created. Common reasons for updating the Ship To address include:

- A jobsite address has changed or was incorrectly entered.
- Delivery needs to be redirected to a centralized warehouse for consolidation.
- The client has requested direct shipment to their location.
- Field logistics or scheduling has changed mid-project.
- An error occurred during PO creation.This guide walks you through the correct procedure, permissions, and options for editing the Ship To address on a Purchase Order in Contractor Foreman.

This article explores the key benefits of using sub-contracts in Contractor Foreman and how they contribute to better project management. 1. Tracking Committed Costs
One of the primary benefits of using sub-contracts is the ability to track committed costs in a project. When you enter into an agreement with a subcontractor for a specific work package, such as electrical installation or plumbing, the total value of that agreement becomes part of the project’s committed costs. For example, if you sign a subcontract worth $20,000 for plumbing work, this amount will be reflected as a committed cost in the project financials. This helps ensure that project budgets remain accurate and that all expected expenses are properly accounted for. 2. Streamlining the Billing Process
Contractor Foreman allows users to generate bills directly from sub-contracts, ensuring a seamless billing process.

body: In Contractor Foreman, you can convert a lead into a customer either manually or through an automated process.
text:
Directory & Contacts > How to Convert a Lead to a Customer?

In Contractor Foreman, you can convert a lead into a customer either manually or through an automated process.
title: How to Convert a Lead to a Customer?

heading: Manual Conversion of a Lead to a Customer
body:
There are two primary methods for manually converting a lead into a customer. Both methods are simple and can be completed directly from the Directory or Leads module.
Method 1: Convert a Lead from the Directory
Start by accessing the Directory module from the main menu in Contractor Foreman. Here, you will see all your contacts, including leads, employees, customers, and more. Find the lead you want to convert. You can either scroll through the list or use the filters to narrow down the contact types to Leads only.
Click on the lead’s name to open their profile. In the lead’s profile, click on the three dots located at the top right corner of the screen. Click Convert to Customer.

Method 2: Convert a Lead from the Leads Module
From the main menu, go to the Leads module where all leads are listed. Locate the lead you wish to convert and click on the three dots to the right of the lead’s name. From the options, click Convert to Customer.
