heading: Automated Lead Conversion in Contractor Foreman
body:
Contractor Foreman also has an automated process that converts a lead into a customer when certain actions are completed.
When you create an Estimate for a Lead, submit the Estimate for Approval, If the lead approves the estimate, Contractor Foreman will automatically convert the lead into a customer.
Not only will the lead be converted into a customer, but Contractor Foreman will also automatically create a project based on the approved estimate. This step eliminates the need for manual entry and ensures that your workflow is as efficient as possible.
Another way to convert the Lead into a customer is when you issue an invoice to the Lead.

body: If a contact is no longer needed, you can easily delete them from your directory. Start by opening the Directory module from the main menu in Contractor Foreman. This is where all your contacts, including employees, customers, leads, contractors, vendors, and miscellaneous contacts, are stored. Scroll through the list or use the filters at the top of the page to locate the specific contact you want to delete. Once you’ve located the contact, click on the three dots located to the right of the contact’s name. This will open a menu with various options. Click on the Delete option. A prompt will appear asking you to confirm the deletion by typing the word “delete.” This step ensures that deletions are intentional and prevents accidental removal of important contacts. After typing “delete,” confirm the action, and the contact record will be permanently removed from your directory. Deleted contacts cannot be recovered, so be sure you want to remove the contact before confirming the action. Deleting a contact may affect related records, such as project assignments or estimates where that contact was involved, so it’s essential to double-check before deleting.

heading: How do I get a report from Contractor Foreman that shows the total amount of hours and the payout amount based on the Wage Rate?
body: Go to the Main Menu, Documents section, Reports. Once here, at the bottom of the screen you can see a whole section named “Time Card Report”. Expand the section and you will have the option to download 4 different reports. In this article, we encourage you to download and try the report “Time Activity (Most Popular)”. Click on the blue view button of the “Time Activity (Most Popular)” report and a pop-up window will appear. Select the Date Range, the Employee(s), Project(s), pick your Optional Columns, use the Labor Rate of your preference and group the information however you would like to get this report, then click on the blue button “Generate Report”. If you picked the Excel format, you will get a spreadsheet that will contain all the information that comes from the Time Cards Module. Another thing to remember is that the reports can be exported from Contractor Foreman and imported into a payroll processing system such as Gusto for wage payments. Also, if you integrate Contractor Foreman with QuickBooks, Time Card data only syncs one-way from Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks. We do not transfer how much your employee is to be paid – QuickBooks handles that.

heading: Locate and Open the Submittal You Want to Send
body:
From the Submittals list:

- Scroll or search for the specific submittal you wish to email.
- Click directly on the submittal title to open its full detailed view.
Each submittal can include one or more related items. These might be individual products, equipment components, system descriptions, or technical drawings that require approval or record-keeping.
To begin attaching an item to the submittal:

- Navigate to the appropriate submittal record from your project dashboard or Submittals module.
- Once inside the submittal detail’s view, locate and click the “+ Item to Submittal” button. This initiates the item creation process and opens the form used to capture item-specific data.Why this matters: Grouping items under a submittal helps keep related information centralized. This improves traceability and ensures that project stakeholders can easily locate all documentation associated with a particular product or phase of work.

title: Attaching Items to a Submittal

heading: Fill out Submittal Item Details
body:
Once the item form is open, you will be prompted to enter key information. These fields help define and categorize the item within the submittal package and must be completed accurately. Complete the form with the following details:

- Item #: This can be a simple numeric or alphanumeric code (e.g., 001, A2, or HVAC-01). Use a consistent numbering format to make referencing easier across documents and communications.
- Name: A descriptive title for the item
- Plan Sheet Numbers: Enter the drawing or blueprint references that correlate to this item (e.g., “M1.1”, “S2.3”). This allows reviewers to cross-reference the submittal item with design documents.
- Manufacturer: Include the name of the manufacturer or supplier providing the product or material.
- Spec Section: Indicate the applicable specification section from the project’s construction specifications (e.g., “Division 23 – HVAC”).
- Description: Provide a summary of the product, component, or drawing.
- Files: Upload any supporting documentation that may be needed for review or reference.

heading: Sync Methods
body:
Do Not Send to QuickBooks – This prevents data from being sent to QuickBooks for the modules it is applied to
Send to QuickBooks – This sends data from Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks but not from QuickBooks to Contractor Foreman.
Sync Both Ways (Preferred) – This allows changes made in one system to be sent to the other system so that both retain the same data.
NOTE: Contractor Foreman does not allow you to edit your Chart of Accounts within our system. We prefer you to continue doing that within QuickBooks. We allow you to point to and reference it (which is all most people will ever need). We also do now sync changes made in QuickBooks Time Cards back to Contractor Foreman due to the way time values are stored. Any changes that need to be made to a time entry should be made within Contractor Foreman.

body:
The integration with Zapier makes it easy for you to send data from Contractor Foreman to other systems (such as MailChimp, Constant Contact, Zoho, Dropbox, OneDrive, and more). Although this process is fairly easy, we are unable to provide support for any settings or configuration outside of our system. Zapier will be able to assist with those questions. Getting Started: If you do not already have an account, you will need to create a free Zapier account at https://zapier.com/sign-up

- From your Contractor Foreman account, go to Menu > Settings > Integration > Zapier
- From there, click on the Integration URL
- Shortly after you’ll be asked to copy the API key displayed on the screen.
- Click on the Zapier App link given there
- Accept Invitation
- Go to Zapier.com and login (or create a free account if you do not have one)
- Click on New Zaps (on the left) and then click Create Zap (on the right)
- In the Trigger box, search for and select Contractor Foreman.
- Select “Lead” from the Trigger Event list.
- Click Continue
- Click “Sign in to Contractor Foreman”
- Paste the API Key copied earlier into the popup.
- Click “Test Trigger”
- If you see, sample Lead details – You’re almost done.
- Now continue and select Action.
- Search “MailChimp”
- Selection Action (Create New Lead or Update)
- Sign into MailChimp
- Map the fieldsThe step below are the same as the ones above but with visual references.

Copying text from one source (such as Word) into Contractor Foreman is a huge time saver. Visually, most everything looks correct. But in the code, Word brings over a lot of nasty code that has a tendency to break things. That is true for many systems (not just Contractor Foreman). So how do you correctly bring over text from Word into Contractor Foreman without retyping it?

- Copy the text in Word
- Go to https://html5-editor.net/
- Paste the copied text into the right side
- Click the Clean button
- Optional: You can format the text here as desired
- Copy the HTML (left side)
- Paste it into the HTML preview in Contractor Foreman. Click the </> icon to go to HTML view (this makes the text background black instead of white)
- Click </> to move back to review mode
- Make necessary formatting changesOnline text editors do not have the same powerful features that you find in applications like Word. Cleaning the text will increase the chance of the output looking as intended and reduce the chance of you or your client having a problem opening the document.
If you need more assistance, email support@contractorforeman.com

body:
At this time, Contractor Foreman does not support the ability to track customer or vendor credits directly within the system. This means that if there is an overpayment or refund involved—whether from a customer or a vendor—it cannot be recorded as a credit that can be automatically applied to another invoice or bill within Contractor Foreman. How to Handle Overpayments and Credits
The system currently does not offer native credit functionality. QuickBooks Integration Note
If you are using QuickBooks Online and have it integrated with Contractor Foreman, it’s important to understand how overpayments are treated in that environment. QuickBooks allows overpayments: You can post a payment in QuickBooks that exceeds the amount of the invoice or bill, and QuickBooks will recognize and hold that extra amount as a credit. Contractor Foreman does not: If you try to do the same thing in Contractor Foreman (i.e., enter a payment greater than the invoice or bill total), the system will allow you to enter it, but QuickBooks will reject the sync due to the mismatch in expected amounts.

heading: Overview
body:
The Document Writer is a powerful tool designed to create customized documents that automatically merge data stored within your Contractor Foreman account.
This allows you to generate professional, data-driven documents quickly and accurately without needing to manually re-enter information.
text:
Document Writer > What is the purpose of the Document Writer? :: Overview

The Document Writer is a powerful tool designed to create customized documents that automatically merge data stored within your Contractor Foreman account.
This allows you to generate professional, data-driven documents quickly and accurately without needing to manually re-enter information.
title: What is the purpose of the Document Writer?

heading: How It Works
body:
The Document Writer functions similarly to a mail merge. You create your document, insert merge field handles, and then select the specific record (such as a Project, Subcontract, or Contact) to populate those fields automatically.
The system will pull the relevant data from your account and insert it into the document—saving you time and ensuring consistency across your forms and templates.

Using Templates in Document Writer
Purpose:
To explain the availability, usage, and customization of document templates within the Document Writer module. Background:
Contractor Foreman’s Document Writer module allows users to generate company documents directly within the platform. These can be used as-is, edited, or replaced with custom templates built to suit your company’s specific needs. Templates are designed to maintain consistency across internal and client-facing documents while saving time and reducing manual formatting. Key Points to Remember:

- Stock templates are provided for general use but can be fully edited to match your branding, formatting, and legal requirements.
- You can also create custom templates based on your existing documents.
- Templates may contain merge fields for project-specific or customer-specific data.
- Custom templates can be saved and reused across multiple projects or departments. Steps to Use or Create Templates in Document Writer:
1. Accessing Templates:

- Navigate to:
Main Menu > Document Writer

- Browse the list of existing documents or templates if available.2.

Creating a document within the Document Writer is a very simple process. You can create your own document (starting with a blank screen) or you can paste an existing document. Once the document has been added, you will then be able to quickly make edits and generate copies if it is for your agreements, contractors and other needs. To create a new document, go to the Document Writer and follow these steps;

- Click on the “+Add Document” button located at the top left side of the screen.

- Then add the “Document Name” and select the Module it is associated with (such as Contractors, Customers, Employees, etc.)

- Select the publication Status:

Unpublished: The document will not be available for your use in any of the modules above listed
Published: The document will be available for your use in the documents above listed. Archive: This status archives the document. This is a good function you can use if you do not want to delete it but at the moment you do now want to use it. Archiving it will “hide” the document for its future use.

- Select to Show Header or Show Footer (If this is enabled, the header and footer image you added to Settings > Profile will appear in the document.

heading: Overview
body:
If your document formatting looks incorrect after pasting text into the Document Writer, it’s likely due to formatting that was carried over from applications like Microsoft Word. Word and other document editors use proprietary formatting that doesn’t always transfer cleanly into web-based text editors.
In most cases, the issue is caused by hidden formatting (such as highlighted, bolded, or styled text) embedded in the original file.
Below are two methods to fix this issue.
text:
Document Writer > The formatting of my document is not correct :: Overview

If your document formatting looks incorrect after pasting text into the Document Writer, it’s likely due to formatting that was carried over from applications like Microsoft Word. Word and other document editors use proprietary formatting that doesn’t always transfer cleanly into web-based text editors.
In most cases, the issue is caused by hidden formatting (such as highlighted, bolded, or styled text) embedded in the original file.
Below are two methods to fix this issue.
title: The formatting of my document is not correct

heading: Option 1: Remove Formatting Inside Document Writer
body:
- After pasting your text into the Document Writer , highlight all of it.
- In the toolbar, click the Eraser icon (Remove Font Style).
- This will clear any imported formatting and usually resolves most issues.

title: The formatting of my document is not correct

heading: Option 2: Clean the Text Before Pasting
body:
If formatting problems persist, use an online tool to remove the extra styling before pasting your text.
Steps:

- Copy your text from Word.
- Paste it into one of the cleaning tool websites and click Clean .
- Copy the Clean HTML output.
- In Document Writer , click the </> (Code View) icon in the toolbar.
- Paste the clean HTML code into this view.
- Click the </> icon again to return to the normal document view and continue editing.

- Click the </> icon again to return to the normal document view and continue editing.
title: The formatting of my document is not correct

heading: If Issues Continue
body:
If the formatting is still incorrect after trying both options, please contact Support.
While we don’t offer document editing services, we’re happy to review your document to identify potential issues.

Tip: In some cases, it’s faster and cleaner to create a new document directly in Document Writer rather than copying from another file—especially when copying text from PDFs, since their structure often transfers poorly.

Purpose:
To explain how to locate, resend, or download a document that has already been generated and sent using the Document Writer. Overview:
Once a document has been created and merged using the Document Writer and then sent, it is no longer stored within the Document Writer interface itself. - Use the search bar or available filters to narrow down results by:

Document name
Project
Date sent
Customer or recipient name3. Resend the Document:

- Once you find the document in the list:

- Choose “Email PDF” . Enter the recipient’s information or adjust the message as needed. Click Send to resend the document.4. Download the Document:

- From the same three-dot menu , select “Download” to save a copy of the document to your device.

- Cover Page
- Company Overview
- Testimonials
- Detailed Scope of Work
- Estimate Page (auto-generated)
- Terms & Conditions or Final NotesEach document must be:

- Published
- Assigned to the Estimate Module
(You can do this when creating or editing the document.)
2. Configure the Proposal Document Batch
This determines the order and combination of documents that appear in the final merged proposal. Steps:

- Navigate to Estimate > Settings > Document Batch .

- Click Edit to open the Document Batch Configuration window.
- Review the list of available documents (these must be published and assigned to Estimates).
- Check the box next to each document you want to include.

Using the Hidden Markup in the Cost Items Database

Navigation: How to Access Hidden Markup

- Go to the Main Menu

- Click on Cost Items Database

- Use the search bar or filters to locate the item you want to edit

- Click on the item to edit its contents

Purpose
The Hidden Markup field allows you to include additional markup that is not visible on the estimate or invoice but still impacts the total cost. This helps you account for:

- Shipping and handling from warehouses
- Internal logistical expenses
- Sales negotiation leeway
- Margin control in competitive bidding

Use Case Examples
ScenarioUse Hidden Markup To…
Materials stocked in your warehouseCover Internal shipping & storage costs
Sales NegotiationSet a buffer that allows discounts without cutting profits
Freight or Delivery MarkupsPass costs internally without customer visibility

How to Add Hidden Markup to an Item

- Open the Cost Items Database

- Find the item you want to edit and click on it.
- Scroll to the Hidden Markup (%) field

- Enter the desired percentage (e.g., 7.5%)
- Click Save to save the changesOnce applied, this hidden markup will automatically be factored into the item’s price anytime it is used in:

- Estimates
- Invoices
- Purchase Orders
- Change OrdersNote: Hidden Markup is not visible to the client on shared documents.

body: In Contractor Foreman, there are several ways to view and manage the schedule status of a project, whether you need to create, edit, or simply monitor the project’s timeline. The system provides various views and tools to track the progress of tasks, whether through a Gantt chart, list format, or calendar view.
text:
Projects > How to view the schedule status of a Project?

In Contractor Foreman, there are several ways to view and manage the schedule status of a project, whether you need to create, edit, or simply monitor the project’s timeline. The system provides various views and tools to track the progress of tasks, whether through a Gantt chart, list format, or calendar view.
title: How to view the schedule status of a Project?

heading: Creating/modifying/viewing Gantt chart schedules from the Schedule Module
body:
The most comprehensive way to view and manage a project’s schedule is through the Schedule Module. This module allows you to create, edit, and customize the Gantt chart, offering a detailed view of the project’s timeline. Go to the Menu and select the Schedule module, then it will open the full scheduling interface where you can build and adjust the project’s timeline. You can create the initial Gantt chart here, input tasks, set milestones, and adjust dates.
Click here to see more about creating Gantt charts.

Within this module, the Gantt chart is the primary tool used to manage and track tasks. You can set and see the schedule in a graphical format that displays the duration of tasks, task dependencies, and project milestones. You can also switch to a list format or monthly view to get a different perspective on the schedule.

title: How to view the schedule status of a Project?

heading: Viewing the Schedule from the Projects Module
body:
In addition to the Schedule Module, you can view and make edits to the project’s schedule directly from the project’s Schedule Tab. Navigate to the specific project by selecting it from the Projects menu. Within the project, select the Schedule tab. Here, you will see the Gantt chart where you can view and modify task details, such as start and end dates, task dependencies, and other schedule information.

While you can make basic edits to the schedule directly from this page (similar to the Schedule Module), creating the initial Gantt chart is not possible here. To start the schedule, you must first go to the Schedule Module. Once the Gantt chart has been created, you can then return to the Schedule Tab of the project to make adjustments as needed.

heading: Viewing the Schedule in the Calendar Module
body:
For an alternative view of your project’s schedule, the Calendar Module provides a calendar format that allows you to see tasks, deadlines, and milestones from all projects. This view is helpful when you want to see how various projects are overlapping or impacting each other.

Navigate to the Calendar Module by going to the Menu and selecting Calendar. You can customize the calendar view by adjusting the Display Options. This allows you to see information coming from different modules. Make sure you have switched Schedule on to see tasks coming from your Gantt charts. This is a particularly useful tool when managing multiple projects, as it helps you visualize task schedules and other tasks in a broader context.

When a Change Order needs to be generated for a subcontractor, the process begins with assigning the appropriate subcontractor to the Change Order items, within the Change Order record.
*** Even if the Change Order record is not meant to be sent to the client/owner, you need to create first a No Cost Change Order. Also, the No Cost Change Order needs to be unbilled/approved. When you add items to your change order manually, In the pop-up box where line items are entered, Contractor Foreman includes an “Assigned to” field. It is in this field where the user must enter or select the name of the subcontractor who will be responsible for completing the added work. This ensures that the Change Order is properly tracked and mapped to the subcontractor who will execute the new tasks or provide the required materials. If you import items from somewhere, once the item is imported, click on the preview icon to open the pop-up box to access the “Assigned to” field and follow the same steps. Once the line items are added and the subcontractor is assigned, the next step is to integrate the Change Order into the subcontract. To do this, navigate to the Subcontracts module within Contractor Foreman.

body: Once the line items are added and the subcontractor is assigned, the next step is to integrate the Change Order into the subcontract. To do this, navigate to the Subcontracts module within Contractor Foreman. It is important to ensure that the status of the relevant subcontract is set to “Draft”. If the status is marked as “Approved,” changes cannot be made. Adjusting the status to “Draft” enables the user to add items to the subcontract. The system provides a seamless option for adding the assigned Change Order items into the subcontract. By selecting the “Add Items to Subcontract” option, the user can import the necessary details from change orders by selecting the Import from Change Order option. This feature, labelled Import from CO, allows for the easy transfer of line items that were previously assigned to the subcontractor, ensuring that all relevant details are properly imported into the subcontract. The last thing to do is to resend the Subcontract to your subcontractor for approval, or simply click on the status “Approved” for the changes to be applied.

A Baseline schedule is a key project management tool used to capture your original planned schedule. It represents what you initially said was going to happen in terms of tasks, timelines, and durations. By setting a Baseline, you can easily compare the actual progress of the project to the original plan, which helps in identifying any deviations, such as schedule delays or early completions. This allows for better visibility into where your project has slipped or gained ground, enabling you to make informed decisions for corrective actions. How to Use a Baseline Schedule in Contractor Foreman
Open the Schedule module from the Main Menu. In the Gantt chart interface, start by adding your project tasks. For each task, you will have the option to enter a start date and a duration. You will also see an option to set a Baseline for your task. Once you click Set, you will get the option to add a Baseline start date and a Baseline duration for the task. This is where you capture the planned schedule. Use ‘Scheduled/Planned’ to represent the actual duration of the project—what happened in reality. Use ‘Baseline/Actual’ to refer to the original plan of action.

In Contractor Foreman, the status of a bill is automatically updated based on the payment activity associated with it. There is no need to manually change a bill’s status from Open to Paid—this transition happens automatically when the full payment has been posted. How Bill Status Works
When a bill is created, its initial status is typically set to Open, indicating that it has not yet been paid in full. The system monitors all payments posted to that bill and updates its status as payments are made. If a bill has an outstanding amount it will remain in Open status. When a payment of the full outstanding amount is posted to the bill, the status will automatically change to Paid. If only a partial payment is made, the bill will remain Open until the remaining balance is paid. How to Post a Payment
To trigger the automatic status change, you simply need to post a payment to the bill:
Open the bill from the Bills module or from within the Subcontracts or Purchase Orders module if it’s tied to a sub-contract. Click on the 3 dots to the top right of the bill and click Post Payment. Enter the payment amount and payment details. Click Confirm.

A Compliance Notice is used to formally notify a subcontractor, vendor, or team member that they are not meeting the requirements outlined in the project plans, specifications, or contract documents. It serves as an official record that a performance, safety, or quality issue has been identified and must be corrected.
Compliance Notices help you:

- Document work that is incorrect, incomplete, or outside of scope
- Address poor workmanship or installation errors
- Communicate when specifications or contract requirements are not being followed
- Create a traceable record of the issue and the steps taken to resolve it
This type of notice is an important part of project documentation, helping ensure accountability, maintain quality standards, and protect your company if disputes arise.

body: A Milestone is an important goal or checkpoint you set in your project schedule. The main distinction between a task and a milestone is that a task has a specific start date and a duration, while a milestone only marks a specific point in time with no associated duration. Tasks typically involve work that needs to be done, whereas milestones signify the completion of key phases or the achievement of critical goals. They are used to mark key events or decision points, helping you track progress toward important goals. heading: Method 1: Link QuickBooks and Contractor Foreman through QuickBooks Integration (Recommended)

heading: Method 2: Export and Import Cost Codes Manually
body:
If you prefer not to use the QuickBooks integration, you can manually export cost codes from QuickBooks and import them into Contractor Foreman using the CSV template. Export Cost Codes from QuickBooks:
In QuickBooks, go to Reports and generate a report of your existing Products and Services. Export this report as a CSV file. In Contractor Foreman, go to the Cost Codes section from the main settings. From the Action drop-down menu, select View Import Template. This will allow you to download the CSV template file that Contractor Foreman uses for importing cost codes. Add Your Cost Codes to the Template:
Open the exported QuickBooks file and the Contractor Foreman template in a spreadsheet program (e.g., Excel). Copy the cost codes from QuickBooks and paste them into the appropriate columns of the Contractor Foreman template. Ensure that each column is correctly filled in according to the template’s instructions (e.g., CSI Code, CSI Name, Status). Import the CSV into Contractor Foreman:
Once your cost codes have been added to the template, save the file. In Contractor Foreman, go back to the Action drop-down menu and select Import Cost Codes (From File). Select your CSV file and upload it.

Optional Items in an Estimate provide flexibility by allowing the customer to choose whether they want certain items included in the final approval. This feature is particularly useful when offering additional services or components that may or may not be necessary for the customer, depending on their preferences or budget. Instead of committing to the item upfront, the customer can decide during the approval process if they would like to include the optional item, giving them more control over the scope and cost of the project. To Create an Optional Item, navigate to the Estimates Module by going to the main Menu and selecting the Estimates module. If you want to create a new estimate, click the +Estimate button to begin. If you’re editing an existing estimate, find and select the estimate you wish to modify. Click here to view more on how to create an Estimate
Once inside the estimate, locate the Items tab on the left panel. This is where you can see the list of items included in the estimate. Next, find the specific line item you want to make optional. Click the preview button (represented by an eyeball icon) to the right of the item. A pop-up window will appear on the side.

body: Accurate project cost tracking is critical to managing a successful construction project. Contractor Foreman provides tools to help distinguish between Bills and Expenses, each serving a specific purpose in tracking job costs. Understanding when and how to use each one ensures better budget control, accurate financial reporting, and improved project forecasting.
text:
Bills > What is the difference between a Expense and a Bill?

Accurate project cost tracking is critical to managing a successful construction project. Contractor Foreman provides tools to help distinguish between Bills and Expenses, each serving a specific purpose in tracking job costs. Understanding when and how to use each one ensures better budget control, accurate financial reporting, and improved project forecasting.
title: What is the difference between a Expense and a Bill?

heading: When to Use Bills
body:
Bills are best used for quantified, planned purchases that are tied directly to the project estimate. These purchases are often agreed upon in advance and are typically generated through a Purchase Order (for materials and supplies) or a Subcontract (for labor or trade services).
Examples of When to Use a Bill:

- Ordering 10 cubic yards of concrete from a vendor.
- Paying for “Furnish and Install 15 windows” by a subcontractor.
- Procuring 500 square feet of vinyl plank flooring for interior finishes.Because these items are often pre-planned and budgeted, using Bills ensures these committed costs are tracked against the original estimate. This allows project managers to monitor performance against budget expectations, ensuring cost control and visibility into how planned costs are being spent.

Bills are best used for quantified, planned purchases that are tied directly to the project estimate. These purchases are often agreed upon in advance and are typically generated through a Purchase Order (for materials and supplies) or a Subcontract (for labor or trade services).
Examples of When to Use a Bill:

- Paying for “Furnish and Install 15 windows” by a subcontractor.
- Procuring 500 square feet of vinyl plank flooring for interior finishes.Because these items are often pre-planned and budgeted, using Bills ensures these committed costs are tracked against the original estimate. This allows project managers to monitor performance against budget expectations, ensuring cost control and visibility into how planned costs are being spent.
title: What is the difference between a Expense and a Bill?

heading: When to Use Expenses
body:
Expenses are intended for unplanned, incidental, or smaller purchases that are typically not listed within the original project estimate. These are often immediate or unexpected costs necessary to keep the project moving smoothly, and they may not always be tied to a formal agreement or quantity-based deliverable.
Examples of When to Use an Expense:

- Purchasing fuel for equipment at a nearby gas station.
- Replacing a broken hand tool needed for daily work.
- Buying lunch for the crew on an extended workday.While these costs may seem minor individually, they can add up over the course of a project. Tracking them through Expenses helps capture real-time financial activity, giving you a full view of actual costs—even those outside the scope of the original estimate.

heading: Impact on Job Costing
body:
Understanding how both Bills and Expenses affect your job costing is essential for maintaining financial clarity throughout the project lifecycle.
Bills:

- Most likely, it will be linked directly to planned line items from the estimate.
- Help track spending against committed and budgeted costs.

body: Let’s define these two terms that are broadly used in Contractor Foreman:
text:
Projects > What is the difference between Committed Cost and Actual Cost?

Let’s define these two terms that are broadly used in Contractor Foreman:
title: What is the difference between Committed Cost and Actual Cost?

heading: Actual Costs
body:
These are costs that have already been incurred or paid for a project or activity. They are recorded in the financial accounts once a payment is made or an expense is formally recognized.
Examples in Contractor Foreman are Labor costs for hours worked, materials purchased and received (Bills), or expenses created and submitted by our field team.
***Actual costs reflect reality and are tangible, measurable amounts that have occurred.
text:
Projects > What is the difference between Committed Cost and Actual Cost? :: Actual Costs

These are costs that have already been incurred or paid for a project or activity. They are recorded in the financial accounts once a payment is made or an expense is formally recognized.
Examples in Contractor Foreman are Labor costs for hours worked, materials purchased and received (Bills), or expenses created and submitted by our field team.
***Actual costs reflect reality and are tangible, measurable amounts that have occurred.
title: What is the difference between Committed Cost and Actual Cost?

heading: Committed Costs
body:
In Contractor Foreman these are costs that the organization has agreed to incur in the future, usually due to contracts, purchase orders, or other commitments.
For example a signed agreement to purchase materials (Purchase Orders), a contract to hire subcontractors (Subcontract), or lease agreements for equipment (Purchase Orders).
*** Committed costs are not yet realized but represent future obligations to the organization.
text:
Projects > What is the difference between Committed Cost and Actual Cost? :: Committed Costs

In Contractor Foreman these are costs that the organization has agreed to incur in the future, usually due to contracts, purchase orders, or other commitments.
For example a signed agreement to purchase materials (Purchase Orders), a contract to hire subcontractors (Subcontract), or lease agreements for equipment (Purchase Orders).
*** Committed costs are not yet realized but represent future obligations to the organization.
title: What is the difference between Committed Cost and Actual Cost?

heading: Key Differences
body:
Timing: Actual costs occur in the past; committed costs are future obligations.
Financial Impact: Actual costs directly affect the current financial statements, while committed costs may impact future financial periods.
Control: Once actual costs are incurred, they cannot be changed. Committed costs may be negotiable if the agreement permits revisions.
Understanding the distinction is crucial for budget tracking, cash flow management, and accurate project cost forecasting.

In Contractor Foreman, an allowance is a pre-determined amount of money allocated for a specific item or scope of work within an Estimate. Allowances help inform the customer how much budget has been allocated for a particular item and provide flexibility for product selection or upgrades.
Important: Contractor Foreman does not currently have a client selection section. This means that while you can include allowances in an Estimate as line items, they cannot automatically update based on a client’s choice of product or material. Any adjustments must be tracked manually via Change Orders.

In Contractor Foreman, you can easily manage retainage deductions as your project progresses and hits key milestones.
From the Main Menu, go to the Projects module and select the project for which you want to set or adjust the retainage rate. Once I nside the project, click on the Details tab from the left panel. There you will find a section called Additional Details. If the section is collapsed, click on View All in the top right of that section to expand it.

In this expanded section, you’ll find an option to set up or modify the retainage rate for your invoices. Input the desired retainage percentage that will be withheld on future invoices.
If you’ve reached a contractual milestone and need to reduce the retainage rate, simply modify the rate in the Additional Details section by following the same steps outlined above.
The updated retainage rate will only apply to future invoices. The retainage already withheld for previous invoices will remain unchanged.

body: Creating an Expense Account (also referred to as an Expense Category) depends on whether your account is integrated with an accounting system such as QuickBooks.
text:
Expenses > How I can create an expense account ? :: Overview

Creating an Expense Account (also referred to as an Expense Category) depends on whether your account is integrated with an accounting system such as QuickBooks.
title: How I can create an expense account ?

heading: If You Are Integrated with an Accounting System
body:
When your Contractor Foreman account is integrated with an external accounting system (such as QuickBooks), Expense Accounts must be created directly within that accounting system.
Contractor Foreman will automatically display the list of existing Expense Accounts that are synced from your accounting system.
However, Contractor Foreman does not allow the creation of new Expense Accounts from within the platform in this case. This restriction ensures that there are no conflicts or duplicate records when data is synced between systems.

title: How I can create an expense account ?

heading: If You Are Not Integrated with an Accounting System
body:
If your account is not integrated with an external accounting system, you can create Expense Accounts directly in Contractor Foreman.

- Go to the Expenses Module .
- Click on Add Expense Category (or Add Expense Account depending on your version).
- Enter the name and details for your new Expense Account.
- Click Save .Once saved, the new Expense Account will appear in your Expense Categories list and can be selected when recording new expenses.

Tracking past due bills is an important part of managing your company’s cash flow and ensuring timely vendor and subcontractor payments. There are a few easy ways you can quickly identify overdue bills using the tools available in the Bills module.
This article will walk you through how to locate and monitor past due bills effectively.
text:
Bills > How can I see if any Bills are past their due dates?

Tracking past due bills is an important part of managing your company’s cash flow and ensuring timely vendor and subcontractor payments. There are a few easy ways you can quickly identify overdue bills using the tools available in the Bills module.
This article will walk you through how to locate and monitor past due bills effectively.
title: How can I see if any Bills are past their due dates?

heading: Option 1: Use the “Past Due Bills” Widget
body:
When you go to the Bills module, you will notice a widget labeled “Past Due Bills” just above the list of Bills. This widget:

- Displays a quick summary of recently past due Bills.
- Helps you immediately identify some of the most critical overdue payments.
Note: This widget only shows a few of the most recent past due Bills. It is not a full list, but it provides a helpful starting point.

title: How can I see if any Bills are past their due dates?

heading: Option 2: Sort the Bills List by Due Date
body:
To manually identify all past due Bills, follow these steps:
Navigate to the Bills module from the main menu. Locate the column titled Due Date at the top of the Bills list.

Click on “Due Date” to sort the list by that column.

- Clicking once sorts the list from the oldest to newest due dates (ascending).
- Clicking again will sort from newest to oldest (descending).Look for any Bills where the due date is earlier than today’s date—these are your past due Bills.
This method gives you a broader view of due dates across all open Bills and helps you identify which ones need immediate attention.

Linking Estimates to Opportunities is important because it helps you keep everything organized from the very start of a potential job. In residential construction, this means you can easily track which leads have quotes, what stage each opportunity is in, and how much potential revenue is on the table. It also prevents confusion between multiple clients or projects, since the estimate stays tied to the right opportunity. This way, when the customer approves the estimate, it can smoothly turn into a project without needing to re-enter any information, saving time and reducing mistakes. There are a couple of ways to create an estimate and link it to an opportunity in Contractor Foreman. Option 1:
When creating a new Estimate, you will be prompted on the right side of the screen to select a Project. In this dropdown menu, you will see both your existing Projects and Opportunities. Simply use the search bar, type the name of the opportunity, and select it. Once selected, any estimate you create will automatically be linked or associated with that opportunity. Option 2:
You can also create the estimate directly from within the opportunity itself.

It makes sense to use the Opportunity record when you’re dealing with a potential project that isn’t official yet — meaning you haven’t signed a contract, but there’s real interest and progress in the conversation.
In residential construction, this is especially helpful for tracking jobs that are in the advanced stage of the sales process. You might already have a relationship with the customer or lead, and you’ve started gathering important details like estimates, photos, drawings, blueprints, or site visit pictures. Instead of mixing this information with active projects, Opportunities let you keep everything organized and separate until the deal becomes official.

Using Opportunities ensures you’re ready to hit the ground running once the client approves the proposal — all the key details are already in place. It’s a smart way to stay organized, avoid double work, and smoothly transition from potential job to active project.

heading: Can my clients create change order request from the Client Portal?
body:
Your clients will have the ability to create a Change Order Request from their client portal account if you have given them permission. Within Project > Settings > Client Access, you will have the ability to set the default settings that apply to all projects. Those defaults are then carried over to the Project record within the Client Access tab. If the box “Create a New CO” is checked, your client will be able to create a new Change Order Request.

They will do so by logging into their Client Portal account and clicking on the Financial tab and clicking the the Submit Change Order button. You will then receive an email notification and the pending CO will be visible in your account for your review.

Submitting a Change Order for approval in Contractor Foreman is a straightforward process, ensuring that any alterations to the original contract are properly authorized and tracked before work proceeds.
Once a Change Order is created and the required details have been entered, the user can submit it for approval by opening the change order record and clicking the three dots located in the top right corner of the screen. This menu contains several options, and one of the key actions for Change Orders is the “View/Email PDF” option.

When selected, this option allows the user to select a template to generate the Change Order. Depending on how you want your change order to look like from the approver’s perspective, choose a template from the list.

Once you selected a template, click “Submit for Approval” below your generated document to send it for approval. After the Change Order has been emailed, the recipient can review the details and, if satisfied, provide their electronic signature to approve the change order. The “Approved” status will then be applied to the Change Order record within Contractor Foreman, allowing the user to proceed with the next steps in the project.

Before you can invoice a Work Order, the first requirement is to make sure that the Work Order has been included in the Schedule of Values for the project. The Schedule of Values serves as a breakdown of all project items, including Work Orders. For more information about the Schedule of Values, please read this article: Basics of Schedule of Values (SOV)
To verify that the Work Order is in the Schedule of Values, navigate to the Project where the Work Order was created, go to the Schedule of Values tab. Review the list of items to confirm that the Work Order has been added. If it has not been added, you can import the Work Order manually into the SOV using the Import From Work Order option. Once you have verified that the Work Order is in the Schedule of Values, the next step is to create an invoice. From the main menu, navigate to the Invoices module. Inside the Invoices module, click on the + Invoice button in the top right to Create a New Invoice. After the new invoice is created, you will be taken to the invoice page. To add details to the invoice, you need to switch to Edit Mode by clicking the Edit button. In the Edit Mode, look for the drop-down menu labeled Add Item to Invoice.

body: After the new invoice is created, you will be taken to the invoice page. To add details to the invoice, you need to switch to Edit Mode by clicking the Edit button. In the Edit Mode, look for the drop-down menu labeled Add Item to Invoice. From this drop-down menu, select Import from Schedule of Values. At this point, the system will present a list of all items that are currently included in the Schedule of Values for the selected project. This includes Work Orders, Change Orders, Approved Estimate Items, and other items. Review the list of items and select the Work Order(s) that you want to include in the invoice. Once the relevant Work Order is selected, click Save & Close. The Work Order items will be imported into the invoice along with any associated quantities, prices, and descriptions. Once you have reviewed and made any necessary adjustments to the invoice, it is important to save your changes.

body: In Contractor Foreman you can restrict the access to the Financial Details of the Project to your employees simply by making sure that the Role assigned to them does not have access to the Financials of the Project. The first thing we will do is to confirm the Role that our employee has. Go to the Directory Module, open the employee’s profile and confirm their role. In our example Charles Smith has the “Office Support” role, now it is time to make sure that he does not have access to the Financials in the Projects Module. It is time to go to the System Settings, Roles, and open the”Office Support” role. Please remember that this is the example, you can do this with any other role. Click on the edit button for the role you want to open and scroll down to the Projects Section. Once there, make sure that they have no access to “Financial (Tab)”, “Reports (Tab)”, “Project Balance Remaining (Field)” and “Project Budget Amount (Field)”. By doing this, you will restrict the access to the financial details of your project to your employees with the assigned role. Do not forget to click on the blue Save Button.

body: In Contractor Foreman, a Work Order cannot be used as a standalone project. Every Work Order must be tied to an existing project in order to function properly within the system. This ensures that costs, labor, materials, and other items are tracked consistently across all reports.
text:
Work Orders > How can I use a Work Order as a project

In Contractor Foreman, a Work Order cannot be used as a standalone project. Every Work Order must be tied to an existing project in order to function properly within the system. This ensures that costs, labor, materials, and other items are tracked consistently across all reports.
title: How can I use a Work Order as a project

heading: What can you do instead?
body:
If you want to manage a small job, for example, repairing a fence, installing a single window, or completing a minor service request, you should use a Service Ticket or still create a Project first. Once the project is created, you can then add a Work Order to capture the specific scope of work.
This way you get:

- Accurate cost tracking tied back to the project.
- Flexibility to add more Work Orders later if the client requests additional work.
- Consistent reporting across all projects, big or small.
Think of the Project as the container, and the Work Orders as the tasks or scopes of work inside that container. Even if it’s just a small project, setting it up properly will keep your records clean and your reports accurate.

In Contractor Foreman, you have the flexibility to handle different types of Change Orders, including those that don’t impact the overall contract value of a project. This is particularly useful when you have a “No Cost” Change Order, where the work is performed but does not result in any additional charges to the client. To ensure that the Change Order amount does not affect the overall contract value, when you are creating or editing the Change Order, there is a checkbox labelled “No Cost Change Order” in the bottom right corner of the change order. By selecting this option, the Change Order will not contribute to the overall contract value for the project.

heading: What Is the Purpose of a Request for Information (RFI)?
body:
A Request for Information (RFI) is used in construction to obtain clarification when plans, drawings, specifications, or agreements contain gaps, conflicts, or missing details. When something in the construction documents is unclear, incomplete, or contradictory, an RFI provides a formal way for contractors, subcontractors, and designers to communicate and resolve the issue.
RFIs ensure that all project stakeholders receive the same information, reducing misunderstandings and helping the work proceed correctly. By documenting these questions and their responses, RFIs also create a clear project record that supports accountability, accurate decision-making, and future reference.

In short, the purpose of an RFI is to clarify information so the project can move forward smoothly, accurately, and in compliance with the design intent.

In Contractor Foreman, adding markups to items in a Change Order can be done either automatically to multiple items at once or manually on an item-by-item basis, depending on your needs. This functionality helps to ensure that you can quickly add costs for additional work or materials by applying a markup percentage, which reflects profit, overhead or any other type of indirect cost on top of the base costs. To apply markups in bulk: When you’re in the Change Order, navigate to the “Add Item to Change Order” dropdown. From there, select the option labelled “Apply Automatic/Bulk

Markup.” This feature allows you to apply a markup percentage to the types of items you want to adjust, such as materials, labour, or equipment. Simply input your desired percentage for each category, and once you’re finished, select an option from “Apply to all items where markup is not set (or is set to 0)”, “Apply to all items where markup is set and greater than 0%”, or “Apply to all items (with or without an existing markup)”, and click “Apply” to implement the changes. Make sure to save the record to ensure that the changes are reflected in the Change Order.

text:

Cross-referencing a permit with an inspection record in Contractor Foreman ensures that every inspection is properly documented and tied to the official approval process for your project. This is more than just paperwork, it’s about compliance, accountability, and meeting construction standards.
title: How do I cross reference a Permit to the Inspection record?

heading: Why is this important?
body:
- Inspectors use permit numbers as their primary way of tracking inspections. If they do it that way, contractors and builders should too.
- Easy backtracking : By linking the inspection to the correct permit, you’ll always know which permit covered which inspection, saving time in audits, disputes, or project reviews.
- Compliance made simple : Building departments often require inspections to be tied to specific permits. Cross-referencing helps you stay aligned with local regulations.
- Meeting construction standards : Proper documentation ensures your work is not only done right but also provable, which protects you, your client, and your team.

body: In Contractor Foreman, it is not possible to permanently delete a cost code. However, you can archive any cost code that is no longer in use. Archiving a cost code removes it from active use but keeps it in the system for future reference, which is useful for tracking past projects or historical data. To Archive a Cost Code, go to Settings from the Main Menu and select Cost Codes. Browse through your list of cost codes to find the one you wish to archive. Click the Archive icon (next to the green pencil edit icon) for the specific cost code you want to archive. A confirmation prompt will appear. Confirm that you want to archive the cost code. Once archived, the cost code will no longer appear in the active list when creating new estimates or entering financial data. You can view archived cost codes by filtering for them in the Cost Codes section if needed. Archiving is an effective way to manage unused cost codes without losing historical data. Cost codes cannot be deleted directly in Contractor Foreman.

heading: Important Notes
body:
- If a line item is marked as an Optional Item in the estimate, it will not appear in the Schedule of Values after approval.
- Only approved items are carried into the SOV. If a line item is missing, first check whether it was marked as optional.
- If the issue is not related to optional items and the line still does not appear in the SOV, further troubleshooting may be needed. In some cases, the estimate may need to be rechecked or recreated to properly display in the Schedule of Values.
Best Practice: Always review your estimate carefully before approval to confirm which items are marked as required vs. optional. This ensures that the Schedule of Values is generated correctly and avoids missing line items later on.

body: In the context of Sales and Project Management, a “Lead” and an “Opportunity” typically represent different stages in the business development process.
text:
Leads > What is the difference between a Lead and an Opportunity?

In the context of Sales and Project Management, a “Lead” and an “Opportunity” typically represent different stages in the business development process.
title: What is the difference between a Lead and an Opportunity?

heading: Lead:
body:
A lead is usually a potential client or company that has shown initial interest in your products or services.

It often refers to the early stage of engagement, where there may be some interest or need, but there hasn’t been a detailed discussion or commitment yet.

Leads can be individuals or organizations that you’ve identified as potential customers, but you’re still in the process of establishing a connection and gauging their requirements.
When a Lead is generated in Contractor Foreman, it can be found in the Leads Module or in the Directory under the Leads Contact Type. Leads can be converted into Customers. If this happens, the Lead will no longer be under the Leads module, however we will be able to see it in the Directory under the Customers Contact Type.
You can create an Estimate from the Lead’s profile.

If this happens, the Lead will no longer be under the Leads module, however we will be able to see it in the Directory under the Customers Contact Type.
You can create an Estimate from the Lead’s profile.
title: What is the difference between a Lead and an Opportunity?

heading: Opportunity:
body:
An opportunity, on the other hand, is a more advanced stage in the sales process.

It usually means that there has been some level of discussion, and there is a specific project or need that the potential client is considering.

Opportunities often arise when a lead progresses to a point where there is a concrete chance of securing a contract or project with the client. It’s a more qualified prospect. Also, Opportunities are commonly used for when you have already done business with somebody in the past and you have another opportunity to do another project with them.
While a Lead can be converted into a Customer, an Opportunity can be converted to a Project. If this happens, the Opportunity will no longer be under the Opportunities Module, it will be moved and converted to a Project, under the Projects Module.
In summary, a lead is a potential customer in the early stages of engagement, while an opportunity is a more qualified prospect where there is a specific project or contract on the table, and there’s a real chance of moving forward.
You can create an Estimate from the Opportunity. Also, Opportunities can be created for existing Customers or for potential Clients; Leads.

heading: Why Do We Cross-Reference a Change Order in the RFI Record?
body:
Many times an RFI will trigger a Change Order, or a Change Order will trigger an RFI. Because these two documents are often directly connected, Contractor Foreman provides a field within the RFI to link it back to the related Change Order when one is created.
Cross-referencing ensures that anyone reviewing the RFI can immediately see if the clarification resulted in a change to the project’s scope, cost, or schedule. It also keeps your project records organized, provides a clear paper trail, and makes it easier to track the history of a decision during billing, audits, or dispute resolution.

In short, the cross-reference field helps maintain clarity, accountability, and consistency between your RFIs and any resulting Change Orders.

heading: Why Is Adding Events Important?
body:
Adding events helps keep your team aligned and your projects running smoothly. It ensures that everyone knows what’s happening, when, and who’s responsible. Using the calendar regularly helps you prevent scheduling conflicts, improve communication, and maintain accountability across all active jobs.
You can create an event from almost any module in Contractor Foreman, not just from the Dashboard.
Here’s how to do it:

- Locate the Calendar icon — it’s usually found at the bottom right corner of the screen (as shown in the screenshot below).
- Click the Calendar icon to open the calendar view.
- Double-click on the date where you want to create a new event.
- Enter your event details and save — that’s it!
It’s extremely simple and quick to use.
Tip: Remember, you can access and create events not only from the Dashboard but also from almost any module in Contractor Foreman. This flexibility allows you to stay organized no matter where you’re working within the system.

body: Once connected to QuickBooks, you will have a Transaction Log that appears in the Menu within the Financial column. Clicking it will show a list of successful and failed transactions. If a transaction did not sync, it is usually due to one piece of the link not being synced. In order for a Payment to sync, the invoice must have already been synced. Start with the cost code and confirm that it has been linked and then look at the customer, project, invoice, etc. If there is an error, that means that QuickBooks rejected it for the reason stated within the error log.

If you are using Stripe to accept online payments, an entry is created in Contractor Foreman and then the entry is synced to QuickBooks.
title: How does the Payment information sync with QuickBooks?

The decision to convert an Opportunity into a Project depends on each construction company’s workflow.
For example, imagine an architectural firm that also builds homes. A client asks for three custom home designs. The firm first creates an Opportunity to track the potential job. Once the client confirms they’ll move forward with the design work, the firm converts the Opportunity into a Project to start tracking real work—such as the time spent by designers and engineers, work orders, and associated costs.
This conversion allows the company to manage budgets, record hours, and maintain all preconstruction information in one place. Later, when the client chooses one design and the estimate is approved, the financial values automatically populate the Project, keeping everything accurate and organized from design to construction.

Overtime is calculated either weekly or daily based on defined values. After enabling it in Settings, it is calculated at 1.5x after a certain set of hours that is defined by the administrator. How to enable the Overtime Feature? Let’s go to the Time Cards Module and open the settings. Once in the settings, scroll down to the section “Overtime Configuration” and click on the green pencil icon to edit. Click on the grey button “Off” to enable it and right away you will see there three more options that were hidden. Overtime Rules – Weekly

This function allows us to set up a maximum number of hours that our employees can work before becoming overtime. For example, if my employees work tens (10 hours daily) from Monday to Thursday, that is a total of 40 hours per week. They have the “day off” on Friday. If I need them to work on a Friday, since they already worked 40 hours this week, the first hour on Friday becomes overtime. Overtime applies at 1.5 times the rate of the employee. If my employee’s rate is $50.00 USD per hour, the first 40 hours will represent an actual cost to my project of $50.00 USD/hour. However the first hour on Friday, it will cost 1.5 x $50.00 = $75.00 USD.

body:
If my employee’s rate is $50.00 USD per hour, the first 40 hours will represent an actual cost to my project of $50.00 USD/hour. However the first hour on Friday, it will cost 1.5 x $50.00 = $75.00 USD. Overtime Rules – Daily

The Daily function is very simple to understand. Using as reference the regular rate for our employee at $50.00 USD per hour, when our employees work daily 8 hours, they will cost us 8 hours x $50.00 USD = $400.00 USD. However, if they continue working, the 9th hour becomes overtime. This triggers the equation 1.5 times the regular rate. Let’s say we set our Overtime Configuration as shown above, after 8 hours working the 9th hour is overtime. Our employee clocks out at the 9th hour, that means that he will cost our project 8 hours x $50.00 USD + 1.5 x 1 hour x $50.00 USD = $475.00 USD. Overtime Rules – Mixed

The last option is the Mixed rule. This option allows us to keep track of the daily overtime (if it takes place, as described above) and also, in the event that we need to work more that 40 hours (think of it as in working on a Saturday or Sunday), it allows us to represent that cost to our project.

Retainage (or retention) is a common practice in construction contracts, where a percentage of the subcontractor’s payment is withheld until project completion or until specific milestones are met. This ensures that subcontractors complete their work according to contract requirements before receiving full payment. In Contractor Foreman, you can specify retainage when creating or managing a Sub-Contract, ensuring that the retained amount is tracked correctly and deducted from payments until it is due. This article will guide you through the process of setting up retainage in a Sub-Contract and how it affects billing. Access the Sub-Contracts Module

- Log in to Contractor Foreman.
- Navigate to the Sub-Contracts module from the Main Menu.
- Select an existing Sub-Contract or create a new one by clicking the + Sub-Contract button. Specify Retainage Percentage in the Sub-Contract

- Once inside the Sub-Contract, locate the Retention % field in the details widget.
- Enter the percentage of retainage you want to apply (e.g., 10%). By entering a retention percentage, Contractor Foreman will automatically calculate the withheld amount for each Bill created against this Sub-Contract.

Roles and the Directory are directly linked in Contractor Foreman. The Directory is where you create and manage all your contacts, which are employees, contractors, vendors, customers, leads, and any miscellaneous contacts. Also, it’s also where you can create user accounts for your employees and contractors by allowing login access so they can login to their own accounts under your company. So, what is the relationship between creating users in the Directory and Roles?

- Allowing login access enables an employee or a contractor to access Contractor Foreman with their own account with a username and password. When you allow login access to someone, that person becomes a user. To allow login access, you need to give that person a username and a password, and most importantly, you need to assign a role.
- The Role you assign defines that user’s permissions, controlling what data and features they can access and interact with.

No — a Service Ticket does not have to be associated or linked with a Project in Contractor Foreman.
This is because Service Tickets are designed to capture smaller, standalone jobs or tasks that don’t necessarily require the full scope of project management. For example, fixing a leaky faucet, repairing a small patch of drywall, installing a light fixture, or performing routine maintenance doesn’t need to be tied to a larger construction project.
By keeping Service Tickets independent, you gain flexibility to:

- Track small jobs for existing customers without creating a full project.
- Serve leads or new customers who may not have an active project but need quick service.
- Avoid cluttering your project list with minor tasks that don’t require project-level management.In short, projects are best used for larger, ongoing scopes of work, while Service Tickets are ideal for one-off, quick-turn, or specialized services. This separation keeps your system organized and ensures each workflow is used for the right purpose.

Retainage Cost Codes play a vital role in managing the retainage amounts for both subcontracts and invoices in Contractor Foreman. Retainage refers to a portion of the contract amount that is held back until the project is fully completed to ensure the work is finished to satisfaction. Setting up Retainage Cost Codes ensures that the retainage amounts are always directed to the correct cost code and that this process integrates smoothly when syncing with QuickBooks. How to Set Up Default Retainage Cost Codes:
From the Main Menu, navigate to Settings and then choose Cost Codes. Open the Action drop-down menu on top left and select Add & Set Retainage Code. This action will take you to the financial settings area. Once in the financial settings, find the section titled Automatically select to ‘Tax’ these item types. Click on the green pencil icon to enter Edit mode. Here, you can set up default cost codes for two key areas:
Sub-Contract Retainage Cost Code: This code applies to the retainage held from subcontracts. Invoice Retainage Cost Code: This code is used for retainage on invoices. For both of these, select the appropriate cost code from your existing list of cost codes.

Tags in a Time Card are used as another way to categorize or to sort your time cards. One clear example of it is to tag a time card to items that are not already present in the Cost Code section.
If there is a time card started for a Change Order, for example, then a tag called Change Order Work would be beneficial so the employee who started the Time Card would not be mistaken for doing the work of a Project they are assigned to.
In this manner, tags help segregate and compartmentalize work in the app.
How do I create my own Tags?
Go to the System Settings by clicking on the Main Menu>Settings and Support > Settings and then, click on Custom under the System Settings.

Once there, there is a panel on the left hand side and towards the bottom of it, you will see the option Tags. Click on it to have the option to work with them.

In order to create a new Tag, just click on the “Add Custom Entry” button and then name the Tag and tick the checkbox to show it on the Time Cards. The status needs to be Active.

Next time you or your employees clock in, they will have the option to select that tag.

When managing contracts in Contractor Foreman, it is important to understand the differences between Sub-Contracts and Purchase Orders (POs) and when to use each. While both are essential for tracking project costs and commitments, Sub-Contracts offer greater contractual clarity, flexibility, and control in managing agreements with subcontractors.
This article explores the benefits of using a Sub-Contract instead of a Purchase Order and when a Purchase Order may be more appropriate.
text:
Sub-Contracts > What are the benefits of using a Sub-Contract instead of a Purchase Order?

When managing contracts in Contractor Foreman, it is important to understand the differences between Sub-Contracts and Purchase Orders (POs) and when to use each. While both are essential for tracking project costs and commitments, Sub-Contracts offer greater contractual clarity, flexibility, and control in managing agreements with subcontractors.
This article explores the benefits of using a Sub-Contract instead of a Purchase Order and when a Purchase Order may be more appropriate.
title: What are the benefits of using a Sub-Contract instead of a Purchase Order?

heading: Key Benefits of Using a Sub-Contract
body:
1. Greater Contractual Clarity with Detailed Terms & Conditions
A Sub-Contract includes detailed terms and conditions that provide a clear legal agreement between the contractor and subcontractor. These typically include:

- Scope of Work – Clearly defines what tasks and responsibilities are included.
- Inclusions & Exclusions – Specifies what is covered in the contract and what is not.
- Clarifications – Provides additional details to prevent misinterpretations.
- Payment Terms – Defines billing schedules and conditions for payments. In contrast, a Purchase Order (PO) is primarily used for material purchases and does not provide the same level of legal and contractual protections as a Sub-Contract. 2. Ability to Include Change Orders
A significant advantage of using Sub-Contracts is that they allow for Change Orders.

- If there is a change in the project scope, you can import items from Change Orders to update the contract value and scope accordingly.
- This ensures subcontracts are properly managed with additional work and that the project remains contractually aligned. Purchase Orders, on the other hand, do not support importing from Change Orders. 3.

The different rates that Contractor Foreman has are always in hours and the definitions are found below:
Wage Rate: The wage rate refers to the base amount paid to a worker or employee for their time, usually calculated per hour, day, or project. It represents the cost of labor without accounting for any additional overheads or benefits.
Burden Rate: The burden rate refers to the additional costs associated with an employee’s wages, such as taxes, insurance, benefits, and other overhead expenses. It is often expressed as a percentage added to the wage rate to reflect the true cost of employing that person.
Billing Rate: The billing rate is the amount charged to the customer for labor services. It includes not only the wage rate and burden rate but also any additional markup or overhead charges, and can vary based on the type of service, project, or client agreement.
In Contractor Foreman, the Burden Rate is the summary of the Wage rate + the Burden rate. This is the Actual cost of an employee per hour.

When marking up items in Contractor Foreman, whether you’re working on estimates, invoices, or other financial documents, you have two options for applying a markup to each line item: by percentage (%) or by dollar amount ($). Here’s the difference between the two:
1. Percentage (%) Markup:
This method allows you to apply a percentage markup based on the cost of the item.
Example: If you enter a cost of $1,000 and choose a 10% markup, Contractor Foreman will automatically calculate a markup of $100, making the total price $1,100.

Use this when you know the percentage you want to mark up over the cost and want Contractor Foreman to calculate the final total for you.
2. Dollar ($) Markup:
This method allows you to manually set the final total price, and Contractor Foreman will calculate the markup percentage for you.
Example: If the item cost is $1,000 and you want the final price to be $1,230, you enter $1,230 as the total price. Contractor Foreman will then calculate and display a 23% markup.

Use this when you have a target final price in mind and need Contractor Foreman to calculate the corresponding markup percentage based on that final price.

The Duration field in a Service Ticket is the dispatcher’s best estimate of how long it will take the technician or crew to complete the job. This could be one hour, four hours, or however long you expect the work to take.
When entered, the Duration serves two main purposes:

- Gives technicians an idea of the time expected on-site – Helps them plan their day and understand how long they should dedicate to that service call.
- Blocks out time in the Crew Schedule – Contractor Foreman uses this field to show the technician as “unavailable” for the set duration. This keeps your scheduling accurate and helps avoid double-booking.

In Contractor Foreman, Progress Billing Invoices allow you to invoice for portions of work as they are completed, tracking the percentage of work invoiced over time. The Schedule of Values (SOV) is the key tool for managing this, as it contains all the project items and tracks the percentage invoiced for each item. You can create an invoice from two places. From the Financials tab of a project: Open the project and navigate to the Financials tab, then click on the +Invoice button. From the Invoices module: Go to the Invoices module from the main menu, then click on the +Invoice button. Creating the Invoice:
When you create a new invoice, you will be prompted to enter the usual invoice details (such as project, customer, terms, etc.). Once these are filled in and the invoice is created, you’ll have the option to add items to your invoice by navigating to the items tab of the invoice from the left panel. To ensure proper tracking of progress billing, select “Import from Schedule of Values” when adding items to your invoice. The SOV keeps track of all project items and previous invoicing percentages. Importing from the SOV allows you to maintain a consistent billing record.

body: To ensure proper tracking of progress billing, select “Import from Schedule of Values” when adding items to your invoice. The SOV keeps track of all project items and previous invoicing percentages. Importing from the SOV allows you to maintain a consistent billing record. Once items are imported from the SOV, you will see the invoiced and remaining percentage for each item based on previous invoices. Adjust the percentage for each item from the Invoice (%) column to reflect the current progress of work being invoiced. The system will automatically calculate the remaining percentage to invoice for future billings. Ensure that you always import items from the Schedule of Values for progress billing invoices. Gross Profit is a critical financial metric that represents the revenue generated from a project minus the costs incurred. In Contractor Foreman, this is automatically calculated based on the data entered into the platform. In contractor Foreman, gross profit is calculated using the below formula. Gross Profit = Invoiced to Date − Actual Costs
This calculation helps determine the profitability of your project, allowing you to make informed decisions about resource allocation, budgeting, and financial planning. You can view the current gross profit in the Summary tab of the project. The summary provides a quick overview of the project’s financial status, including gross profit, invoiced to date, and actual costs incurred. For the gross profit calculation to be accurate, it is essential that all financial items related to the project are properly entered and approved. In addition to the gross profit, you can also access your current Estimated Gross Profit in a project, go to the the Financial tab, which is located on the left panel. This tab contains all the financial data associated with your project, such as invoices, estimates, and other cost records.
