title: How do I choose what syncs with QuickBooks?

heading: QuickBooks
body:
Menu > Settings > QuickBooks > Advanced Configuration. From there you will see the screen below that allows you to select the modules that should be sycned.

- If the module is not checked, no transactions will sync
- Do not Send to QuickBooks = The Transaction will import from QuickBooks but changes (or new records) will not sync to QuickBooks
- Send to QuickBooks = Records will be sent to QuickBooks but new records created in QuickBooks will not sync to Contractor Foreman
- Sync Both Ways = This is the most popular option as it synces updates both ways so that the records on both systems match.
- Sync Existing Entries to QuickBooks = If selected, this will sync existing entries within Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks.Changes made in Contractor Foreman typically sync to QuickBooks within a few seconds but changes made in QuickBooks can take up to 5 minutes. In both cases, give the system at least 5 minutes to sync. If the item does not sync, refer to the Menu > Transaction Log for error details.

You have the option of allowing your company to share the same calendar among all users or allowing each user to have their own calendar within Contractor Foreman. Shared is default. This means if one user enters an activity, then all users will see that activity. Private, means that the users will only see those activities assigned to them.
To change your calendar from Shared to Private, do so from Menu > Settings > Integrations > Calendar and change from Shared to Private.
Once the calendar has been set to Private, each user can connect to their own Google or Outlook calendar by going to Settings > My Profile.
If you decide to change back to a Shared calendar, you can do by changing Settings > Integration > Calendar from Private back to Shared.

Retention is a widely used financial mechanism in construction contracts that ensures subcontractors complete their work to the agreed standard before receiving the full payment. Contractor Foreman allows you to not only hold retention through subcontracts but also manage and release it efficiently—whether partially during the project or fully at the end.
This article explains how to release and pay retention on a Sub Contract after generating a bill.
Click here to see how to set up retention for a sub-contract.
text:
Bills > How do I pay full or partial retention on a Sub Contract?

Retention is a widely used financial mechanism in construction contracts that ensures subcontractors complete their work to the agreed standard before receiving the full payment. Contractor Foreman allows you to not only hold retention through subcontracts but also manage and release it efficiently—whether partially during the project or fully at the end.
This article explains how to release and pay retention on a Sub Contract after generating a bill.
Click here to see how to set up retention for a sub-contract.
title: How do I pay full or partial retention on a Sub Contract?

heading: How to Release and Pay Retention
body:
Once you’re ready to release either a portion or the full amount of retention for a subcontractor, the process is handled directly through the Subcontracts Module. Step 1: Generate a Bill from the Sub Contract

- Go to the Subcontracts module from the main menu.
- Open the specific Sub Contract you want to work with.
- Click on the three-dot menu (top right) and select “Create Bill”.
- You will automatically be redirected to the newly created bill.Step 2: Add Retainage for Payment

- Inside the new bill, click on “Add Item to Bill”.
- From the dropdown options, choose “Add Retainage (Partial or Full) for Payment”.
- A new window will appear prompting you to enter the amount of retention you want to release. You can release the entire retainage amount if the work is completed, or just a portion if only part of the scope has been fulfilled. Step 3: Save and Close

- After entering the retainage amount, click “Save & Close”.
- This action will add the retainage release as a line item to the bill, making it part of the amount that will be processed and paid.Contractor Foreman makes it easy to manage retention at every stage of a subcontract.

body: It’s easy to get the two confused but knowing the difference between the two can greatly impact the profitability of your next project. So, what is the difference between Markup and Margin. MARKUP is the percentage amount by which the cost of a product is increased to arrive at the selling price or proposed price to the CUSTOMER. If you look at the combined totals, you will see the total selling price is $15,000 and the total estimated cost is $8000. Total Markup is $7,000. You may also see this referred to as ESTIMATED PROFIT. The total MARKUP % is 88%, which is calculated as PROFIT / ESTIMATED COST, or $7000/$8000, or 88%. Once the ESTIMATE is Approved and the CUSTOMER agrees to the proposed price of $15,000, now we start referring to the targeted PROFIT as “GROSS PROFIT” and we express this in terms of MARGIN or MARGIN %. MARGIN (or GROSS PROFIT) is equal to the Selling Price minus the Cost of Construction. We sold the above Office Relocation Project at $15,000. We estimated the cost to be $8,000. So our MARGIN or GROSS Profit is $7,000. The MARGIN % or GROSS PROFIT % is calculated as PROFIT / SALES PRICE, or $7,000/$15,000, or 47%.

MARKUP is the percentage amount by which the cost of a product is increased to arrive at the selling price or proposed price to the CUSTOMER. If you look at the combined totals, you will see the total selling price is $15,000 and the total estimated cost is $8000. Total Markup is $7,000. You may also see this referred to as ESTIMATED PROFIT. The total MARKUP % is 88%, which is calculated as PROFIT / ESTIMATED COST, or $7000/$8000, or 88%. Once the ESTIMATE is Approved and the CUSTOMER agrees to the proposed price of $15,000, now we start referring to the targeted PROFIT as “GROSS PROFIT” and we express this in terms of MARGIN or MARGIN %. MARGIN (or GROSS PROFIT) is equal to the Selling Price minus the Cost of Construction. We sold the above Office Relocation Project at $15,000. We estimated the cost to be $8,000. So our MARGIN or GROSS Profit is $7,000. The MARGIN % or GROSS PROFIT % is calculated as PROFIT / SALES PRICE, or $7,000/$15,000, or 47%.
title: Markup vs Margin: What is the Difference?

We sold the above Office Relocation Project at $15,000. We estimated the cost to be $8,000. So our MARGIN or GROSS Profit is $7,000. The MARGIN % or GROSS PROFIT % is calculated as PROFIT / SALES PRICE, or $7,000/$15,000, or 47%. When you hear a contractor say “I need to make 35 points on my jobs to run a profitable business, he is referring to MARGIN %, or a GROSS PROFIT % of 35%.”
Our new FINANCIAL Summary reflects ESTIMATED PROFIT as both a MARKUP % and a MARGIN % so our users can see the relationship

Confusing PROFIT MARGIN vs. MARKUP can lead to accounting and sales errors. If you Markup your costs 25% when you prepare a quote, you are only generating 20% in Margin and that 5% could make the difference between a company making any real company profits or not once administrative costs and overhead are paid.

heading: Purpose:
body:
Often each project has a particular labor rate. Contractor Foreman handles this based on the Job Cost Labor calculation.
The purpose of this article is to know other ways to setup our Contractor Foreman Account to be able to use different rates for our Labor Force and not only the ones shown in the Directory.
Why would you like to have a different rate for the Labor Items? Not only because every Project is different but also, because some of them require to have a Prevailing Wage. According to the Department of Labor: The prevailing wage rate is the average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment.

title: Prevailing Wage, how to use different Labor Rates for different Projects?

heading: What to do in Contractor Foreman?
body:
The first thing to do is to change the Labor Calculation Method. In order to do that, we have to go to the Main Menu > Settings & Support > Settings > System Settings > Financial. Once there, we make sure to click the green pencil on the top right side of the screen under the Financial Settings. Look for the option “Job Cost Report: Labor Calculation” and change it to “Approved Estimate” and then click the blue button Save.

The next thing to do is to create the Estimate adding the Labor Items and assigning a Cost Code to each Labor Item with its perspective wage. See below picture as an Example.

When the Estimate gets approved, it will create the Project in Contractor Foreman allowing your field team to clock in into that Project, using the Cost Code given to that Project-Specific wage you want to have in the system.

heading: Can I get a report from Contractor Foreman factoring different rates?
body:
The quickest way to see your job cost reports of your projects, is to go to the Projects module, then click on the Reports option of the left panel.

Once here, you will have the freedom to see the different rates you have in a project, from the Wage Rate, Burden Rate, Billing Rate and the Rates set up by you using your Estimates and Cost Codes.

Remember that in the module Cost Items Database you can add the different rates you will have for your employees (laborers or field team) so you do not have to create them every time you add an Estimate.
Just go to the CIDB Module and once there, click on the tab Labor, then click on the “Select Option for Labor Items” drop down menu as shown below, and click on “Add Labor” to add the rate in there manually.
***Note that this is the way we can keep track of double time (Overtime Configuration).

You have a couple different options for configuring who should be allowed to make online payments. Project Level Approval

Within the Project Details, you have the ability to allow online payments for any invoice associated with that project. Invoice Level Approval

Within ‘Invoice > Settings’, you have three options for defining when an invoice can be paid online:

- Yes (All Invoices) = Online payments will be enabled for all invoices.
- Yes (Ask me per Invoice) = A checkbox will be shown allowing you to toggle online payments on/off per invoice.
- No = Paying online isn’t available (useful if the feature needs to be temporarily disabled). 2) Configuring the Invoice Template

2) Configuring the Invoice Template
Once integrated with Stripe, you’ll have a new element (enabled by default) within your template that causes the Pay Online option to appear in the Invoices that you send. It will also allow the client to pay an invoice through the Client Portal (if enabled). heading: Showing a Single Line Item per Change Order in Invoices
body:
By default, when adding Change Orders to an invoice, Contractor Foreman includes every line item from the Change Order.
However, some users prefer to display one single summarized line for each Change Order instead.
To consolidate Change Orders into one line per CO:

- Go to Settings → Change Orders .
- Under General Settings , click Edit (top-right corner).
- Locate and turn on the “Consolidate on Invoice” option.Once enabled, all future invoices will display a single line item per Change Order instead of showing all itemized entries.

heading: Step 1: Create the Schedule of Values (SOV)
body:
Once Retention is set, the next step is to create your Schedule of Values (SOV).
Read this article for more information: [Basics of Schedule of Values (SOV)]
To create the SOV:

- Go to your Project .
- From the left panel, select Schedule of Values .
- Click on Add Item to SOV .
- Choose Manual Project Item .
- Enter the description “ Total Value of the Project ” and set the total amount to $10,000.00 USD .

heading: How Do We Release the Retention?
body:
At the end of the Project, you can release the held Retention by creating a final invoice.

- Go to the Invoices Module .
- Click Add New Invoice .
- Click on the menu Add Item to Invoice .
- Select Add Retainage (Partial or Full) for Payment .A pop-up window will appear. Here, you can enter the percentage of Retention you wish to release.
In our example:

- The Project Retention was 10% of $10,000.00 = $1,000.00 USD .
- Enter “ 0 ” in the box to release all retained funds

body: Contractor Foreman is proud to be one of the only construction management software companies that provides its customers with a Price-Lock Guarantee. Your commitment to us means a lot and we will not raise the price you are paying just because we need to for new customers. Fun Fact: We still have customers who are paying the same rate as they did when we launched in 2017. What does that mean for you? Will my price change? When we have a price increase, the price paid by an existing customer will not change as long as their account remains active. What does that mean? If you signed up in 2021 and cancelled in 2023 and then signed up again after a price increase, you would have to pay the current advertised rate. If your account continues to remain active and you do not need to change your plan, you will continue to pay the same price. What if I need to upgrade? If you need to upgrade, you would need to select one of the plans that exist on the website at that time. If there is an announced price increase that will be taking place soon, it is recommend that you go ahead and upgrade before the price change. How do I upgrade? You can request an upgrade to your account from here.

heading: DRAFT
body: In the construction industry in the United States, the order in which you create a project and an estimate can vary based on the project management approach and the contractual arrangement with the client. Let’s break down the process for different project types:
text:
Knowledge Base > Do I set up a Project before the Estimate? :: DRAFT

In the construction industry in the United States, the order in which you create a project and an estimate can vary based on the project management approach and the contractual arrangement with the client. Let’s break down the process for different project types:
title: Do I set up a Project before the Estimate?

heading: Cost Plus Projects:
body:
Procedure: For cost-plus projects, where the final cost is not known upfront, it’s common to create the project first. This allows you to establish the project framework, including timelines, milestones, and overall scope. Once the project is defined, you can then work on the estimate based on the detailed project requirements. Additions or Scope added to the Project must be recorded by using Change Orders in Contractor Foreman.
Advantages: Creating the project first allows for better project planning and management. It provides a clear structure for all parties involved and helps in setting expectations.
Disadvantages: The disadvantage could be that you may need to revisit the project plan if the estimate significantly influences the scope or timeline.

heading: Fixed Cost Projects:
body:
Procedure: For fixed cost projects, where the project cost is predetermined, it’s common to start with the estimate. This involves detailed cost breakdowns and analysis to arrive at a fixed cost for the entire project. Once the estimate is agreed upon, the project is created based on the fixed cost.
Advantages: Starting with the estimate allows for precise budgeting and cost control. It helps in presenting a clear and fixed cost to the client from the beginning.
Disadvantages: The disadvantage could be that if there are changes to the project scope later on, it may impact the fixed cost, potentially leading to disputes.

heading: Time and Material (T&M) Projects:
body: Procedure: Time and material projects involve billing clients based on the time spent and materials used. In this case, you might create the project first to define the overall structure, and then estimate costs based on hourly rates and material costs. Advantages: Creating the project first allows for effective tracking of time and materials against a defined project structure. Using Contractor Foreman you have another bunch of advantages such as; setting up your Job Cost Report with the MLESO budget, setting up groups of Subcontractors and Vendors to create Subcontracts and Purchase Orders and having the ability to create theCMP Gantt Chart Schedule, among others. Disadvantages: The disadvantage is that clients might prefer fixed costs, and there could be challenges in presenting a clear estimate for T&M projects. In summary, the order of creating a project and an estimate can depend on the project type and management approach. For cost-plus projects, creating the project first is common, while for fixed cost projects, starting with the estimate is typical. For Time and Material projects, it might be a mix of both, with an emphasis on defining the project structure first.

heading: Work Orders :
body:
Purpose: Work Orders are documents used to authorize and track additional work that goes beyond the original scope of the contract. They may have a financial impact on the overall project cost.
Financial Impact: Work Orders often involve changes that can impact the contract amount. This could include additional work, modifications, or adjustments to the project scope, and they typically result in a change in the overall project cost.
Employee Assignment: Work Orders are commonly used to assign specific tasks or work items to employees or subcontractors. They provide clear instructions on what needs to be done as part of the additional scope.
Example Scenario: If during the construction process, the client decides to add a new room to a building, a Work Order would be created to document and authorize this additional work, along with any associated cost adjustments.

title: What is the difference between a Work Order and a Service Ticket?

heading: Service Tickets :
body: Purpose: Service Tickets are used to track specific services, often of a smaller scale, such as maintenance, repairs, or handyman-type tasks. They may not necessarily impact the overall contract amount. Financial Impact: Service Tickets may or may not have a financial impact on the project’s overall budget. They are often associated with routine or minor services rather than major changes to the project scope. Warranty Scope: Service Tickets can also be utilized to track warranty-related work. This involves addressing issues covered by the project’s warranty, ensuring that any necessary repairs or adjustments are documented. Example Scenario: If there’s a need for routine maintenance, such as fixing a minor plumbing issue or addressing a paint touch-up, a Service Ticket would be created to capture and monitor this specific task. In summary, Work Orders are typically associated with changes that impact the project’s overall cost and scope, often requiring approval and documentation of additional work. On the other hand, Service Tickets are more focused on tracking routine services, repairs, and warranty-related tasks that may not significantly alter the original contract amount.

heading: Draft
body:
Yes, you need to use Change Orders in construction for several important reasons:
Scope Changes: Change orders are necessary when there are changes to the original scope of work. They document any additions, deletions, or modifications to the project, ensuring clarity on what work is included. Financial Impact: Change orders outline the financial implications of any alterations to the project. They detail the cost adjustments associated with changes in materials, labor, or other factors, preventing disputes over payment. Contractual Agreement: Change orders serve as formal amendments to the original contract. They require approval from all parties involved, establishing a clear agreement on the revised scope and associated costs. Project Transparency: Change orders provide transparency and a clear record of project changes. This helps in tracking the project’s evolution, managing expectations, and avoiding misunderstandings among contractors, subcontractors, and clients. Risk Mitigation: Change orders help manage risks by ensuring that any deviations from the initial plan are documented and agreed upon. This reduces the likelihood of disputes and legal issues down the line.

In Contractor Foreman a Cost Code helps categorize costs in your estimates and projects. This is primarily used for tracking costs (budget vs. actual) and linking financial data to QuickBooks.
Example:
01010 – Site Preparation

04000 – Masonry

09300 – Tiling
A Cost Code consists of two parts:
Cost Code Number → The numeric or alphanumeric identifier (e.g., 01010)

Cost Code Name (or Description) → The work category it represents (e.g., Site Preparation)

Together, they form a Cost Code.

When you navigate to the Financials Tab within a project, you’ll immediately encounter two critical visual aids, Cost Comparison By Type and Financial Summary charts. These two charts offer a summary view of key financial metrics, but there is much more depth to explore beneath the surface. Cost Comparison By Type Chart
The first chart you’ll see is the Cost Comparison By Type, which provides a breakdown of the budgeted, committed, and actual costs categorized by item type. These categories are Material, Equipment, Labor, Subcontractor, Other, and Unassigned (which refers to items without a type attached). This chart serves as a visual comparison of how much has been budgeted versus how much has actually been spent, and it shows you what commitments have been made but not yet paid. The three columns displayed are:
Budgeted Costs – This is the total amount estimated for each type of item when the estimate was created. Committed Costs – These represent the costs that have been agreed upon but not yet paid. For example, this could include purchase orders that have been placed but not yet billed or subcontractor agreements that have been signed but not yet billed.

body:
Committed Costs – These represent the costs that have been agreed upon but not yet paid. For example, this could include purchase orders that have been placed but not yet billed or subcontractor agreements that have been signed but not yet billed. Actual Costs – This shows the actual expenses that have been incurred to date. By comparing these three figures, you can quickly identify areas where costs are exceeding the budget or where commitments have been made but not yet billed. These columns provide a much deeper dive into the project’s financial standing. For instance, the Remaining Committed and Remaining Actual columns show the difference between what was estimated or committed and what has actually been spent. The percentage columns (Remaining Committed % and Remaining Actual %) help quantify the remaining balance as a percentage of the estimated cost. Turning the Chart into a Table
For users who prefer to view this information in a table format, there’s an option to switch from the chart to a table by clicking the icon in the top-right corner of the chart. Once the table view is activated, more detailed columns will appear.

Turning the Chart into a Table
For users who prefer to view this information in a table format, there’s an option to switch from the chart to a table by clicking the icon in the top-right corner of the chart. Once the table view is activated, more detailed columns will appear. For each of these columns, there is an “i” icon next to it that provides additional details on where the data is coming from and how it is calculated. Estimated Cost – Total Estimated Cost (no markup) from Approved Estimate, SOV items, Approved Change Orders, Approved Work Orders, and Service Tickets that are related to the project. Committed Cost – This will pull data from Expenses, Purchase Orders (Approved, Paid, Submitted, Received), Sub-Contracts (Committed, Submitted, Approved), Time Cards, and Daily Log Equipment. Actual Cost – This will pull data from Bills (no markup), Expenses, Time Cards, and Daily Log Equipment. Remaining Committed – Difference between Estimated and Committed. Remaining Actual – Difference between Estimated and Actual. Remaining Committed % – (Remaining Committed*100)/Estimated Cost. Remaining Actual % – (Remaining Actual*100)/Estimated Cost.

body:
Converting the Financial Summary to a Table
Similar to the Cost Comparison chart, the Financial Summary can also be converted into a table for a more detailed view. For each of the column headings, hovering over the “i” icon provides further clarification on the data source and calculation methods:
1. Estimates Revenue – Items total with markup. 2. Estimated Cost – Items total without markup. 3. Estimated Profit – Total markup of items (Estimates Revenue – Estimated Cost). 4. Estimated Markup – (Estimated Profit*100)/Estimated Cost. 5. Estimated Margin – (Estimated Profit*100)/Estimated Revenue. The rows in this table are based on the original contract amount, change orders, work orders, service tickets, and the total project amount. Below these figures, you will also find details like the amount invoiced, amount paid, amount unpaid, retention held, remaining to the invoice, due in 30 days, and past due. This detailed breakdown helps not only track the project’s financial performance but also understand exactly where profits and costs are coming from.

Efficient financial management is crucial in the construction industry, and integrating Contractor Foreman with QuickBooks streamlines estimating and accounting processes. This article outlines the process of how an estimate transitions from Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks, ensuring a smooth transfer of financial data. Creating an Estimate in Contractor Foreman

The process begins by generating an estimate within Contractor Foreman. Estimates can include multiple sections and line items such as labor, subcontractors, materials, equipment, and other, what we call MLESO items.
https://kb.contractorforeman.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/GMT20251229-185600_Clip_Cesar-Macedos-Clip-12_29_2025.mp4
Since QuickBooks does not categorize line items in the same manner as Contractor Foreman, it is essential to ensure proper mapping. The cost codes used in the estimate must be predefined in both Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks to maintain consistency and accuracy. Cost Codes and Product Mapping
Contractor Foreman utilizes cost codes to categorize project expenses. These cost codes must be matched with the corresponding product and service items in QuickBooks.

While tracking salaried employees isn’t a direct feature in some project management or time-tracking software, you can still accurately account for their time and allocate costs using a simple workaround.
Start by calculating the employee’s hourly equivalent rate based on their annual salary. For example, divide the yearly salary by 2080 (standard full-time hours per year) to get their hourly rate. You can then apply this rate as either a burdened rate (including overhead, taxes, etc.) or a straight hourly rate for job costing.
Have your salaried employees clock in and out using time cards and assign their time to specific cost codes or tasks throughout the day. This ensures that every hour worked is documented and allocated properly to jobs, phases, or cost activities.

By doing this, you gain visibility into how much salaried labor is spent on each job or task. This not only improves your job costing accuracy but also helps in analyzing productivity and managing project budgets more effectively.

heading: Critical Requirements for Proper Synchronization and Job Costing in Contractor Foreman
body:
There is a critical caveat: for the bill to be fully usable within Contractor Foreman—especially for job costing purposes—it must be entered into QuickBooks in a very specific way.
When a bill is created in QuickBooks, the following general details are synchronized and appear correctly in Contractor Foreman:

- Supplier (interpreted as Vendor or Subcontractor in Contractor Foreman)
- Terms
- Bill Date
- Due Date
- Bill Number
These details ensure that the basic structure of the bill is captured accurately across both platforms.

- Item Details

title: How do Bills sync from QuickBooks to Contractor Foreman

heading: 1. Category Details – Not Recommended
body:
The Category Details section is the default and most commonly used method, especially by accountants. In this section, you select a general expense account (category) for each line item.

While bills entered using Category Details will still sync into Contractor Foreman, some information will be missing in Contractor Foreman:

- Item type always will be “Other”
- There is no unit cost and there is no QTY, by default QTY is 1 and Unit Cost is the total amount
- No units in QuickBooks, means no units in Contractor Foreman.
- No cost code.

With that in mind, there is a major issue:
No Cost Codes will transfer, and the bill will be locked in Contractor Foreman, meaning you won’t be able to edit or assign cost codes manually afterward.

This severely limits the ability to perform proper job costing and project financial tracking within Contractor Foreman.

body:
The second method is using the Item Details section. This is the preferred and recommended way to enter bills if you plan to integrate with Contractor Foreman.
Why?

- These Products/Services are mapped to your Parent and Child Codes in Contractor Foreman.
- When entered this way, each line item carries over with the correct quantity, rate, total, and most importantly, the Cost Code.

This structure allows Contractor Foreman to read and assign the data properly, giving you full access to itemized costs within the platform and enabling detailed job costing.

heading: Important Note About Sync Limitations
body:
While the sync between Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks is robust, there is one key limitation to be aware of:
We do NOT currently support syncing Bills from QuickBooks to Contractor Foreman if those Bills are associated with multiple Projects (i.e., split transactions are not supported).
This means if a single bill in QuickBooks is split between more than one project, it will not sync properly back into Contractor Foreman. However, if a Bill in Contractor Foreman is tied to one project, it will sync successfully with QuickBooks.

heading: Important Differences in Item Handling
body:
The most significant difference lies in how items are managed between the two systems:

- In Contractor Foreman , items are structured with a type (e.g., Material, Labor, Equipment, Subcontractor and Other), a name, and associated cost details.
- In QuickBooks , all items imported from Contractor Foreman appear under the Item Details section, not under Category Details .
This is critical to note, as many QuickBooks users are more familiar with entering bills using Category Details. The switch to Item Details may require a shift in workflow for some users.
Additionally:

- In QuickBooks, the Product/Service reflects the parent code and child code from Contractor Foreman.
- The Description matches the item name.
- Quantity and Rate transfer correctly, allowing QuickBooks to calculate the Amount (Quantity × Rate).
- The Customer field in QuickBooks is automatically populated with the project name from Contractor Foreman.

Step-by-Step in Contractor Foreman:

- Open the Bills Module in Contractor Foreman and locate the bill in question.
- Click on the 3-dot icon in the top-right corner of the screen.
- Select “Post a Payment” from the dropdown menu.
- Fill in the required payment details—amount, date, payment method, etc.
- Once saved, the payment will appear at the bottom of the bill screen.This payment will sync automatically to QuickBooks. The screenshot below shows how a posted payment is reflected on the bill in Contractor Foreman.

You can also record partial payments in Contractor Foreman. These will be noted as such, and the system will indicate that the payment was recorded in Contractor Foreman.
At the very bottom of the screen, you’ll also see a legend:
“Synced with QuickBooks”, along with the date, time, and a direct link to view the bill in QuickBooks.

When using Contractor Foreman integrated with QuickBooks, it’s possible to create estimates in QuickBooks and have them sync over to Contractor Foreman. While the integration works well, there are some important limitations to understand, especially if you’re used to creating lump-sum estimates in QuickBooks.
This article walks you through the full process, what transfers, what doesn’t, and how to get the most out of the integration.
*Contractor Foreman recommends creating the Estimate in Contractor Foreman and not in QuickBooks, see more information about workflows here.

When using Contractor Foreman integrated with QuickBooks, it’s possible to create estimates in QuickBooks and have them sync over to Contractor Foreman. While the integration works well, there are some important limitations to understand, especially if you’re used to creating lump-sum estimates in QuickBooks.
This article walks you through the full process, what transfers, what doesn’t, and how to get the most out of the integration.
*Contractor Foreman recommends creating the Estimate in Contractor Foreman and not in QuickBooks, see more information about workflows here.
title: How an Estimate Transfers from QuickBooks to Contractor Foreman

heading: Step 1: Create an Estimate in QuickBooks
body:
Start by creating a new estimate in QuickBooks using your preferred method. Be sure to include all the essential information:

- Customer
- Email
- Billing Address
- Estimate Date
- Expiration Date
- Estimate Number⚠️ Important: The Estimate Number must be unique. If that number has already been used in Contractor Foreman, the sync will fail.

heading: Limitations of QuickBooks → Contractor Foreman Estimate Sync
body:
QuickBooks doesn’t support several fields that are essential for fully utilizing Contractor Foreman’s estimating features. As a result, when the estimate is synced to Contractor Foreman:

- ❌ No Title is transferred (QuickBooks doesn’t have a title field)
- ❌ Item Type defaults to “Other” (no way to set this in QuickBooks)
- ❌ Units and Markups do not transfer (QuickBooks doesn’t support these)
- ✅ Item Names , Cost Codes , Quantity , Unit Cost , and Total all transfer seamlessly
- ✅ Attachments added in QuickBooks do transfer to Contractor ForemanAdditionally, while the estimate might show as Pending in QuickBooks, in Contractor Foreman it will automatically appear as Approved. However, no Project is created from the synced estimate unless done manually.

Once the estimate has synced to Contractor Foreman, open it and scroll to the bottom. There, you’ll find a legend:
“Synced with QuickBooks”, showing the date, time, and a link that takes you directly to the estimate in QuickBooks.

body:

heading: Step-by-Step: Creating an Invoice in QuickBooks
body:

- Billing Information
- Invoice Number
- Invoice Date
- Due Date
- Terms
- Add line items :

- In Contractor Foreman:

Parent Code = Product
Child Code = Services
Description in QuickBooks becomes the Item Name in Contractor Foreman
Quantity , Rate , and Amount all sync directly.
- Once all data is entered, click Save . ✅ This action triggers the sync automatically.

heading: Step-by-Step: Posting a Payment in Contractor Foreman
body:

Payment Amount

Payment Notes

Reference Number

All payments posted to this invoice

Payment dates, amounts, types, and statusesTip:You can post multiple payments to a single invoice if needed.
Each payment represents an income transaction— money your customer has paid you.

heading: Payment
body:
When a payment is received in Contractor Foreman, it is transferred to QuickBooks as a payment record. The payment includes the reference number, payment amount, customer name, payment method, and payment date. It is deposited into the same account selected in Contractor Foreman and remains linked to the corresponding invoice.
Additional details—such as the invoice due date, original invoice amount, open balance, and applied payment—are preserved during the sync. The payment description entered in Contractor Foreman is transferred to QuickBooks under the Memo field, ensuring full context is retained.
All information transfers seamlessly, allowing you to continue your accounting workflows in QuickBooks without interruption or manual re-entry.

heading: How to Create an Expense in QuickBooks
body:
Use your preferred method to create an expense within QuickBooks. Once you are inside the expense form, complete the following fields:

- Payee: This is the Vendor field in Contractor Foreman.
- Payment Method
- Reference NumberAfter these basic details are entered, you will encounter two sections:Category DetailsandItem Details. For the purpose of transferring expenses correctly to Contractor Foreman,you must use only the Category Details section, not the Item Details. WithinCategory Details, complete the following fields:

- Category: This will transfer as the Category in Contractor Foreman.
- Description: This will transfer as the Expense Name in Contractor Foreman.
- Amount: This will transfer as the Total Amount in Contractor Foreman.
- Customer: This will link the expense to the correct Project in Contractor Foreman.Memo:This will transfer as the Reason field in Contractor Foreman. Once all required information is entered, clickSave and Close. Allow approximately five minutes for the synchronization between QuickBooks and Contractor Foreman to occur. After the sync, you will find the expense available within Contractor Foreman.

When you open the expense in Contractor Foreman, you will notice that the following information successfully transfers:

- Project (linked through the Customer field in QuickBooks)
- Vendor (through the Payee field)
- Bank Account
- Expense Name (from the Description)
- Reason (from the Memo)
- Reference Number
- Total Amount
- CategoryHowever, you will also notice that some fields remain blank:

- Employee: This field remains empty because QuickBooks does not have a direct field for it during expense creation.
- Item Type: This field will not be populated, as expenses created in QuickBooks using Category Details do not define item types.
- Cost Code: As mentioned earlier, QuickBooks does not allow the entry of Cost Codes for expenses. It is a best practice to manually assign a Cost Code once the expense appears in Contractor Foreman to maintain accurate and organized job costing.
title: How Do Expenses Transfer from QuickBooks to Contractor Foreman

heading: Quick Recap
body:
- Use Category Details (not Item Details) when creating expenses in QuickBooks.
- Save and allow about five minutes for the sync to Contractor Foreman.
- Use the Transaction Log in Contractor Foreman to confirm the sync.
- Manually update the Cost Code inside Contractor Foreman for complete job costing data.By understanding this workflow, you can maintain a clean and synchronized financial system between QuickBooks and Contractor Foreman, ensuring your project costs are always accurate and up to date.

Understanding how Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks share project data is crucial for maintaining clean records and efficient job costing. This article explains how Projects are transferred between Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks, assuming the systems are properly integrated. How Projects Transfer from Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks
When you create a Project in Contractor Foreman, it automatically syncs to QuickBooks, but not as a standalone project. Instead, it appears as a sub-customer under the corresponding Customer in QuickBooks. Example:

If you have a customer named Michael Thompson in Contractor Foreman, and you create a project called 400 Boren – Time & Material, QuickBooks will register 400 Boren – Time & Material as a sub-customer of Michael Thompson Customer. What Gets Synced:
The project name and its relationship to the customer are the primary data points transferred. Address also syncs. Best Practices
Important: For best results and proper job-costing structure, it’s recommended to create all Projects directly in Contractor Foreman.

body:
Purchase Orders created in QuickBookscan sync to Contractor Foreman, but there are limitations that can affect accuracy—especially in job costing.

Important Note:
If you enter Purchase Orders directly in QuickBooks, you must use the Item Details section, not the Category Details.

Attention QuickBooks users. Intuit now requires that users that have access to the integration configuration settings to be automatically logged out after 30 minutes of inactivity. This change was recently rolled out and we do apologize for the delay in sharing this information. We do understand that this is frustrating, but it is a requirement from Intuit that we must follow. If you are not already doing so, you can use a password manager and set it to auto-login so that when you revisit the page, it will log you in automatically. To help minimize the inconvenience, we highly recommend using a secure password manager like LastPass. With LastPass, you can:
Store your QuickBooks credentials securely
Enable auto-login to save time and avoid repeated manual logins
Access your login information across devices
Maintain compliance with security best practices
By setting up auto-fill with LastPass, your credentials will be entered automatically when you revisit the login page, making the transition back into QuickBooks smooth and hassle-free. If you are not already using a password manager, this is a great time to start. LastPass offers both free and premium options, and it’s easy to set up.

Starting May 29, 2025, customers who signed up with Contractor Foreman prior to October 2024 will be moved to our new billing system.
On your credit card statement, the descriptor will be “PADDLE*CFAPP.AI“.
Paddle.com the merchant that is securely processing the payment. We are limited to 10 characters for the text that follows the * so you will see CFAPP.AI.
Once you are moved to Paddle, you will be able to manage your subscription from Settings > Subscription Details. From there, you can see your invoices (that generate after the switch), upgrade, downgrade, change card, etc.
We do not anticipate anything being needed from our customers as the subscription details will be moved from the old system to the new system. The renewal date will stay the same.
If you have any questions, contact billing@contractorforeman.com

Navigation: How to Access Bulk Markup Tool

- Go to the Main Menu

- Click on Cost Items Database

- Select an Item type

- In the top-right corner, click the dropdown menu

- Select Automatic / Bulk Markup

Purpose
The Bulk Markup feature allows you to apply or update markup percentages across multiple items at once, saving time and ensuring consistency across your pricing data.

When to Use This
Use the Bulk Markup tool when:

- You want to update markup across all Material , Labor , Equipment , Subcontractor , or Other items
- You’re adjusting pricing strategies across the board
- You want to standardize margins for an entire category or item type
- You’ve recently updated cost structures or pricing models
Tips

- This action overwrites the current markup values for selected items
- Changes apply immediately , so double-check your inputs before confirming
- You can export your Cost Items list before applying changes for backup

heading: Tips for Better Submittal Organization
body: A well-organized submittal system reduces confusion, enhances collaboration, and speeds up both internal and external reviews. Contractor Foreman offers multiple views and categorization tools to help you stay organized.

title: Submittals Settings, Revisions & Tips for Better Organization

heading: Use the Card View for Visual Clarity
body:
To improve visibility and distinguish between different types of submittals, you can switch to the Card View layout.
●Click the Card View icon at the top left of the Submittals module.

●This layout separates submittals into visual cards, allowing for an at-a-glance view of:

○Submissions – brand new or initial submittals

○Resubmissions – revised versions of previously rejected or updated submittals
Why use Card View?
It makes it easier to see which submittals are in progress, which are awaiting approval, and which are resubmitted versions, helping you keep a clean workflow and avoid duplication.

heading: Leverage Custom Fields for Tailored Tracking
body:
Every project has unique data requirements. Use Custom Fields to ensure that your submittals reflect the needs of your project team and stakeholders.
Examples of custom fields you can create:
●Location: Indicate which building area, floor, or section the submittal applies to

●Discipline: Useful for multi-trade projects (e.g., HVAC, Electrical, Plumbing)

●Urgency or Priority: Flag time-sensitive submittals for quicker processing

●Phase or Milestone: Link the submittal to a specific stage of construction (e.g., Rough-In, Final Install)

Pro Tip: Custom fields can also be used in filters and reports, giving you more powerful ways to search, sort, and analyze your submittals.

heading: Approval Workflow Flexibility: Optional Internal Step
body:
Contractor Foreman supports a flexible approval flow that can be adjusted based on your project or company policy.
By default, the submittal approval process includes an internal review step prior to sending documents to external parties. However, if your project team prefers to streamline this process, you have the option to bypass the internal-only step.

heading: Combined Approval Process Option:
body:
●Instead of sending to internal and waiting, you can release a submittal to both internal and external reviewers at the same time.

●This is particularly helpful when:

○You’re working under tight timelines

○Internal and external reviewers collaborate closely

○Your team is confident in the quality of the submission

While this can accelerate your approval timeline, be sure that all documentation is thoroughly reviewed before sending, since skipping internal review could increase the chance of revision requests later.

Change Order Request

body:
To begin, navigate to the Change Orders module and click on the + icon, then select Change Order Request. You’ll be prompted to complete a brief form with key details:

- Select Project (required): Start by choosing the correct project that this request is associated with. This ensures the COR is logged under the proper job and connected to all relevant project documentation.
- Choose the Customer: Next, identify who the request is being sent to—typically the owner, client, or general contractor. This person or company will be listed on the official documentation.
- Enter a Subject (required): Provide a clear and concise subject line that summarizes the nature of the requested change. This helps make the COR easy to identify later.
- Enter the COR # (required): Each Change Order Request must have a unique identifying number. This may auto-populate based on your numbering system or can be entered manually to maintain a sequence.
- Select the Date: Specify the date when the COR is being created.

Cost Items Database: Pull predefined materials, labor, or services directly from your Cost Items Database. This saves time and ensures consistency in your pricing and descriptions. Estimate: If the item was originally scoped in the estimate and now requires adjustment, import it directly to preserve continuity. Another Change Order Request: If the same or similar change was previously requested in another COR, you can pull it in to avoid re-entry. Another Change Order: Similarly, import from a past Change Order if you’re updating or extending previously approved changes.

Add Manual Change Order Items: Manually enter new items with custom descriptions, quantities, unit prices, and totals. This is useful for unique or one-off changes that aren’t stored in your database. Add Discounts: You can apply line-item or overall discounts to show goodwill, correct errors, or align with negotiated pricing.

body:
Saving a Change Order or Change Order Requests as a Template
If you find yourself repeatedly creating similar Change Ordersor Change Order Requests, perhaps for recurring work items, common scope changes, or standardized pricing, it can be helpful to save one as a template for future use. This not only saves time but ensures consistency in how you present and structure your Change Ordersor Change Order Requests. Once you’ve either created a new Change Order or Change Order Requests or opened an existing one, scroll down to the bottom of the record. There, you’ll find a checkbox labeled “Save as Template.”

- Check the box to save the current Change Order or Change Order Requests, including its structure, items, and settings, as a reusable template.
- After checking the box, simply save the Change Order or Change Order Requests as you normally would. Behind the scenes, Contractor Foreman will add that entry to your list of available templates. The next time you go to create a new Change Order or Change Order Request, you’ll see a “Use Change Order Template” dropdown menu in the creation form. Click the dropdown, and you’ll be able to select from the list of saved templates.

body: Cross-referencing a Change Order in an RFI (Request for Information) record is an important best practice in construction project management. It creates a direct, traceable link between a question raised during construction and any resulting change to scope, cost, or schedule.
text:
RFI & Notices > Why Do We Cross-Reference a Change Order in the RFI Record?

Cross-referencing a Change Order in an RFI (Request for Information) record is an important best practice in construction project management. It creates a direct, traceable link between a question raised during construction and any resulting change to scope, cost, or schedule.
title: Why Do We Cross-Reference a Change Order in the RFI Record?

heading: Why This Matters
body:
During a project, RFIs are often created because of:

- Missing or unclear information
- Conflicting plans or specifications
- Unexpected field conditions
- Design clarificationsThese clarifications can sometimes lead to impacts that must be formally documented through a Change Order—whether it affects the budget, schedule, materials, or scope of work.

During a project, RFIs are often created because of:

- Missing or unclear information
- Conflicting plans or specifications
- Unexpected field conditions
- Design clarificationsThese clarifications can sometimes lead to impacts that must be formally documented through a Change Order—whether it affects the budget, schedule, materials, or scope of work.
title: Why Do We Cross-Reference a Change Order in the RFI Record?

heading: How Cross-Referencing Helps
body:
By cross-referencing a Change Order inside the RFI record, you:

- Maintain clear documentation Connect the question with the resulting change for easy tracking.
- Avoid confusion or duplicate entries Anyone reviewing the RFI can immediately understand what changes occurred because of it.
- Improve transparency across teams Project managers, subcontractors, and office staff can see the full history of the issue.
- Support billing, audits, and dispute resolution If questions arise later, you have a clean paper trail showing why the Change Order was issued.
- Increase accountability It’s always clear who requested clarification, who authorized the change, and what decision was made.

Compliance Notice vs. Schedule Notice
Contractor Foreman includes two types of prebuilt notice forms designed specifically for formal construction project correspondence: Compliance Notices and Schedule Notices. While both are used to document issues and communicate expectations with subcontractors or vendors, they serve different purposes. Compliance Notice
Purpose:

A Compliance Notice is used to formally notify a subcontractor or vendor that their work is either not meeting contractual standards or is outside the agreed scope. It’s an essential tool for documenting performance issues, holding parties accountable, and giving them a chance to correct the problem before more serious steps, like back charges or change orders, are taken. When to Use:

Use a Compliance Notice when work being performed is:

- Out of Scope
- Out of Compliance with specifications
- Done with Poor Workmanship
- Not Meeting Contract Requirements
- Or when another issue arises (labeled as “Other”)Example Scenario:

Let’s say a subcontractor installs interior trim and stain, but the stain comes out blotchy and inconsistent. You notify them verbally, but they refuse to fix it.

body:
It also establishes a documented paper trail in case the issue escalates, protecting your company from financial or legal disputes. Schedule Notice
Purpose:

A Schedule Notice is used to communicate scheduling-related changes or problems that may affect project timelines. Whether it’s an unexpected delay or a proactive update, this notice ensures that all parties are aware of and can respond appropriately to shifting timelines. Types of Schedule Notices:

- Schedule Update – Used when a new schedule or adjustment needs to be shared immediately.
- Schedule Delay by Subcontractor – Sent when a subcontractor’s actions (or inaction) are causing delays.
- Schedule Delay by Weather – Used to formally document project delays due to weather events.Example Scenario:

You notice that the framing subcontractor is consistently two days behind schedule, which is starting to delay follow-up trades like plumbing and electrical. You send a Schedule Delay by Subcontractor notice along with a screenshot or export of the affected section of the schedule. This formally communicates the problem and serves as proof in case further action is needed.

Purpose
The Bill History feature in Contractor Foreman provides a clear, chronological record of all billing and payment activity tied to a specific Purchase Order (PO). It is especially useful for tracking:

- Partial payments
- Multiple invoice submissions
- Delivery-related billing
- Discrepancy resolutionBy viewing the Bill History, you gain full visibility into how much has been invoiced, paid, or remains outstanding, ensuring accurate financial reporting and supplier accountability. Why Use Bill History? In real-world job costing and procurement workflows, a single Purchase Order may span several billing cycles. Vendors may send invoices in phases, based on delivery, milestone completion, or progressive draws. The Bill History tab becomes a centralized ledger that helps you:

- Monitor how much of the PO total has been billed
- Verify past payments against delivery records
- Prevent overbilling or duplicate payments
- Support audits or disputes with documentation
Permissions Required
To access Bill History:

- You must have View Access to the Purchase Order module.
- To create or manage bills , you must have Billing or Admin permissions depending on company settings.

- Payment status

3. Review and Track Invoices Over Time

- As vendor invoices are received, your team can generate bills tied directly to the Purchase Order.

- Invoice Amount : The value of the invoice tied to the PO.
- Paid Amount : How much has been paid toward that invoice.
- Outstanding Balance : Any remaining amount left unpaid.
- Invoice/Payment Date : For chronological tracking.
- Bill Status : Draft, Submitted, Approved, or Paid.

Purpose
The Custom Tab in Contractor Foreman allows your organization to adapt the Purchase Order (PO) workflow to your unique operational or data-tracking requirements. Whether you need to track internal reference numbers, jobsite delivery windows, special vendor terms, or other non-standard information, the Custom Tab makes it possible to extend the PO form without altering the core structure of the system. What Is the Custom Tab? The Custom Tab is a configurable section within a Purchase Order where you can create and display user-defined fields. These fields are fully customizable and can be designed to capture any extra data that your team or project requires. Custom fields may include:

- Delivery Instructions – Specific times, staging notes, or access restrictions
- Warehouse Reference Codes – Useful for logistics coordination
- Internal Cost Codes – For alignment with accounting systems
- Compliance Indicators – Such as environmental approvals or insurance verifications
- Custom Status Tags – For tracking internal review stagesThese fields are visible inside each PO and can also be leveraged in reports or exports, depending on how your organization uses them.

Purpose
The Pricing Request feature in Contractor Foreman allows you to gather quotes from multiple suppliers before issuing a formal Purchase Order. This approach provides greater flexibility during the procurement phase and is especially helpful when you need to compare costs, negotiate terms, or validate budget estimates after bidding but before vendor selection is finalized. Rather than committing to one vendor up front, you can generate a single Pricing Request tied to a project, list the materials or services you need, and invite several suppliers to submit pricing proposals. Purpose:

To explain how to record additional amounts paid to employees (e.g., travel expenses, mileage, per diem) in Contractor Foreman without creating a Change Order or affecting the contract value. Background:

Occasionally, companies need to reimburse employees or pay additional fees for specific reasons that are not part of their regular payroll (e.g., travel, lodging, meals during a project). In Contractor Foreman, these costs can be recorded as Expenses assigned to the employee. This method ensures the cost appears in expense reports and job costing but does not show on the employee’s profile or alter the contract total. These expenses typically fall under Overhead & Profit (OH&P) and are not explicitly listed in the estimate unless marked as billable. Key Points to Remember:

- No Change Order is needed for these costs.
- Contract totals remain unchanged.
- Expenses will appear in the Expenses Report for accurate job cost tracking.
- The employee’s profile will not display the expense.
- Use the Billable toggle only if the cost will be invoiced to the client.
- Payments to employees are handled through payroll or accounts payable outside of Contractor Foreman.

Purpose:

To explain the recent improvements made to the employee clock-out process in Contractor Foreman, making it easier for Time Card admins to manage entries while reducing unnecessary modification requests. Background:

Previously, employees with modification privileges could unintentionally trigger change request emails when clocking out, creating additional work for Time Card admins. To streamline the workflow, the clock-out process has been updated. Employees now have clearer options and visibility into their recorded time, which helps prevent confusion and unnecessary adjustments. Key Points to Remember:

- Clock-out questions have been modified to simplify the process .
- Users with modification privileges will no longer send automatic change request emails when clocking out.
- Employees will now be explicitly asked whether they want to modify their time or simply clock out .
- The start and stop times are displayed on the clock-out screen for transparency.

Purpose
Contractor Foreman allows administrators and managers to track employee login activity, including when users log in, log out, or perform actions in different modules. This helps maintain accountability and provides visibility into user activity. Where to Find Login Activity
All employee login and activity records are stored under the Logs section in Settings. How to View Employee Logins

- Go to Settings

From the main menu, open Settings .

- Open Logs

In the Settings menu, select Logs .

- Filter and Search

Use the filters at the top to narrow results:

User – Select a specific employee. Module – Filter by module activity (e.g., Daily Logs, Time Cards, To-Do). Date Range – Select a custom range to view activity within specific dates.
- Review Activity Records

The log displays:

User – The employee name. Action – Example: Login, Logout, Created, Updated. Module Name – Where the action took place (e.g., Time Cards, Daily Logs). Record ID – The system reference number. Date & Time – When the action occurred.
- Export Data (Optional)

Click Export to CSV (top right of the log table) to download activity records for reporting or auditing purposes.

We’re excited to introduce a new feature for our Time Card administrators: the ability to make Cost Codes mandatory on all time cards.
This update helps reduce manual entry from the office by ensuring that employees select the correct cost code when filling out their time cards. With this feature, you can improve accuracy, reduce administrative work, and streamline reporting.

🔧 How to Enable Mandatory Cost Codes

- Navigate to Time Card Administration in your system settings.

- Look for the Cost Code Requirement option.

- Enable the setting to require a cost code on all submitted time cards.
- Save your changes.Once enabled, all users will need to select a cost code before submitting their time card entries.

Benefits of this Feature

- Ensures consistent and accurate reporting.
- Reduces the need for manual adjustments by admins.
- Saves time for office staff by preventing incomplete submissions.
- Helps align labor tracking with project budgets.

When working with files and photos in the system, there are two different types of limits to be aware of:

1. Files Displayed in PDF Templates (Forms, Estimates, Daily Logs, Invoices, etc.)

- The current limit is 120 files that can be shown or displayed on a single PDF.
- Exceeding this limit may cause errors when viewing, downloading, or emailing the PDF.
- Example: If you attach more than 120 photos to a Daily Log, the system may fail when generating the PDF. 2. Uploading Files and Photos into the System (Files and Photos Modules)

- Uploads are subject to two limits:

File size limit: 150 MB per upload. File count limit: Maximum of 50 files per upload.
- If either limit is exceeded, the upload will fail.
- Example: If you try to upload 75 photos at once, the system will not accept the upload. Key Takeaways

- Files in PDFs: Maximum of 120 files per PDF (e.g., daily logs, estimates, invoices).
- Uploads into system: Max 50 files per upload and 150 MB total.We recommend keeping within these limits to ensure smooth uploading, viewing, and PDF generation.

body: Adding and managing permits in Contractor Foreman ensures your projects stay compliant and organized. Here’s how you can create a new permit and why it matters.
text:
Permits > How to Add a New Permit?

Adding and managing permits in Contractor Foreman ensures your projects stay compliant and organized. Here’s how you can create a new permit and why it matters.
title: How to Add a New Permit?

heading: Creating a New Permit
body:
- Go to the Permits Module from your main menu.
- On the Permits Dashboard, click on + Permit .
- A popup window will open on the right. Fill in the following fields:

Project (mandatory) – Select the project the permit belongs to.

Permit # (mandatory) – Enter the official permit number.

Type (mandatory) – Identify the permit type (e.g., Electrical, Plumbing, Fire Marshall, Waterproofing). In order to add a new permit type, type it and hit enter.

Fee (optional) – Record the cost of the permit. Note: Fees do not feed into financials.

Agency – Indicate the issuing or inspecting authority (e.g., city inspections, fire marshal).

- Click Create Permit . You’ll be redirected to the Permit Record screen.

- Click Create Permit . You’ll be redirected to the Permit Record screen.

heading: Key Permit Record Fields (Details Tab)
body:
- Pulled Date – When the permit was issued. Useful for compliance timelines.
- Approved Date – Confirms the permit passed review and is valid.
- Expires Date – Tracks when the permit will no longer be valid.
- Must Be Pulled By Date – Deadline to secure the permit before work begins.
- Referenced Inspections – Links the permit to its related inspections for easy backtracking.

Overview
Understanding how tasks connect in a schedule is essential for keeping projects organized and on time. In Contractor Foreman, you can define dependencies, predecessors, and lead/lag times to control the sequence and timing of your project’s activities.
text:
Schedule > Schedule Dependencies

Overview
Understanding how tasks connect in a schedule is essential for keeping projects organized and on time. In Contractor Foreman, you can define dependencies, predecessors, and lead/lag times to control the sequence and timing of your project’s activities.
title: Schedule Dependencies

heading: What Are Schedule Dependencies?
body:
A dependency defines the relationship between two tasks — how the start or finish of one affects the other.
For example, you can’t begin painting until drywall installation is complete. Dependencies ensure your project flows logically and efficiently.
text:
Schedule > Schedule Dependencies :: What Are Schedule Dependencies?

A dependency defines the relationship between two tasks — how the start or finish of one affects the other.
For example, you can’t begin painting until drywall installation is complete. Dependencies ensure your project flows logically and efficiently.
title: Schedule Dependencies

heading: Types of Dependencies
body:
There are four main types of task dependencies in Contractor Foreman. Each defines a different relationship between two activities.

- Finish-to-Start (FS) – Most common type

Task B starts only after Task A finishes.

Example: You can’t pour concrete (Task B) until formwork is complete (Task A)
- Start-to-Start (SS)

Both tasks can start around the same time, but Task B can’t start until Task A has started.

Example: Excavation (Task A) and foundation preparation (Task B) may start together.
- Finish-to-Finish (FF)

Task B can’t finish until Task A finishes.

Example: Electrical and plumbing inspections often complete at roughly the same time.
- Start-to-Finish (SF) – Least common type

Task B can’t finish until Task A starts.

Example: Temporary power must remain active until permanent power installation begins.

title: Schedule Dependencies

heading: What Are Predecessors?
body:
A predecessor is the task that must occur before another one.
When you assign a predecessor in Contractor Foreman, the system automatically links both activities according to the chosen dependency type.
Example:
If “Drywall” lists “Framing” as its predecessor (Finish-to-Start), the drywall task will begin only after framing is completed.

heading: Lead and Lag Time
body:
Dependencies can be adjusted using lead or lag time to fine-tune your schedule:

- Lead Time → Allows tasks to overlap.

Example: Start painting 2 days before drywall is fully done (lead = –2 days)
- Lag Time → Adds a delay between tasks.

Example: Wait 3 days after concrete curing before starting framing (lag = +3 days)

Overview
The Contract Minus Costs value shows how much budget remains for a project after subtracting all incurred costs. It helps determine the project’s profitability and financial health in real time.
Formula
Contract Minus Costs = Contract Amount – Actual Costs
Breakdown

- Contract Amount : This total comes from the project’s Estimate , plus any Work Orders , Change Orders , and Service Tickets .
- Actual Costs : These include all expenses recorded through Time Cards , Expenses , Bills , and Equipment Timecards .Example
If a project’s total contract value (including approved changes) is $250,000 and the total cost incurred to date is $190,000, then:
Contract Minus Costs = 250,000 – 190,000 = $60,000 remaining

Where to Find It
You can view Contract Minus Costs in the Job Cost Detailed Report, located under:
Projects → Reports → Job Cost Detailed Report

This report summarizes contract values, costs, and remaining balances for each project.

Working with Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks offers a flexible two-way sync that allows companies to adapt the system to their internal processes. Because every construction company operates differently, there is more than one way to move data between both platforms.
However, after years of training thousands of users, we have identified one workflow that consistently delivers the fewest sync issues, the fastest processing time, and the cleanest financial data. This article outlines that recommended workflow.
Before we begin, it is important to clarify the following:
text:
Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks > Recommended Workflow to Work with Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks

Working with Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks offers a flexible two-way sync that allows companies to adapt the system to their internal processes. Because every construction company operates differently, there is more than one way to move data between both platforms.
However, after years of training thousands of users, we have identified one workflow that consistently delivers the fewest sync issues, the fastest processing time, and the cleanest financial data. This article outlines that recommended workflow.
Before we begin, it is important to clarify the following:
title: Recommended Workflow to Work with Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks

heading: Contractor Foreman does not provide training on how to use QuickBooks
body:
We are experts in Contractor Foreman, and our responsibility is to help you use our platform correctly and efficiently. While the integration allows both systems to communicate, we cannot advise on accounting practices or how QuickBooks should be applied to your specific financial processes, your accountant can guide you on those decisions. For QuickBooks-specific questions related to functions, workflows, accounting practices, or system behavior, please reach out to your QuickBooks accountant; Smart Business Solutions is also available for a fee if additional assistance is required.
What we can do is show you the proven, reliable way to work in Contractor Foreman so your information syncs cleanly to QuickBooks.

For QuickBooks-specific questions related to functions, workflows, accounting practices, or system behavior, please reach out to your QuickBooks accountant; Smart Business Solutions is also available for a fee if additional assistance is required.
What we can do is show you the proven, reliable way to work in Contractor Foreman so your information syncs cleanly to QuickBooks.
title: Recommended Workflow to Work with Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks

heading: Why We Recommend Working From Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks
body:
Although the integration supports two-way synchronization, the workflow that produces the best results has always been:

- Enter your operational data in Contractor Foreman.
- Allow Contractor Foreman to send that data to QuickBooks.This approach significantly reduces sync delays, manual re-entry, missing or duplicated records, and conflicts between systems. When records are created and completed in Contractor Foreman, they are transmitted to QuickBooks almost immediately, provided the data is entered correctly.

heading: Modules That Do Not Sync
body:
Some features in Contractor Foreman are operational, not financial, and therefore do not sync to QuickBooks. This is expected because QuickBooks does not have equivalent modules. Examples include:
• Daily Logs
• Punch Lists
• Safety Meetings
• RFIs
• Files & Photos
• Crew Schedule
These features can be used entirely inside Contractor Foreman without affecting the financial sync.

These features can be used entirely inside Contractor Foreman without affecting the financial sync.

heading: Step 1: Create an Estimate in Contractor Foreman
body:
Create your estimate in Contractor Foreman. Assign proper cost codes to every line item. Missing or incorrect cost codes are the most common cause of sync failures.
When the estimate is complete, change the estimate status to Approved.
The Approved status triggers the sync. Contractor Foreman sends the estimate to QuickBooks, and QuickBooks creates a Sub-Customer. You must manually convert this Sub-Customer into a Project in QuickBooks.
At the same time, Contractor Foreman automatically creates a Project when the estimate is approved.
At this point:

• You have a project created in Contractor Foreman
• You have converted the Sub-Customer into a Project in QuickBooks
With both projects established, you can begin creating commitments and managing financial transactions.

In Contractor Foreman, files are downloaded, not exported — but the process is very similar. You can easily download one or multiple files at once within the Files and Photos module.

·Go to the Files and Photos module from the main menu.

·Locate the project or folder containing the file(s) you want to download.

This article explains the basics of AIA contracts, a brief history of where they come from, how AIA invoicing works, and how to create AIA-style invoices inside Contractor Foreman. What Are AIA Contracts? AIA contracts come from the American Institute of Architects, which has been producing standardized agreements since the late 1800s. These documents are designed to:

- Create a consistent framework for construction contracts
- Reduce disputes
- Clarify responsibilities between owner, architect, GC, and subcontractors
- Standardize invoicing and progress reportingAIA billing is most commonly used on:

- Commercial construction
- Public projects
- Architect-led builds
- Jobs requiring formal progress billingThe most commonly referenced forms for invoicing are:

- AIA G702 – Application for Payment
- AIA G703 – Continuation SheetContractor Foreman does not reproduce copyrighted forms, but it does generate AIA-style invoices that mirror the structure, including schedule of values, percent complete, stored materials, and balance to finish.

Managing Roles and Security Settings in Contractor Foreman
Managing Roles and security settings in Contractor Foreman is a critical component of maintaining accurate permissions, protecting company data, and ensuring that employees access only the features required for their job responsibilities. Proper Role configuration prevents unauthorized edits, reduces operational risk, and promotes efficient workflows by providing each user with an interface tailored to their function within the organization. What Are Roles? Roles in Contractor Foreman define the level of access a user has throughout the system. Each Role determines whether a user can view, create, edit, or delete records across all modules, including Estimates, Projects, Timecards, RFIs, Daily Logs, and more. Roles allow administrators to control permissions at a granular level, ensuring that employees see only what is necessary to perform their assigned duties. Roles are directly connected to the Directory, where each employee is assigned a specific Role. Once a Role is assigned, all permissions defined in the Role are automatically applied to that user.

In Contractor Foreman, managing your subscription’s user capacity is straightforward and directly tied to operational efficiency. The platform counts users based on those with active login access, ensuring your plan aligns with the number of team members who need to interact with the system. This approach prevents overages while allowing flexibility for your crew’s size, helping you avoid unexpected costs as your projects scale. Understanding User Counting in Subscriptions
User limits are enforced per subscription plan to balance accessibility with resource allocation. Only individuals granted login credentials contribute to the count, meaning inactive or external collaborators without accounts do not impact your quota. This method promotes precise team management, where you can onboard foremen, estimators, or admins as needed without inflating numbers unnecessarily. The core principle is simple: The user number is counted based on the number of users that have access to login to the app. Every account has a limit on how many users can be created, and the more employees have login access, the count drops according to the plan you have.

Understanding the user limits tied to your subscription plan is essential for scaling your team effectively within Contractor Foreman. This flexibility allows construction businesses of varying sizes to select a tier that matches their workforce without overcommitting resources or underutilizing features. By aligning your plan with your operational needs, you ensure seamless access for all team members while optimizing costs. Overview of Subscription Plans and User Limits
Contractor Foreman structures its pricing around plans that directly correspond to the number of active users, providing clear scalability as your projects grow. This tiered approach accommodates everything from small crews to large enterprises, with each level unlocking progressively more users alongside core platform capabilities like project management, scheduling, and invoicing. The number of users that can be created depends on the plan you select. Options include limits of 3, 8, or 15 users, as well as unlimited access, tailored to your specific requirements.

- Standard Plan : Supports up to 3 users, ideal for solo operators or small teams just starting out.

body:
Accessing the Directory displays a comprehensive list of current contacts, allowing quick searches or additions that integrate directly with scheduling, time tracking, and project assignments across the platform. Create a New Contact
With the Directory open, initiate the addition of a basic profile. This foundational step captures essential details, transforming a simple entry into a robust record ready for user elevation, ensuring all subsequent features—like timecards or notifications—leverage accurate information from the outset.

- Click the + Contact button at the top right of the page. The + Contact button launches a form optimized for quick input, focusing on core identifiers to expedite setup without overwhelming optional fields.
- Select the contact type, such as employee or contractor. Choosing the appropriate type—employee for internal staff or contractor for external collaborators—applies relevant defaults, like payroll integrations or vendor associations, aligning the record with operational contexts.
- Enter basic information, including name and contact details; complete all required fields marked with an asterisk (*).
