Adding or updating your email signature in Contractor Foreman ensures that every message sent from the platform—whether from estimates, invoices, change orders, or general correspondence—carries a consistent, professional closing. This signature automatically appends to outbound emails, reinforcing your branding and providing recipients with immediate contact details without requiring manual entry each time. Access Your Personal Settings
The email signature is managed at the individual user level, giving each team member control over their own professional sign-off while maintaining uniformity across the company when desired.

- From the main navigation Menu , select Settings . The Settings module serves as the central location for all personal account adjustments, including communication preferences that affect how you interact with clients and team members.

- Click on My Details in the left sidebar. My Details opens your personal profile page, where user-specific customizations such as contact information and communication settings are consolidated for easy access. Locate and Edit the Email Signature
Once in My Details, scroll to the dedicated signature field.

title: How Do I Set or Edit My Email Signature?

body:
My Details opens your personal profile page, where user-specific customizations such as contact information and communication settings are consolidated for easy access. Locate and Edit the Email Signature
Once in My Details, scroll to the dedicated signature field. This placement keeps the feature readily available without cluttering the interface, ensuring quick updates as roles or contact details change.

- Scroll down to the Email Signature section. The Email Signature area features a rich text editor that supports formatting, links, and basic styling—ideal for creating a polished, multi-line signature that reflects your professional identity.
- Enter or modify your signature using the built-in editor. You can include your name, title, phone number, website, or even a short tagline. The editor allows bolding, italics, hyperlinks (e.g., to your company site), and line breaks to achieve a clean, organized layout.
- Click Save at the bottom of the page to apply the changes. Saving instantly activates the updated signature across all future emails sent from within Contractor Foreman, with no delay or additional confirmation required.

title: How Do I Change the Color Theme for the Templates?

body:
Templates houses branding and appearance options that influence how your company is represented in system-generated materials. Modify the Color Theme
Within Templates, locate the dedicated control for template theming. This streamlined interface makes it simple to update the look of all PDFs in one action.

- Find the field labeled Header Text Color & Header Background Color . The Header Text Color & Header Background Color option determines the primary accent color used in headers, borders, buttons, and other design elements throughout every PDF template.
- Click the color picker or enter a hex code to select your desired color. Choose a color that matches your logo or brand guidelines (e.g., #003366 for a deep navy or #E63946 for a bold red). The change previews instantly and applies to all existing and future templates.
- Click Save at the bottom of the page to commit the update. Saving immediately activates the new theme across the entire account, so the next time any user generates a PDF—from an invoice, change order, or certificate of insurance—the updated color scheme will appear automatically.

In Contractor Foreman, Assigned Projects and Default Projects serve as powerful filtering mechanisms to streamline visibility and focus your team’s attention on relevant data alone. By limiting views to specific projects, these tools reduce clutter, enhance productivity, and prevent accidental access to unrelated information—ideal for supervisors overseeing select sites or subcontractors collaborating on isolated jobs. However, they require careful application: avoid assigning or defaulting projects to admins or users who need broad access, as this can inadvertently hide essential records like estimates or invoices tied to unassigned areas. Understanding Default Projects
The Default Project acts as a persistent filter in your personal view, automatically narrowing all modules—such as estimates, timecards, or schedules—to data from one designated project. This setup is particularly beneficial for prolonged engagements on a single site, where immersion in project-specific details minimizes navigation errors and speeds up daily tasks. Once activated, the system exclusively surfaces content linked to that project, ensuring a tailored dashboard without manual adjustments each session.

Assigned Projects extend the filtering concept to individual users, granting targeted visibility to prevent information overload and enforce role-based access. For instance, assigning a handful of projects to a site supervisor ensures they interact only with pertinent records, safeguarding sensitive details from unrelated personnel. This is especially useful for subcontractors, who benefit from a streamlined interface focused solely on their contributions, or for teams in multi-site operations where cross-project confusion could lead to errors. Administrators should exercise caution: never assign projects to yourself or full-access users, as this can obscure newly created items if they’re linked to unassigned projects, creating the illusion of “vanished” data. The records remain secure and accessible—just temporarily filtered from view. To configure Assigned Projects, navigate to the user’s profile for precise, user-specific adjustments. This directory-based workflow integrates with broader personnel management, allowing admins to align access with evolving team roles.

- From the main navigation Menu , select Directory .

Managing your Contractor Foreman subscription—from viewing essential account information to initiating upgrades or cancellations—is handled exclusively through the Account Details section. This centralized area ensures that only authorized personnel, specifically the primary contact, can make critical changes, safeguarding your plan’s integrity while providing transparent insights into billing, usage, and status. Whether you’re scaling your team with a higher tier or preparing to wind down, this feature streamlines administrative tasks, applying adjustments with prorated fairness to align with your business needs. Accessing Account Details
The Account Details section is tucked away in the Settings module, designed for quick reference by the account’s primary contact. This placement keeps sensitive subscription controls separate from everyday project tools, promoting focused management without cluttering your workflow.

- Open the Menu . The Menu serves as your platform’s navigational backbone, offering one-tap access to all modules and configurations from any screen.
- Select Settings .

Adding files to folders in the Files and Photos module is quick and easy.
Follow these steps:

- Go to the Files and Photos module from the main menu.

- Open the project and then the folder where you want to upload your files.

- Once inside the folder, you have two options to add files:
- Drag and Drop: Simply drag files from your computer and drop them into the upload area labeled “Drag and drop files or to browse.”
- Browse and Upload: Click the upload area or the “+ Add New Files” button to open your file browser and select the files you want to upload.

- Your selected files will begin uploading automatically and will appear in the folder once complete.

Tip: Every folder in the Files and Photos module has the same upload options, so you can easily add files from anywhere within the module.
That’s it! You’ve successfully added files to a folder in Contractor Foreman.Adding files to folders in the Files and Photos module is quick and easy.

In Contractor Foreman, files are downloaded, not exported — but the process is very similar. You can easily download one or multiple files at once within the Files and Photos module.
Follow these steps:

- Go to the Files and Photos module from the main menu.

- Locate the project or folder containing the file(s) you want to download.

- Select the file(s):
- Hover over each file and check the box in the top left corner, and/or
- Use the Select All option to choose all files within that folder.

- Once selected, several options will appear at the top of the screen.
- Click on the Download Zip button.
- A ZIP file will be generated, and you’ll receive an email with the download link once it’s ready.

Tip: You can download files from within a project, a specific folder, or even across multiple projects.
That’s it! Whether you’re downloading one file or many, the process is quick and simple.

body:
How do I move files from one folder to another within Files and Photos?

Important: Only copies of the files can be moved to different folders, since the original files are unchangeable records. Within the system, you will be able to create copies if needed.

To move files between folders in the Files and Photos module, follow these steps:

- Go to the main menu and open the Files and Photos module.

- Locate the project where your files are stored. On the left-hand side of the screen, you’ll see a list of all your projects. Click on the project of your interest.

- Once inside the project, open the folder that contains the file(s) you want to move.
- Hover over the file and click the checkbox in the top left corner of the file preview.
- After selecting one or multiple files, several action buttons will appear at the top of the screen.
- Click on Generate a Copy for the selected file.

- Select the folder where you would like to store the copy of the document.
- Choose the destination folder where you want to move your file(s), and confirm the action.

- And this is how we can move the copies generated from other documents.

Deleting a file in Files and Photos is simple. Follow these steps:

- Go to the Files and Photos module from the main menu.

- Locate the project or folder containing the file(s) you want to delete.
- Locate the file you want to delete within the Files and Photos module.

- Hover your cursor over the file. You’ll see a small checkbox appear in the top-left corner of the file.
- Select the file by checking the box.

- Once selected, a new toolbar will appear below the blue banner (where your company name is displayed).
- On the right-hand side of that toolbar, you’ll see several options — such as Copy , Move , Email , Download Zip , Email Zip File , Delete , and Save .
- Click on the trash bin icon (Delete) to remove the file. Deleting multiple files
To delete multiple files at once:

- Continue checking the boxes next to each file you wish to delete.
- Alternatively, click Select All (top-left corner below the “Files and Photos” title) to select all files in that folder.
- Then click Delete to remove them all at once.

body:
Deleting multiple files
To delete multiple files at once:

- Continue checking the boxes next to each file you wish to delete.
- Alternatively, click Select All (top-left corner below the “Files and Photos” title) to select all files in that folder.
- Then click Delete to remove them all at once. Important Notes

- You can only delete files that were uploaded directly to the Files and Photos module .
- If you try to delete a file that was uploaded through another module (e.g., Submittals , Estimates , or Projects ), you’ll receive a message stating that the file is associated with another record and cannot be deleted here .

- To delete those files, go to the original module where they were uploaded (e.g., Submittals, Estimates, or Projects) and follow the same steps there.You can identify where a file was uploaded by checking the tag displayed under the file thumbnail — for example:

- A tag that says Project means it was uploaded under the Project module.
- A tag that says Estimate means it was uploaded under the Estimates module. Only files uploaded directly in Files and Photos can be deleted from this module.

You can easily search for files and photos in Contractor Foreman, but it’s important to know where this feature is available. The search function is currently available in the main Files and Photos module, not inside the Project-level Files and Photos section.

Steps to Search for a File

- Go to the Files and Photos module from the left-hand menu.

- At the top-left corner of the screen, you’ll see a search bar .
- Type in any keyword, tag, note, or part of the file name related to the document you’re looking for.
- The system will instantly display all matching files, helping you locate your document quickly.

Important Note
At this time, the search bar is not available within the Files and Photos section inside a specific Project.
If you want to search for a file related to a project, use the main Files and Photos module instead. This will still display all files across projects, allowing you to find what you need much faster.

Tip
Use clear file names, tags, and notes when uploading documents — this will make them easier to locate later using the search bar.
text:
Files and Photos > How do I search for a file within a specific Project?

You can easily search for files and photos in Contractor Foreman, but it’s important to know where this feature is available. The search function is currently available in the main Files and Photos module, not inside the Project-level Files and Photos section.

Steps to Search for a File

- Go to the Files and Photos module from the left-hand menu.

- At the top-left corner of the screen, you’ll see a search bar .
- Type in any keyword, tag, note, or part of the file name related to the document you’re looking for.
- The system will instantly display all matching files, helping you locate your document quickly.

Important Note
At this time, the search bar is not available within the Files and Photos section inside a specific Project.
If you want to search for a file related to a project, use the main Files and Photos module instead. This will still display all files across projects, allowing you to find what you need much faster.

Tip
Use clear file names, tags, and notes when uploading documents — this will make them easier to locate later using the search bar.
title: How do I search for a file within a specific Project?

body: A step-by-step guide that connects the software to the real-world construction process.

A step-by-step guide that connects the software to the real-world construction process.

heading: Think of Contractor Foreman like building a house.
body:
Before pouring concrete, installing drywall, or scheduling crews, there’s a plan, a price, and a process. Contractor Foreman follows that same logic, step by step, just like a successful project in the field.
The workflow shown in the diagram is not just a list of modules, it’s the natural lifecycle of a construction job, from the first phone call with a potential customer to the final invoice and inspection.

Before pouring concrete, installing drywall, or scheduling crews, there’s a plan, a price, and a process. Contractor Foreman follows that same logic, step by step, just like a successful project in the field.

heading: 1. Customer Relationship Management (CRM): Finding the Job
body:
Construction always starts with someone needing work done.
In Contractor Foreman, that starts with a Lead, a potential customer. Leads can be:

- Entered manually
- Captured through the website lead form
- Imported using a templateFrom there, you can create:
A To-Do list
Follow-ups (Task Activities)
An Opportunity (meaning this job has potential)
This keeps your sales process organized instead of relying on memory, sticky notes, or text messages.

This addition allows teams to more accurately track inspection timelines, maintain clearer project documentation, and ensure that inspection tasks are completed within the expected schedule. These changes represent the first phase of broader upgrades that will continue into the next release cycle. The goal is to make the Inspections module more intuitive, more flexible, and better aligned with the evolving needs of field and office personnel.

body: The Q4 2025 release introduces a new Bulk Action Toolbar within the Estimates module, designed to significantly reduce the time required to manage and update estimate line items. This enhancement allows users to modify multiple items simultaneously, eliminating the need for repetitive, item-by-item edits when applying the same change across several rows. When more than one estimate item is selected, the Bulk Action Toolbar automatically appears and opens a focused editing panel. Rather than exposing all editable fields at once, users first select which field they want to modify. This approach reduces the risk of accidental changes while maintaining speed and precision. Supported fields include item name, cost code, quantity, unit cost, unit, and assignee. Once a value is applied, the update is immediately reflected across all selected items. There is no delay, batch processing step, or additional confirmation screen. This makes the feature particularly effective when refining pricing, updating assignments, or correcting quantities on larger estimates.

Creating bid packages from estimates is now faster and more efficient with the ability to generate bid packages directly from the Bulk Action Toolbar. This enhancement allows users to convert selected estimate items into a bid package without leaving the estimate or manually reselecting items in a separate workflow.
Users can multi-select the relevant estimate items and initiate bid package creation in just a few clicks. The selected items are immediately loaded into a new bid package, preserving their values and structure. This reduces setup time and minimizes the risk of missing or duplicating items during bid preparation.

This update is especially beneficial for estimates that contain multiple subcontracted scopes, as it allows estimators to remain focused within the estimate while preparing bid packages quickly and accurately.

body:

If an error occurs, users can easily review the history and correct the entry while maintaining full accountability.

This enhancement ensures that all bid data can be accurately captured and audited within Contractor Foreman, even when submissions originate externally.

body:
Effective coordination between Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) trades is not optional—it is essential to keeping construction projects on schedule, within budget, and running efficiently in the field.
In this webinar, MEP Coordination and Trade Sequencing, we explore real-world jobsite scenarios where poor coordination and incorrect trade sequencing led to delays, wasted labor, rework, and unnecessary friction between teams. The goal is not to assign blame, but to understand where coordination typically breaks down and how to prevent small issues from turning into major project disruptions.

body:

This includes:

- Identifying which trade must start first
- Understanding dependencies between activities
- Ensuring prerequisite work is fully complete before the next trade beginsWhen sequencing is unclear:

- Trades block each other physically
- Installed work must be removed to allow access
- Decision-making becomes reactive and stressfulSuccessful sequencing is about visualizing workflow, not just listing tasks.

body:

heading: Step 6: Manually Calibrate the Scale
body:
To manually calibrate the scale:

- Exit the measurement tool.
- Click the blue Calibrate Scale button.
- Zoom in as needed and place the first point precisely at one end of a known dimension.
- Place the second point at the opposite end of that same dimension.
- Enter the exact dimension value (for example, 9 feet, 0 inches ) and click Save .

Automatic takeoffs are designed to accelerate the estimating process by identifying quantities directly from uploaded drawings. However, accuracy does not come from automation alone, it comes from understanding how those takeoffs are generated and applying a structured review process.
This article explains how automatic takeoffs are created and how to properly evaluate, adjust, and validate the results before using them for estimating.
title: Understanding Automatic Takeoffs & Reviewing Auto-Generated Takeoffs

heading: How Automatic Takeoffs Are Created
body:
For this example, the drawing Extended Design – First Floor Plan (A1.1X) is opened inside the takeoff tool in Contractor Foreman.
As soon as drawings are uploaded, the system analyzes the plan and automatically generates three primary groups within the Legend:

- Spaces
- Objects
- WallsThese groups are created based on how the software interprets drawing boundaries, symbols, and annotations. No manual input is required at this stage.

heading: Footprint
body:
When the Footprint option is enabled, the system displays what it believes to be the total project area. This boundary is generated by identifying the outer limits of the structure on the drawing.
The footprint provides a fast baseline, but it is only a starting point. It must always be reviewed.
In this example, part of the front porch or deck is either partially included or excluded. This indicates that the automatic takeoff needs adjustment.

heading: The Review Mindset: Supervision, Not Rebuilding
body:
Automatic takeoffs change the workflow. You are no longer starting from scratch, you are supervising work that has already been done.
A best practice is to:

- Turn off all detected elements
- Enable them one at a time
- Review each item criticallyThis approach makes errors easier to identify and correct.

A best practice is to:

- Turn off all detected elements
- Enable them one at a time
- Review each item criticallyThis approach makes errors easier to identify and correct.
title: Understanding Automatic Takeoffs & Reviewing Auto-Generated Takeoffs

heading: Reviewing Rooms Individually
body:
Each room should be reviewed on its own.

- Unknown Rooms Some areas may be labeled as Unknown . By reviewing their location and context, these can often be identified correctly—for example, a closet—and renamed accordingly.
- Non-Usable Spaces Areas identified as rooms may actually represent shelving, mechanical zones, or other non-usable spaces. These should be corrected or excluded as needed.
- Boundary Overlaps In some cases, a room boundary may extend slightly into an adjacent area, such as a hearth or transition zone. These overlaps must be adjusted to reflect true usable space.
- Stairs and Exclusions Stair areas are commonly excluded from usable floor area calculations. If stairs are detected as rooms, they should be reviewed and modified to match estimating standards.
This step-by-step validation ensures that each space accurately represents what will be measured and priced.

Automatic takeoffs provide speed, but accuracy comes from review.
By understanding how the system interprets drawings and carefully validating each detected element, you avoid:

- Incorrect quantities
- Overstated areas
- Missed exclusionsThe most reliable takeoffs result from combining automation with informed human supervision.

heading: Using the Search Elements Function
body:
The Search Elements function is designed to identify repeating symbols on drawings that may not be detected automatically.
In this example, the drawing A1.4X – Extended Design, First Floor RCP Electrical is used. Electrical plans often include symbols, such as outlets or devices, that vary in appearance and are not always captured during automatic takeoff generation.

heading: How Search Elements Works
body:
- Activate the Search Elements tool.
- Select a representative symbol directly from the drawing, such as a GFCI outlet .
- Confirm the symbol selection.
- Click Search .
The system scans the entire drawing, finds matching symbols, and highlights them automatically. All detected elements are added to a new group in the Legend.
The newly created folder can be renamed, for example, GFCI, to clearly identify the item type.
This approach replaces manual, one-by-one selection and significantly reduces time spent on symbol-based takeoffs.

heading: Article: Managing Scope Change & Cost Control — Turning Small Site Changes Into Controlled Outcomes
body:
Construction projects rarely unfold exactly as drawn. Even the most detailed plans cannot anticipate every field condition, weather delay, design clarification, or owner request. Variability is not the exception in construction — it is the norm.
The real question is not whether scope will change.
The question is: How are you managing it?

heading: The Hidden Danger of Scope Drift
body:
Scope drift does not happen overnight.
It happens gradually:

- One outlet moved.
- A minor plumbing reroute.
- A “quick” material substitution.
- A verbal direction to keep work moving.Individually, these changes feel small. Collectively, they can significantly impact:

- Labor hours
- Material costs
- Subcontractor expenses
- Schedule duration
- Cash flow timingWhen these changes are not documented properly, the result is predictable:

- Budget overruns
- Disputes over payment
- Reduced profitability
- Strained client relationshipsMany project managers have experienced this:
Work is executed quickly to maintain schedule momentum, but the paperwork lags behind. Weeks later, nobody clearly remembers who approved what — and whether it was billable.
That is where cost control begins to break down.

body:
In the field, speed matters. Superintendents want progress. Clients want responsiveness. Subcontractors want clarity.
But verbal instructions without documentation create risk.
When changes are:

- Not tracked immediately
- Not tied to a formal change order
- Not associated with cost codes
- Not logged in daily reportsThey become invisible cost leaks.
The discipline required is simple in theory but difficult in practice:

- Capture the change immediately.
- Document the reason.
- Tie it to cost impact.
- Communicate alignment with all stakeholders.
- Track it through approval and billing.Without a structured system, this process becomes inconsistent — and inconsistency is expensive.

heading: Cost Control Is Proactive, Not Reactive
body:
Many teams try to “fix” cost problems after the fact. By the time reports show a budget overrun, it is often too late to recover.
Effective cost control requires:

- Real-time visibility
- Clear cost coding
- Structured documentation
- Defined workflows for change managementWhen scope changes are tracked as they happen, project managers can:

- Evaluate financial impact immediately
- Adjust forecasts
- Protect margins
- Maintain schedule alignmentThe goal is not to eliminate change — that is impossible.
The goal is to control change before it controls your project.

This feature is particularly useful for teams that already store plans, photos, and documents in Dropbox and want to bring those files into Contractor Foreman without duplicating effort.
This article explains how the Dropbox integration works and clarifies the synchronization behavior.
title: Dropbox Integration in Contractor Foreman: Sync Behavior and File Management

heading: Connecting Dropbox to Contractor Foreman
body:
Within the Files and Photos module, users have the option to connect their Dropbox account. Once connected, you can browse your Dropbox folders and select files to upload directly into Contractor Foreman.
This eliminates the need to manually download files from Dropbox and re-upload them into the platform.
text:

Within the Files and Photos module, users have the option to connect their Dropbox account. Once connected, you can browse your Dropbox folders and select files to upload directly into Contractor Foreman.
This eliminates the need to manually download files from Dropbox and re-upload them into the platform.
title: Dropbox Integration in Contractor Foreman: Sync Behavior and File Management

heading: Sync Direction: One-Way Integration
body:
It is important to understand that the Dropbox integration in Contractor Foreman operates as a one-way sync:

- Files are transferred from Dropbox into Contractor Foreman
- Changes made within Contractor Foreman do not sync back to DropboxThis means Contractor Foreman acts as the destination for files selected from Dropbox, rather than a bi-directional synchronization tool.

title: Dropbox Integration in Contractor Foreman: Sync Behavior and File Management

heading: What This Means for Users
body:
Because the integration is one-way, users should consider the following:

- Source of truth : If you need files to remain updated in Dropbox, any edits or updates must be managed directly within Dropbox
- No automatic updates : Updating or replacing a file in Contractor Foreman will not update the original file stored in Dropbox
- Manual re-uploads : If a file is revised in Dropbox, it must be re-uploaded into Contractor Foreman to reflect the latest version

text:
Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks > Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks Integration: What Syncs and What Doesn’t

Once you connect Contractor Foreman to QuickBooks, data starts flowing between the two systems automatically — but not everything syncs, and not everything syncs in both directions. Here’s a plain-language breakdown.
title: Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks Integration: What Syncs and What Doesn’t

heading: What DOES Sync
body:
Contacts:Contacts sync in both directions. A customer or vendor created in either system will appear in the other. Updates to contact information also carry over. Invoices:Invoices sync both ways. Create an invoice in Contractor Foreman and it pushes to QuickBooks. Invoices created in QuickBooks can also come into Contractor Foreman. Invoice Payments: Payments posted against invoices sync in both directions. Record a payment in Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks gets updated — and vice versa. Bills:Bills sync both ways between the two systems. A bill created in Contractor Foreman transfers to QuickBooks, and bills entered in QuickBooks flow back to Contractor Foreman.Important:It’s strongly recommended to create bills in Contractor Foreman, not QuickBooks, to keep your job costing accurate. Expenses: Expenses created in Contractor Foreman transfer to QuickBooks
Estimates:Estimates can transfer in both directions, but they function differently in each system. An estimate created in Contractor Foreman will transfer to QuickBooks, and a QuickBooks estimate can come into Contractor Foreman.

Overview
In some cases, required materials or components—such as wiring, conduit, or low voltage cabling—may not be explicitly shown on project drawings. Contractor Foreman allows users to account for these items by manually defining assumptions or incorporating them into the takeoff process using a combination of drawing inputs and prompt-based logic.
text:
Takeoff > How do I generate a takeoff for items not shown in the drawings?

Overview
In some cases, required materials or components—such as wiring, conduit, or low voltage cabling—may not be explicitly shown on project drawings. Contractor Foreman allows users to account for these items by manually defining assumptions or incorporating them into the takeoff process using a combination of drawing inputs and prompt-based logic.
title: How do I generate a takeoff for items not shown in the drawings?

body:
Contractor Foreman allows users to account for these items by manually defining assumptions or incorporating them into the takeoff process using a combination of drawing inputs and prompt-based logic. When This Applies
This approach is useful when:

- Items are implied but not visually represented (e.g., wiring between devices)
- Quantities depend on standard practices or company-specific rules
- You need to estimate based on relationships (e.g., distance between fixtures)Methods to Include Non-Drawn Items

- Draw and Measure Manually You can represent missing elements directly on the plans:
- Use drawing tools to sketch lines (e.g., cable runs, conduit paths)
- Measure distances to calculate required material lengths
- Assign quantities based on these measurementsThis method provides the most visual accuracy and works well for linear materials like wiring or piping.

- Define Logic in Prompts or Notes You can include assumptions directly in your takeoff logic:
- Specify rules such as “each outlet requires 3 cables at 10 ft each”
- Include capacity or rating details where applicable
- Apply consistent formulas across similar itemsThis allows you to standardize calculations without needing to draw every component.

- Use a Combined Approach For more complex estimates, combine both methods:
- Draw major runs or key distances on the plans
- Use prompts or predefined rules to calculate associated materials
- Adjust quantities based on real-world conditions or project scopeBest Practices

- Standardize assumptions across your team to maintain consistency
- Document any rules used in prompts for future reference
- Validate calculations against past projects or field data
- Use preview or review tools to confirm quantities before finalizingExample
For low voltage installations:

- Draw the main cable path between devices
- Apply a rule such as “each device includes 3 cables at 10 ft”
- Multiply based on the number of devices identified in the takeoffConclusion
Generating takeoffs for items not shown in drawings requires a structured approach that blends manual input with defined assumptions.

Rather than covering how to set up cost codes from scratch, this session goes deeper — exploring the real-world consequences of not using cost codes and time cards correctly, and showing what contractors stand to gain when they use them with discipline. Taha explains that for most construction companies, labor is where the largest profit margin lives, yet it is also the area most commonly left untracked, estimated loosely, or allocated as a flat overhead expense rather than tied to specific projects and cost categories. The session walks through how estimates in Contractor Foreman define both the project budget and the cost code structure, and how time cards — when properly assigned to projects and cost codes — feed directly into the Job Cost Actual Report, giving project managers a real-time view of estimated versus actual labor spend.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Amber draws on her 25 years of QuickBooks experience and 6 years of construction accounting expertise — including over 2,000 integrations completed since 2020 — to walk users through the best workflow practices for running a successful QuickBooks integration with Contractor Foreman. The session focuses on what happens after integration is complete: how to avoid syncing issues, why cost codes are the critical link between the two systems, and how to structure day-to-day workflow so that project data flows cleanly from Contractor Foreman into QuickBooks — without duplications, double entries, or reporting problems. Amber explains that 95% of all syncing issues are not caused by the integration itself, but rather by two common missteps: cost codes not being applied correctly, and teams not understanding the recommended workflow between systems.

Attendees were also offered a complimentary one-on-one training session for deeper, project-specific support.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha draws on his experience as a licensed mechanical engineer and former remote construction project manager to reframe how contractors think about daily logs — not as a checkbox to get through at the end of the day, but as one of the most powerful tools in Contractor Foreman for protecting your business, managing your team, and staying ahead of problems before they escalate. Taha opens by addressing one of the most common patterns he saw on job sites: daily logs filled out hurriedly, with vague task descriptions and a photo or two, that ultimately offer little value when something goes wrong. The session makes the case that when daily logs are filled out with intention — with the right details, the right people, and the right connections to other modules — they become the central record of everything happening on a project. The session covers three core themes.

April 3rd, 2026
Hosted by:César Macedo, Trainer at Contractor Foreman
Topic: Cost Codes Made Simple — Building a Simple, Functional Structure for Job Costing in Contractor Foreman
title: 2026, April 3rd – Cost Codes Made Simple

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, César Macedo walks through one of the most foundational — and most misunderstood — concepts in construction project management: cost codes. Rather than treating them as a technical setup task, César frames cost codes as the critical link between what you estimated you would spend, what you are actually spending, and how that data flows into your accounting system through the QuickBooks integration. The session opens with a clear, jargon-free definition: cost codes are labels used to track where money is being spent on a project. But César quickly expands that definition to show their real purpose — giving owners, project managers, and office staff the visibility to compare budgeted costs against actuals at every stage of a project, and to make informed business decisions based on that data. Whether the question is whether to buy equipment instead of renting it, or understanding why a particular trade is consistently over budget, none of that is answerable without a working cost code structure. A significant portion of the session focuses on the QuickBooks integration and how it changes the rules for cost code setup.

title: 2026, April 10th – Move From Plans to Quantities

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha takes a deep dive into the Takeoff tool — one of the newest features inside Contractor Foreman, currently available in preview — and walks attendees through how to use it to speed up quantity takeoffs, improve estimating accuracy, and reduce the manual effort of reading through construction drawings. Taha opens by grounding the session in a real-world problem: takeoffs are one of the most time-consuming and consequential tasks in construction project management. Getting quantities wrong at the estimating stage can mean submitting a low bid and losing money on the job, or ordering the wrong amount of material and stalling progress on site. He explains that the Takeoff tool is designed to make this process faster and more accessible — whether it’s being used for initial project estimates, change orders, material ordering, or just a quick sanity check on quantities.

heading: Webinar Description
body: He explains that the Takeoff tool is designed to make this process faster and more accessible — whether it’s being used for initial project estimates, change orders, material ordering, or just a quick sanity check on quantities. The session walks through the full workflow: uploading a set of drawings as a PDF, watching the AI automatically label and categorize pages by type (architectural, structural, electrical, etc.), setting the correct drawing scale, and using the AI panel to perform area, linear, and count measurements directly on the drawing. Taha shows how the AI generates an initial takeoff automatically upon upload, and how users can refine it using manual measurement tools, the AI chat prompt feature, and the Search Element tool — which allows users to zoom into a specific element on a drawing (such as a GFCI outlet or an LED fixture), take a snapshot, and have the AI find and count every matching instance on the page. A key theme throughout the session is the importance of human review alongside AI output.

title: 2026, April 17th – Cash Flow Basics: invoicing and Getting Paid

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha draws on his experience as a remote construction project manager to address one of the most common financial pain points in contracting: losing track of what’s been billed, what’s been paid, and whether the money coming in is keeping pace with the money going out. Taha opens by framing cash flow as one of the biggest risks in the construction business — not because contractors don’t understand billing, but because as project managers wear so many hats, the granular details of invoicing can easily slip. A subcontractor bill that doesn’t match its purchase order, a missed line item on a customer invoice, or a payment that was processed but not properly recorded can quietly compound into serious cash flow problems. The session makes the case that Contractor Foreman’s billing and payment modules, used together as a system, eliminate most of that ambiguity. The core of the session walks through how purchase orders, bills, and the payments module work together to create a clear, trackable record of committed costs and actual spend.

heading: Webinar Description
body: The core of the session focuses on the critical distinction between committed costs and actual costs. Taha explains that a committed cost — created through a purchase order or subcontract — is a promise to spend money: it locks in what you agreed to pay before a single bill arrives. An actual cost is what you have already paid. The gap between the two is what most contractors miss when reviewing project profitability mid-job, and Taha walks through a real example where a plumbing subcontractor’s final draw wasn’t invoiced until months after project close — catching the project manager off guard and eroding a profit margin that had already been celebrated. He shows how creating a subcontract from the start would have surfaced that outstanding committed cost and prevented the surprise. Taha then walks through the Project Financials table and the Job Cost Actual Report in detail — showing how estimated costs, committed costs, and actual costs sit side by side per cost code, and how misaligned cost codes (bills filed under the wrong code) distort the picture and make it harder to trust the numbers.

text:
Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks > When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses?

Summary:
This article explains how using the wrong “expense” transaction type and payment module associated to these transactions, can impact the job cost reporting and workflow issues in Both QUICKBOOKS Online and Contractor Foreman.
title: When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses?

heading: Two expense types associated to a “Project.”
body:
• Bills (Vendor/Supplier (PO’s)/Subcontract “invoices” received with terms); When entered will create Accounts Payable (liabilities) and outstanding balances owed.
• Expenses (written “Check”/credit-card charges/cash payments) are payments made for expenses at the point of sale. Expenses are immediately reported on the profit and loss statement.
If a QuickBooks user is unfamiliar with the “Pay Bills” process in QuickBooks, they will use the “Check” module in QuickBooks to manually record a “check” and assume that it will mark the bill created from Contractor Foreman paid.
text:
Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks > When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses? :: Two expense types associated to a “Project.”

• Bills (Vendor/Supplier (PO’s)/Subcontract “invoices” received with terms); When entered will create Accounts Payable (liabilities) and outstanding balances owed.
• Expenses (written “Check”/credit-card charges/cash payments) are payments made for expenses at the point of sale. Expenses are immediately reported on the profit and loss statement.
If a QuickBooks user is unfamiliar with the “Pay Bills” process in QuickBooks, they will use the “Check” module in QuickBooks to manually record a “check” and assume that it will mark the bill created from Contractor Foreman paid.
title: When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses?

heading: Why the QuickBooks “Check” module should not be used to pay a “Bill” entered in Contractor Foreman?
body: Check(s) created through the “Check” module in QuickBooks will create a new Expense in Contractor Foreman, not a payment applied to an existing Bill. To properly pay a Bill in QuickBooks, you must use the “Pay Bills” module, so the Bill Payment can be linked/synced to the Bill in both QuickBooks and Contractor Foreman.
text:
Contractor Foreman & QuickBooks > When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses? :: Why the QuickBooks “Check” module should not be used to pay a “Bill” entered in Contractor Foreman?

Check(s) created through the “Check” module in QuickBooks will create a new Expense in Contractor Foreman, not a payment applied to an existing Bill. To properly pay a Bill in QuickBooks, you must use the “Pay Bills” module, so the Bill Payment can be linked/synced to the Bill in both QuickBooks and Contractor Foreman.
title: When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses?

heading: Why does the transaction type matter?
body:
No Accounts Payable (A/P) linkage: A “Check” does not mark the “Bill” as paid, leaving the “Bill” outstanding and A/P aging overstated.
Duplicate Bill expense: The “Check” creates a separate Expense transaction for the same Bill amount in Contractor Foreman.
Reconciliation & Bank Feeds: “Pay Bills” creates a Bill Payment that links the Bill and Bank transaction; “Checks” do not match, leaving room for duplication by “added” duplicate expenses.
Credits/discounts/partial payments: “Pay Bills” supports applying “Vendor credits,” early-pay discounts, and partial payments against the “Bill.” Using a “Check” bypass’s those features.
Integration and sync issues: Integrations (like Contractor Foreman) expect “Bills” to be cleared via “Pay Bills.” Using “Checks” breaks mappings and causes duplicates or failed syncs.
text:

No Accounts Payable (A/P) linkage: A “Check” does not mark the “Bill” as paid, leaving the “Bill” outstanding and A/P aging overstated.
Duplicate Bill expense: The “Check” creates a separate Expense transaction for the same Bill amount in Contractor Foreman.

Credits/discounts/partial payments: “Pay Bills” supports applying “Vendor credits,” early-pay discounts, and partial payments against the “Bill.” Using a “Check” bypass’s those features.
Integration and sync issues: Integrations (like Contractor Foreman) expect “Bills” to be cleared via “Pay Bills.” Using “Checks” breaks mappings and causes duplicates or failed syncs.
title: When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses?

heading: What “Pay Bills” does, that a “Check” does not
body:
- Applies a payment directly to one or more open Bills (reduces AP and clears specific invoices).
- Records Bill Payment with references to the applied Bill(s).
- Allows applying vendor credits, discounts, and partial payments against the Bill.
- Preserves correct job-cost and vendor balances and a clean audit trail.
text:

- Applies a payment directly to one or more open Bills (reduces AP and clears specific invoices).

- Allows applying vendor credits, discounts, and partial payments against the Bill.
- Preserves correct job-cost and vendor balances and a clean audit trail.
title: When do I use Bills vs Expenses to record project related expenses?

heading: Recommended practice
body:
Enter invoices from Suppliers/Vendors, Purchase Orders, and Subcontracts as a “Bill” in Contractor Foreman to sync to QuickBooks as an unpaid open Bill.
When it is time to pay the Bill, go to “Pay Bills” (Bill Payment) in QuickBooks Online and select the bills to pay for that vendor, which will sync to Contractor Foreman and mark that “Bill” paid.

May 15th, 2026

Topic: From Drawings to Project — The Full Takeoff-to-Estimate Workflow in Contractor Foreman
title: 2026, May 15th – From Plans to Project

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, César Macedo walks through one of the most time-intensive processes in construction — taking a set of drawings and turning them into a complete, cost-coded estimate — and shows how the Takeoff tool in Contractor Foreman compresses that workflow from hours of manual measurement into a streamlined, end-to-end process: drawings, quantities, estimate, project. César opens by setting honest expectations about the Takeoff tool, which is currently available in preview. It is not magic — uploading drawings does not instantly produce a finished estimate. What it does is reduce friction and speed up the measurement work, giving experienced estimators a faster way to capture quantities and a smarter starting point for building their bids. He frames the AI inside the tool as a new estimator who needs to be directed: the better you understand what you need, the better the results you’ll get from it. The session walks through the full workflow live. César starts by uploading a PDF drawing set into the Takeoff module, where the AI automatically reads, categorizes, and labels each sheet by discipline — architectural, structural, electrical, and so on.

title: 2026, May 22nd – Document It Before It Becomes a Problem

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha takes on one of the most personal and consequential topics of the series: safety and documentation on the job site. Drawing from firsthand experience as a remote construction project manager — including incidents that resulted in serious injury to people he worked alongside — Taha makes the case that documentation is not a bureaucratic obligation, but the single most important habit a construction company can build to protect its workers, defend against liability, and stay in business long-term. The session opens with a clear premise: if it isn’t documented, it didn’t happen. Taha explains that this principle applies across the full spectrum of job site events — weather delays, installation details, subcontractor performance, safety meeting attendance, near misses, and accidents. When something goes wrong and documentation doesn’t exist, it is the contractor who absorbs the consequences, regardless of fault.

heading: Critical Workflow Requirement
body: This process should not be handled differently, or it can create reporting issues, duplicate labor costs, inaccurate job costing, and overstated financials. Labor costs in Contractor Foreman are intentionally treated differently than financial costs in QuickBooks because Contractor Foreman is designed for operational labor allocation and job costing while QuickBooks is the official accounting and payroll system of record.

heading: Why Labor Is Separate Between Systems
body: Timecards and labor costs are intentionally not found in the Financial Tab inside Contractor Foreman projects because they do not stand for true financial transactions in QuickBooks. Contractor Foreman tracks time activity and operational burden allocations only. The actual payroll financials, payroll liabilities, payroll taxes, and net pay transactions stay entirely inside QuickBooks.

heading: Employee Directory Labor Rate Setup
body: Burden rates or wage rates are stored directly within each employee directory profile that uses timecards inside Contractor Foreman. Rates may be based on gross wages only or full burden rates depending on how the company chooses to distribute labor costs across projects. Every employee, regardless of how they are paid, must have a labor rate assigned under Project Settings. Only one labor rate can be selected to register labor costs against projects. If labor rates are missing from employee directory records, Contractor Foreman timecards will not calculate labor costs against projects correctly.

title: Timecards & Payroll Best Practices

heading: Calculating Burden Rates
body: Burden rates are calculated using gross wages or salaries, not net pay. For salaried employees or owners taking draws, convert weekly gross wages or salary into an hourly equivalent by dividing weekly gross compensation by 40 hours. The goal is to calculate a true hourly labor cost allocation for operational job costing. Burden rates should include gross wages plus overhead costs such as payroll taxes, workers compensation, benefits, and company labor overhead.

title: Timecards & Payroll Best Practices

heading: Understanding Timecard Labor Burden/Wage vs third party Payroll systems
body:
Timecards in Contractor Foreman distribute gross wages plus overhead burden rates to projects for operational job costing purposes only. Payroll itself is based on employee net pay after taxes and deductions and stays entirely inside QuickBooks. Labor burden/wage allocations from Contractor Foreman will never post back into QuickBooks financial reports.
It is important to note that QuickBooks Time does not integrate with Contractor Foreman Timecards and Timecards in Contractor Foreman will need to be adapted for correct time tracking.

heading: Syncing Time to QuickBooks
body:
Time entries sync from Contractor Foreman into QuickBooks as time activity records only.
The sync does not create payroll expense journal entries, payroll liabilities, or payroll financial transactions. Imported time activities in QuickBooks are used solely to populate payroll hours for payroll processing.

heading: Project Allocation in QuickBooks Payroll
body: If customers need to assign payroll costs to projects directly inside QuickBooks payroll checks, this should only be done using journal entries. Journal entries never sync back into Contractor Foreman. Payroll entered as bills, checks, expenses, or payroll transactions assigned directly to projects may create duplicate labor reporting in Contractor Foreman and sync issues.

heading: Labor Cost Items & Customer Billing
body: Labor rates charged to customers are supported separately inside the Labor Cost Items database in Contractor Foreman. These labor cost items are customer-facing billing rates used on invoices and proposals only. Internal burden rates are operational cost calculations based on gross wage plus overhead allocations per project and should not be confused with customer billing rates.

heading: Avoiding Double Expense Issues
body:
Net payroll checks, payroll taxes, payroll liabilities, and payroll financials should never sync back into Contractor Foreman because labor burden allocations already exist for operational reporting purposes. Syncing payroll financial transactions back into Contractor Foreman would create duplicate labor expenses and distort project profitability reports.
Labor costs are intentionally treated separately between systems to prevent double counting.

heading: Operational Best Practices
body:
Employee records should match exactly between Contractor Foreman and QuickBooks.
Require supervisor review before payroll sync and perform weekly reviews comparing Contractor Foreman labor totals to payroll hours in QuickBooks.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this special guest session, Justin Rastegar — a sales specialist with deep roots in the construction industry — takes on a topic that rarely gets covered in construction software training: the sales process itself. Before a single project is created in Contractor Foreman, there is a pipeline of leads, conversations, follow-ups, and proposals that determine whether the work ever gets won. This session makes the case that how a contractor manages that pipeline is just as important as how they manage the job once it starts. Justin opens by addressing a common objection head-on: the idea that sales is something other people do, or that a full schedule of word-of-mouth referrals makes a formal process unnecessary. He argues that even contractors whose phones ring constantly need a structured process — because an informal approach leads to missed follow-ups, inconsistent presentations, and a first impression that sets the tone for the entire client relationship. Whether you love sales or find it uncomfortable, the goal of the session is the same: define your process, put it in the system, and let the software do the remembering.

body: Offline Time Cards allow employees to continue tracking time even when they lose internet connectivity. This feature is especially useful for crews working in remote areas, locations with poor cellular coverage, or job sites where a stable internet connection is not always available. When enabled, users can create and manage time card entries while offline, and the data will automatically sync back to Contractor Foreman once a connection is restored. To enable Offline Time Cards, navigate to Settings and open the Time Card Settings section. Within the available time card configuration options, locate the Automatic Breaks area. Scroll through the settings until you find the Offline Time Cards Preview option. Enable the Offline Time Cards Preview setting and save your changes. Once activated, eligible users will be able to access the offline time card functionality through the mobile application. No additional configuration is required for individual employees unless your company has specific permission or access controls in place. After enabling the setting, it is recommended to test the functionality using a mobile device.

body: No additional configuration is required for individual employees unless your company has specific permission or access controls in place. After enabling the setting, it is recommended to test the functionality using a mobile device. Open the Contractor Foreman mobile app, create a time card while connected to the internet, and then place the device into airplane mode or disconnect it from the network. Confirm that time can still be entered and saved. Once internet connectivity is restored, verify that the offline entries successfully synchronize back to the system. Keep in mind that offline functionality is designed to temporarily store time card data until a connection becomes available. Users should periodically reconnect to the internet to ensure all recorded time is uploaded and reflected accurately in reporting, payroll, and project tracking. If users do not see the offline time card option after enabling the setting, ensure they are running the latest version of the Contractor Foreman mobile application and have logged out and back into the app after the feature was activated.

body: Service Tickets make it easy to capture a client’s signature directly from the field, helping document completed work, confirm customer approval, and maintain accurate records for future reference. Whether you are using a phone or tablet, signatures can be collected immediately after work is completed and stored directly with the Service Ticket. When a technician arrives on-site and completes the requested work, they can open the Service Ticket from the Contractor Foreman mobile app. Before closing out the visit, review the completed work with the client and confirm that all requested services have been performed to their satisfaction. Within the Service Ticket, scroll to the signature section and select the option to capture a signature. Hand the mobile device to the client and have them sign directly on the screen using their finger or a stylus. Once the signature has been entered, save the Service Ticket to attach the signed approval to the record. The signature becomes part of the Service Ticket and can be referenced later when reviewing project activity, resolving disputes, verifying completed work, or generating documentation for billing purposes.

body: Accurate quantity takeoffs are one of the foundations of successful construction estimating. Every square foot included in an estimate affects material costs, labor requirements, scheduling, and ultimately project profitability. When measuring walls, floors, roofs, or other surfaces in Kamai, there are many situations where certain sections should not be counted toward the final area. Learning how to subtract these sections correctly ensures estimates remain precise and prevents unnecessary material purchases. Subtracting areas is particularly useful when dealing with windows, doors, stair openings, skylights, mechanical penetrations, shafts, or any other space that should be excluded from calculations. Rather than manually adjusting totals outside the software, Kamai allows estimators to remove these sections directly within the measurement process, creating a cleaner and more reliable workflow. The process begins by creating the primary area measurement just as you normally would. Trace the complete outline of the wall, floor, ceiling, or other surface until the total area is established. This measurement represents the full surface before any deductions are applied.

body: The process begins by creating the primary area measurement just as you normally would. Trace the complete outline of the wall, floor, ceiling, or other surface until the total area is established. This measurement represents the full surface before any deductions are applied. Once the primary area exists, identify the portion that should be excluded. This might be a large window opening in a wall, an atrium in a floor plan, or another feature that does not require materials or labor associated with the surrounding surface. Instead of creating separate calculations and performing manual math, use Kamai’s subtraction functionality to define the excluded section. Carefully outline the area that needs to be removed. Precision matters because the deducted measurement directly impacts the final quantity used for estimating. After completing the subtraction, Kamai automatically recalculates the remaining area by deducting the selected portion from the original measurement. The estimator receives an updated total without needing to export data or use external calculations. This workflow offers significant advantages beyond convenience.

heading: How This Appears in QuickBooks Financial Reports
body:
On the Profit and Loss report, Tax on Purchases will appear as a separate Cost of Goods Sold expense. This provides visibility into the amount of sales tax paid on job-related purchases while keeping it separate from labor, materials, and other project costs.
By recording sales tax separately, the total costs in QuickBooks will match the costs recorded in Contractor Foreman, and the combined pre-tax amounts plus the Tax on Purchases amount will equal the total supplier bill payment.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha tackles one of the most financially consequential habits in the construction industry: doing work for free. Whether it’s a $500 extra that seems too small to invoice, an unforeseen condition resolved quietly to keep the project moving, or a scope assumption made without written confirmation, the pattern is the same — and the costs compound quickly. This session walks through the full change management workflow in Contractor Foreman, from the moment a question arises in the field to an approved change order reflected in the project schedule and billing cycle. Taha opens with a candid account of the mistakes he made as a project manager: resolving issues without telling the client, holding onto change orders until the end of the project, and making field assumptions instead of sending RFIs — all in an effort to keep things moving and avoid friction. He explains why each of these habits ultimately backfires, and why the best protection a contractor has against scope disputes, schedule delays, and unprofitable jobs is a paper trail that starts from the first question, not the last invoice.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha Q. walks through one of the most nuanced contract structures in the construction industry — the Cost Plus contract — and shows exactly how to set it up, manage billing, and track financial performance inside Contractor Foreman. Unlike previous sessions focused on fixed-cost projects, this session addresses a workflow where the rules change fundamentally: risk shifts from the contractor to the client, profit is fixed upfront, and financial transparency becomes the foundation of the entire client relationship. Taha opens by framing the key difference between fixed-cost and cost plus contracting. In a fixed-cost project, the contractor absorbs the risk of cost overruns — if lumber prices spike or unforeseen conditions add expense, that comes out of the contractor’s margin. In a cost plus arrangement, those costs pass through directly to the client, and the contractor’s profit is a predetermined service fee.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In a fixed-cost project, the contractor absorbs the risk of cost overruns — if lumber prices spike or unforeseen conditions add expense, that comes out of the contractor’s margin. In a cost plus arrangement, those costs pass through directly to the client, and the contractor’s profit is a predetermined service fee. Taha makes the case that for projects with significant ambiguity, incomplete drawings, or high exposure to unforeseen conditions, cost plus is often the smarter structure — and that COVID-era lumber price swings are a vivid example of why that risk transfer matters. The session walks through the complete cost plus workflow step by step. It begins with the good faith estimate — not a fixed bid, but a transparent projection of expected costs that the client understands may come in higher or lower — and covers a critical setup detail that trips up many teams: line item markups must be turned off entirely in a cost plus estimate, since the contractor’s only profit is the service fee line item. Taha demonstrates how to structure the estimate correctly and flags exactly where the mistake gets made when importing from the cost item database.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, Taha walks through the Takeoff Tool in Contractor Foreman — currently available in preview — from start to finish. Unlike a surface-level feature overview, this session follows a complete workflow: uploading a set of construction drawings, managing and verifying the AI’s initial takeoff, using the AI chat to extract specific quantities and generate supporting documents, exporting data into the estimate, and ultimately using that same information to produce a scope of work and a project schedule. Taha opens with a framing that sets the tone for the entire session: the Takeoff Tool is not something you hand the wheel to and walk away from. He uses the analogy of a car with an auto-parking feature — the technology does most of the work, but your hands are still on the wheel, your eyes are still on the mirrors, and you are still responsible for the outcome. That mindset — trust the tool, verify everything — runs through every step of the demonstration. The session begins with two foundational points before touching the software.

heading: Webinar Description
body: In this advanced training session, César Macedo returns to one of the most foundational topics in construction project management — cost codes — with a format that is deliberately different from a standard feature walkthrough. Rather than presenting a pre-built structure and telling attendees to follow it, the session invites participants to work through the logic together: what cost codes actually are, why most contractors either avoid them entirely or overcomplicate them, and how to build a structure that is simple enough for the whole team to use consistently. César opens with a definition that cuts through the mysticism that often surrounds cost codes: they are labels. More specifically, they are buckets — one for your estimated cost, one for your actual cost — and the purpose of assigning a cost code to every transaction is to see, in real time, how much of your budget has been spent and how much remains. He walks through the analogy live: a $1,000 framing budget, a $300 bill from Home Depot assigned to the framing bucket, and the immediate visibility that gives a project manager — $700 still available, with the project still running.

heading: Webinar Description
body: He walks through the analogy live: a $1,000 framing budget, a $300 bill from Home Depot assigned to the framing bucket, and the immediate visibility that gives a project manager — $700 still available, with the project still running. That visibility is the entire point, and it only works if the team is actually labeling their transactions consistently. A significant portion of the session addresses the distinction between item types and cost codes — one of the most common points of confusion for Contractor Foreman users, particularly those who have the QuickBooks integration. César explains that Contractor Foreman organizes costs by item type (labor, material, equipment, subcontractor, other), while QuickBooks organizes by chart of accounts. These two systems do not map to each other automatically — and that gap is the source of most integration reporting problems. He works through a live example: a drywall cost code used for both a subcontractor bill and a material purchase will send both transactions to the same QuickBooks expense account, which means subcontractor costs and material costs become indistinguishable in QuickBooks reporting.

heading: Webinar Description
body: He works through a live example: a drywall cost code used for both a subcontractor bill and a material purchase will send both transactions to the same QuickBooks expense account, which means subcontractor costs and material costs become indistinguishable in QuickBooks reporting. The fix is to create separate child cost codes by item type — drywall subcontractor, drywall materials — so each maps to the correct expense account. For contractors without QuickBooks, one cost code per trade is perfectly sufficient. The session also covers how to build a simple cost code structure from scratch: starting with the trades or phases that are relevant to your type of work, resisting the urge to create codes for every conceivable scenario, and adding complexity only when the data tells you it’s needed. César revisits the core principle from the April 3rd session: a cost code list that is too long or too granular stops being used by field teams, which defeats the entire purpose. A simple list that everyone follows produces far more useful data than a detailed list that nobody applies consistently.

body: César revisits the core principle from the April 3rd session: a cost code list that is too long or too granular stops being used by field teams, which defeats the entire purpose. A simple list that everyone follows produces far more useful data than a detailed list that nobody applies consistently.
